name: North Buhaya
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: North Buhaya emerged as a cluster of sovereign Haya kingdoms along the western littoral of Lake Victoria in present-day north-western Tanzania. Dominated primarily by the dynamic realm of Kiziba, the polity prospered through intensive banana cultivation, sophisticated iron smelting and interlacustrine trade networks connecting neighbouring monarchies. Dynastic rulers known as bakama exercised sacred kingship over clan-based communities until regional consolidation reshaped the lacustrine interior at the turn of the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdoms; Capital: Kiziba; Common languages: Haya; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Mukama; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Empire of Kitara; Historical region: African Great Lakes

name: Principality of Abkhazia
description: The Principality of Abkhazia existed as an autonomous Caucasian principality along the eastern Black Sea coast under the overarching suzerainty of the Ottoman Empire. Governed by the hereditary princes of the Sharvashidze dynasty, the state navigated imperial pressures from Istanbul while preserving its local feudal institutions and tribal allegiances. Although coastal fortresses such as Sukhumi were garrisoned by Ottoman troops, internal administration and customary mountain law remained firmly in the hands of the indigenous nobility. \n\n Status: Ottoman protectorate; Capital: Sukhumi; Official languages: Georgian; Common languages: Abkhaz and Georgian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy and Sunni Islam; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Sharvashidze; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early modern period

name: Republic of the Seven United Netherlands
description: The Republic of the Seven United Netherlands was a sovereign federal commonwealth formed during the Dutch Revolt against Spanish Habsburg rule. Following the 1581 Act of Abjuration, seven northern provinces joined into an enduring maritime republic governed through provincial estates and the national States General at The Hague. Driven by maritime commerce, banking innovations and global naval expeditions, the state became a foremost European mercantile power during the seventeenth-century Dutch Golden Age before succumbing to the French-backed Batavian Revolution in 1795. \n\n Status: Federal republic; Capital: The Hague; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch, Dutch Low Saxon and West Frisian; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Confederal parliamentary republic; Legislature: States General; Established: 26 July 1581; Disestablished: 19 January 1795; Currency: Guilder

name: Ava
description: Ava functioned as an autonomous rebel stronghold in Upper Burma during a brief insurrection against the expanding First Toungoo Empire. Centred upon the fortified riverside citadel of Inwa, dissident commanders and local nobility established temporary control over the surrounding agricultural plains along the Irrawaddy River. The breakaway administration defied royal authority until imperial forces under King Nanda Bayin mounted decisive military operations that recaptured the city and reimposed centralised Burmese rule. \n\n Status: Rebel polity; Capital: Inwa; Common languages: Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Military junta; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1582; Disestablished: 1585; Preceded by: Toungoo Dynasty; Succeeded by: Toungoo Dynasty

name: Marquisate of Groppoli
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Groppoli was an imperial fief of the Holy Roman Empire nestled in the mountainous Lunigiana region of northern Tuscany. Ruled primarily by branches of the Malaspina family and subsequently acquired by Genoese patricians, the diminutive marquisate occupied a critical mountain transit pass between Liguria, Lombardy and the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. Despite persistent encroachment and competing claims by the Medici of Florence, Groppoli preserved its sovereign imperial immediacy until its formal absorption into Tuscany in the late eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Imperial fief of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Groppoli; Common languages: Italian and Tuscan dialect; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: Malaspina; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Lunigiana

name: Ajatappareng Confederation
description: The Ajatappareng Confederation was a maritime league comprising five allied Bugis principalities situated across the western peninsula of South Sulawesi. Formed primarily by Sidenreng, Suppa, Sawitto, Rappang and Alitta, the alliance grew into a thriving commercial hub by offering safe harbour to international merchants displaced after the fall of Malacca. The confederation maintained regional autonomy and naval strength until it was decisively defeated and subjugated by the ascendant Sultanate of Gowa during the early seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Confederal alliance; Capital: Suppa; Common languages: Buginese; Religion: Traditional Bugis religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Oligarchic confederation; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1583; Disestablished: 1610; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Gowa

name: English North America
description: English North America encompassed the initial, unchartered territorial claims and reconnaissance colonies claimed by the Crown of England along the eastern seaboard of North America during the Elizabethan era. Spearheaded by exploratory expeditions sponsored by Sir Walter Raleigh under royal letters patent, English efforts focused on establishing fortified coastal footholds such as the Roanoke settlements. These pioneer ventures encountered severe supply disruptions and indigenous hostilities, remaining precarious outposts until Crown administration was reorganised following the accession of King James I. \n\n Status: Crown territorial claim; Administrative seat: London; Capital: Roanoke; Common languages: English; Religion: Church of England; Government: Colonial proprietorship; Head of state: Elizabeth I; Historical era: Elizabethan era; Disestablished: 24 March 1603; Succeeded by: British North America

name: Jhabua State
description: Jhabua State was an autonomous princely realm in central India, set across the hilly and forested tracts of the Malwa region. Founded in 1584 by a Rathore Rajput chieftain, the state maintained authority over a population composed largely of indigenous Bhil communities who inhabited its rugged terrain. The ruling dynasty retained local suzerainty through tactical tributary accommodations with neighbouring imperial powers, collecting revenues and defending frontier passes until Maratha incursions reshaped central Indian politics. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Jhabua; Common languages: Malvi, Hindi and Bhili; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rathore Rajput; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1584

name: Cautionary Towns
description: The Cautionary Towns were three heavily fortified Dutch coastal strongholds, Brielle, Vlissingen and Fort Rammekens, held under English military governance during the Eighty Years' War. Pledged to Queen Elizabeth I under the terms of the 1585 Treaty of Nonsuch, the bases served as surety for English financial loans and armed intervention against Spanish forces in the Low Countries. English garrison commanders maintained defensive garrisons and collected local customs until the accession of King James I marked a transition in imperial custody. \n\n Status: English military possession; Administrative seat: Mobile garrison; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: English and Dutch; Religion: Calvinism and Church of England; Government: Military governorship; Historical era: Anglo-Spanish War; Established: 10 August 1585; Disestablished: 24 March 1603

name: Republic of the Seven United Netherlands
description: During the mid-1580s, the Republic of the Seven United Netherlands briefly operated as an English protectorate following the conclusion of the Treaty of Nonsuch. In exchange for direct military and financial assistance against Spanish forces, the Dutch provinces accepted the Earl of Leicester as governor-general and granted English representatives influential voting seats on their Council of State. However, political friction between Leicester and the powerful mercantile estates of Holland led to his recall in 1587 and prompted the Dutch provinces to formalise an independent confederal republic in 1588. \n\n Status: English protectorate; Capital: The Hague; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch and English; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Protectorate council; Head of state: Elizabeth I; Representative title: Governor-General; Established: 20 August 1585; Disestablished: 1588

name: Roanoke Colony
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Roanoke Colony was an early English colonial outpost established on Roanoke Island off the coast of modern-day North Carolina under the sponsorship of Sir Walter Raleigh. Intended as a permanent Protestant agricultural settlement and naval base against Spanish shipping, the venture faced extreme food shortages, severed resupply lines and escalating hostilities with local Secotan communities. When relief vessels finally returned in 1590 after prolonged wartime delays in Europe, the entire settlement was found abandoned without clear trace of the colonists. \n\n Status: English colony; Administrative seat: Fort Raleigh; Capital: Roanoke Island; Common languages: English and Carolina Algonquian; Religion: Church of England; Government: Proprietary governorship; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Elizabethan era; Established: 1586; Disestablished: 1591

name: Cooch Behar State
description: Cooch Behar State was a sovereign kingdom in north-eastern India founded following the dynastic division of the ancient Kamata realm in the late sixteenth century. Ruled by the Koch dynasty from their historic seat at Gosanimari, the state controlled fertile plains bordering the Himalayan foothills south of Bhutan. The kingdom maintained fierce independence against surrounding regional powers and resisted early encroachment by the Mughal Empire before entering into formal vassalage at the start of the seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gosanimari; Common languages: Kamatapuri and Bengali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Koch; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1587; Preceded by: Kamata Kingdom

name: Koch Hajo
description: Koch Hajo was an independent monarchical state established on the northern bank of the Brahmaputra River after the partition of the Kamata kingdom between rival Koch princes. Governed by Maharaja Raghudev and his heirs from Hajo, the realm spanned the fertile riparian territories between the Sankosh and Bhareli rivers. Despite frequent wars with its western sibling state of Koch Bihar and territorial clashes with the Ahom Kingdom, Koch Hajo maintained sovereign authority until Mughal expansion engulfed the region in 1617. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hajo; Common languages: Assamese and Kamatapuri; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Koch; Ruler title: Maharaja; Established: 1587; Disestablished: 1617; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire

name: Sultanate of Mataram
description: The Sultanate of Mataram was a dominant early modern Islamic empire based in the fertile central plains of Java. Founded under the leadership of Senopati and reaching its military zenith during the reign of Sultan Agung, the kingdom unified most of central and eastern Java while exercising suzerainty over Madura and ports across the Java Sea. Although Mataram developed sophisticated agrarian administration and court literature, internal succession struggles and growing intervention by the Dutch East India Company eventually fractured the empire in 1755. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Kota Gede; Common languages: Javanese and Sundanese; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Susuhunan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1587; Disestablished: 13 February 1755; Succeeded by: Surakarta Sunanate and Yogyakarta Sultanate

name: Faza
label: polities of the swahili coast
description: Faza was a colonial Swahili trading enclave situated on the northern shore of Pate Island within the Lamu Archipelago off the East African coast. Following a brutal punitive expedition launched from Portuguese Goa in 1587, Portuguese authorities subjugated the settlement and established a colonial garrison and coastal chapel to oversee maritime trade. The settlement served as a strategic Portuguese listening post and naval anchorage against rival maritime factions until rising Omani influence and local insurgencies dismantled Portuguese authority. \n\n Status: Portuguese colonial possession; Capital: Faza; Common languages: Swahili and Portuguese; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Sunni Islam; Government: Colonial military governorship; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1588; Disestablished: 1751; Historical region: Swahili Coast

name: Babouantou
description: Babouantou was a sovereign Bamileke chieftaincy situated in the rugged Western Highlands of modern-day Cameroon. Governed by a traditional monarch known as a fo, who ruled in concert with secret societies and a council of titled notables, the polity maintained an agro-pastoral economy centred on terraced farming and regional craft markets. Babouantou preserved its political autonomy and customary chieftaincy institutions against neighbouring rival fondoms throughout the precolonial era until German colonial subjugation commenced at the beginning of the twentieth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign chieftaincy; Capital: Bafoussam; Common languages: Bamileke languages and Medumba; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Ruler title: Fo; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1591; Disestablished: 1901

name: Kingdom of Imamo
description: The Kingdom of Imamo was an independent Merina realm established across the western highlands of central Madagascar. Based at the fortified hilltop capital of Ambohitrambo, the kingdom controlled expansive valleys devoted to irrigated rice production and highland cattle husbandry. Guided by ancestral traditions and headed by hereditary royal dynasties, Imamo maintained regional sovereignty and distinct cultural traditions until its territory was unified with the central Imerina kingdom under King Andrianampoinimerina around the start of the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ambohitrambo; Common languages: Malagasy; Religion: Traditional Malagasy religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1591; Disestablished: 1801; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Imerina

name: Pashalik of Timbuktu
description: The Pashalik of Timbuktu was an early modern West African tributary governorship established following the Saadian conquest of the Songhai Empire at the Battle of Tondibi. Administered from Timbuktu by an appointed Moroccan pasha commanding the expeditionary Arma soldiers, the state enforced Saadian overlordship across key riverine cities along the Niger River. The administration oversaw trans-Saharan gold and salt commerce while sending tribute to Marrakech until political turmoil in Morocco allowed the local military elite to govern autonomously after 1604. \n\n Status: Moroccan tributary pashalik; Capital: Timbuktu; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Songhai, Hassaniya Arabic and Soninke; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military governorship; Ruler title: Pasha; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 13 March 1591; Disestablished: 1604; Preceded by: Songhai Empire

name: Jaffna Kingdom
description: The Jaffna Kingdom was a historic Tamil monarchy on the northern peninsula of Sri Lanka that fell under Portuguese imperial protection following a naval expedition in late 1591. Portuguese authorities installed King Ethirimanna Cinkam as a client ruler, compelling the crown to pay annual tribute and tolerate Roman Catholic missionary activity while retaining native civil administration. Although Jaffnan monarchs covertly aided the interior Kandyan resistance against European expansion, overt rebellion by pretenders eventually provoked direct military annexation and the complete dissolution of the kingdom. \n\n Status: Portuguese protectorate; Capital: Jaffna; Official languages: Tamil; Common languages: Tamil and Portuguese; Religion: Shaivism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Client monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Aryacakravarti; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 December 1591; Succeeded by: Portuguese Ceylon

name: Dendi Kingdom
description: The Dendi Kingdom was a sovereign West African state established in the southern reaches of modern-day Niger following the collapse of the Songhai Empire at Tondibi. Founded by surviving Songhai royal lineages who retreated along the Niger River valley to Lulami, the kingdom preserved Songhai imperial court ceremonies, administrative titles and Islamic scholarship. The state resisted Moroccan and Fulani encroachments across three centuries of continuous existence before it was ultimately overwhelmed and incorporated into French West Africa in 1902. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Lulami; Common languages: Dendi and Songhai; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Askia; Ruler title: Askia; Historical era: Post-Songhai period; Established: 1592; Disestablished: 1902; Preceded by: Songhai Empire; Succeeded by: French West Africa

name: Empire of Japan (Military Occupation)
description: The Empire of Japan Military Occupation designated external operational zones and conquered territories garrisoned by Japanese armed forces outside standard domestic administrative boundaries. During the late sixteenth century, Toyotomi Hideyoshi directed extensive field armies across southern and central Korea, maintaining fortified coastal camps known as wajo without establishing a permanent civil capital. These occupation zones served strictly as frontline logistical bases and military commands, enduring through severe combat before retreating forces evacuated following Hideyoshi's death in 1598. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Mobile expeditionary command; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Japanese and Korean; Religion: Shinto and Buddhism; Government: Military administration; Head of state: Toyotomi Hideyoshi; Historical era: Imjin War; Established: 24 May 1592; Disestablished: 24 December 1598

name: Kingdom of Sweden
description: The Kingdom of Sweden was ruled in personal union with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth between 1592 and 1599 following the coronation of Sigismund III Vasa as Swedish monarch. Bound by dynastic ties but deeply divided over religion and royal prerogatives, the Swedish realm retained its indigenous legal institutions, Lutheran state church and the Riksdag in Stockholm. Growing domestic friction culminated in the War against Sigismund, leading to the monarch's deposition by his Lutheran uncle, Duke Charles, and the dissolution of the trans-Baltic union. \n\n Status: Personal union; Capital: Stockholm; Official languages: Swedish; Common languages: Swedish, Polish and Latin; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Vasa; Ruler title: King; Head of state: Sigismund III Vasa; Legislature: Riksdag; Established: 17 November 1592; Disestablished: 1 June 1600

name: Kingdom of Sitawaka
description: The Kingdom of Sitawaka was a prominent Sinhalese polity in south-central Sri Lanka that briefly fell under Portuguese protectorate status in its terminal phase. Following the death of the formidable warrior-king Rajasinha I in 1593, succession crises and internal rebellion shattered the kingdom's military cohesion, allowing Portuguese forces to advance and install a client administration at Avissawella. This puppet protectorate survived for barely a year before Portuguese troops formally annexed Sitawaka's remaining territories, incorporating them directly into Portuguese Ceylon. \n\n Status: Portuguese protectorate; Capital: Avissawella; Common languages: Sinhala; Religion: Theravada Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Client monarchy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1594; Disestablished: 1595; Preceded by: Kingdom of Sitawaka; Succeeded by: Portuguese Ceylon and Kingdom of Kandy

name: Kingdom of Cambodia
description: The Kingdom of Cambodia operated as a tributary vassal under the Kingdom of Siam following the capture and sacking of the royal stronghold at Lovek in early 1594. Governed from subsequent royal capitals at Srei Santhor and Oudong, Cambodian monarchs received formal regalia and military confirmation from the Siamese court at Ayutthaya and later Bangkok. Although retaining indigenous Khmer court ceremonies, Theravada Buddhist religious hierarchies and internal provincial governance, the kingdom repeatedly served as a contested buffer state between competing Siamese and Vietnamese imperial ambitions. \n\n Status: Siamese vassal kingdom; Capital: Oudong; Official languages: Khmer; Common languages: Khmer; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Vassal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Post-Angkor period; Established: 3 January 1594; Disestablished: 1 November 1841; Preceded by: Khmer Empire

name: Kingdom of Siam (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Siam Military Occupation encompassed frontline operational theatres and occupied territories held under temporary martial control by Siamese royal forces across mainland Southeast Asia. During the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, Ayutthaya sent substantial military expeditions into the Mon borderlands, Tenasserim and lower Burma to secure strategic trade corridors and suppress rival garrisons. These military occupations operated without fixed civilian administrative seats, functioning as expeditionary field camps and fortified border garrisons until political treaties or troop withdrawals concluded each campaign. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Mobile military command; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Thai, Mon and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Military command; Historical era: Burmese-Siamese Wars; Established: 1595; Disestablished: 1 February 1596

name: Basra
description: Basra functioned as a Portuguese commercial and colonial enclave situated along the Shatt al-Arab waterway at the head of the Persian Gulf in southern Iraq. In exchange for naval protection against Ottoman provincial authorities and regional nomads, local hereditary rulers permitted the Portuguese Crown to operate a fortified trading lodge, collect customs duties and station naval squadrons in the port. The enclave channelled valuable maritime trade between Mesopotamia, the Arabian Peninsula and Portuguese Goa until shifting regional dynamics and Ottoman consolidation ended Portuguese influence. \n\n Status: Portuguese colonial enclave; Capital: Basra; Common languages: Arabic and Portuguese; Religion: Sunni Islam, Shia Islam and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial commercial protectorate; Representative title: Factor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1596; Disestablished: 1669

name: Dhrol State
description: Dhrol State was an autonomous Rajput princely realm located within the historical Halar region of the Kathiawar peninsula in western India. Founded in 1595 by Jam Hardholji, a younger son of the ruler of Nawanagar, the state established its administrative capital at Dhrol and maintained an independent army to safeguard its agrarian domains. The Jadeja Rajput rulers exercised sovereign local governance and defended their borders against regional rivals for more than two centuries before entering into subsidiary treaty relationships with the British East India Company. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Dhrol; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jadeja Rajput; Ruler title: Thakur Sahib; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1596; Disestablished: 1808; Preceded by: Nawanagar State

name: Imamate of Aussa
description: The Imamate of Aussa was an independent Sunni Muslim state established in the arid Awash River basin of modern-day north-eastern Ethiopia and Djibouti. Formed when remnants of the Adal Sultanate relocated their governmental seat inland to Asaita to escape relentless Oromo migrations, the imamate brought together Harari, Harla and Afar populations under the spiritual and political leadership of hereditary imams. The state governed vital caravan routes between the Red Sea coast and the Ethiopian highlands until dynastic fragmentation enabled the Mudaito Sultanate to seize power. \n\n Status: Sovereign imamate; Capital: Asaita; Common languages: Harari, Afar, Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Imam; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1596; Disestablished: 1735; Preceded by: Adal Sultanate; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Aussa

name: Duchy of Saxe-Coburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Saxe-Coburg was an autonomous Ernestine principality of the Holy Roman Empire centred in the Franconian borderlands of present-day northern Bavaria. Created through dynastic partitions among the Wettin family, the duchy was ruled by Duke John Casimir, who oversaw extensive administrative reforms, judicial modernisation and Renaissance architectural projects from the fortress palace of Ehrenburg in Coburg. The duchy exercised imperial immediacy and sent delegates to the Imperial Diet until the line expired in 1634, prompting successive territorial divisions among neighbouring Saxon houses. \n\n Status: Principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Coburg; Official languages: German; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Wettin (Ernestine line); Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1597

name: Duchy of Saxe-Eisenach
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine
description: The Duchy of Saxe-Eisenach was an autonomous Thuringian principality of the Holy Roman Empire governed by the Ernestine branch of the House of Wettin. With its ducal residence established at Eisenach beneath the historic Wartburg castle, the small state maintained its own provincial chancery, fiscal administration and Lutheran ecclesiastical structures. Despite intermittent dissolutions and reunions triggered by shifting dynastic inheritances during the seventeenth century, Saxe-Eisenach remained an important cultural and musical centre before permanently merging into Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach in 1741. \n\n Status: Principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Eisenach; Official languages: German; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Wettin (Ernestine line); Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1597

name: Qasimid State
description: The Qasimid State was an independent Zaidi imamate established in northern Yemen under the leadership of Imam al-Mansur al-Qasim. Mobilising highland tribes against Ottoman imperial occupation, the Qasimid imams waged sustained military campaigns that culminated in the total expulsion of Ottoman forces from Sanaa and the southern coast by the 1630s. At its zenith, the realm controlled trade ports along the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, but subsequent tribal rebellions and dynastic fragmentation eventually allowed Ottoman forces to reoccupy Sanaa in 1849. \n\n Status: Sovereign imamate; Capital: San'a; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Zaidi Islam; Government: Theocratic imamate; Ruling dynasty: Qasimid; Ruler title: Imam; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1598; Disestablished: 1 August 1849; Preceded by: Yemen Eyalet

name: Principality of Masserano
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Masserano was an autonomous imperial enclave located in the hilly Piedmontese countryside near Biella, united with the Marquisate of Crevacuore. Elevated to a sovereign principality by Pope Clement VIII in 1598, the territory was ruled by the noble Ferrero-Fieschi family, who exercised supreme civil and criminal jurisdiction independent of the neighbouring House of Savoy. The princes operated their own mint and fortified residences until eighteenth-century financial distress and geopolitical pressures culminated in the sale and incorporation of the fief into the Kingdom of Sardinia. \n\n Status: Imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Masserano; Common languages: Piedmontese and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruling dynasty: Ferrero-Fieschi; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 13 August 1598; Disestablished: 1742

name: Dutch Gold Coast
description: The Dutch Gold Coast comprised a network of fortified trading factories and colonial settlements established along the Gulf of Guinea in present-day Ghana. Initiated by merchants of the Dutch West India Company at Fort Nassau and greatly expanded following the capture of Saint George of the Mine at Elmina from Portugal in 1637, the colony anchored Dutch Atlantic commerce in gold and enslaved labourers. Dutch officials maintained intricate diplomatic alliances with the inland Ashanti Empire until declining revenues and the abolition of the slave trade prompted the cession of the territory to Great Britain in 1872. \n\n Status: Dutch chartered company colony; Capital: Elmina; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch, Akan and Fante; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church and traditional African religions; Government: Colonial governorship; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1599; Disestablished: 6 April 1872; Succeeded by: Gold Coast (British colony)

name: County of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt was an autonomous Thuringian state of the Holy Roman Empire created following the partition of the ancestral Schwarzburg patrimony in 1599. Governed from the imposing residence of Heidecksburg in Rudolstadt, the county exercised imperial immediacy and maintained its own territorial administration, court apparatus and Lutheran state church. The counts successfully preserved their realm through the devastation of the Thirty Years' War, continuing to govern their compact domains until the county was formally elevated to an imperial principality in 1711. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Rudolstadt; Official languages: German; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Feudal county; Ruling dynasty: House of Schwarzburg; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1600; Disestablished: 15 April 1711; Preceded by: County of Schwarzburg

name: County of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen was a sovereign imperial county in northern Thuringia that emerged from the dynastic division of the House of Schwarzburg at the close of the sixteenth century. Headquartered at the residential palace of Sondershausen, the county enjoyed imperial immediacy with seat and voice in the Imperial Diet. Despite enduring severe economic disruption and military foraging during the Thirty Years' War, the ruling counts maintained internal administrative stability and patronage of Lutheran religious culture until their elevation to princely dignity in 1697. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Sondershausen; Official languages: German; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Feudal county; Ruling dynasty: House of Schwarzburg; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1600; Disestablished: 13 September 1697; Preceded by: County of Schwarzburg

name: Khandpara State
description: Khandpara State was an independent princely realm situated in modern-day Nayagarh district of Odisha in eastern India. Established around 1599 by a younger brother of the ruler of neighbouring Nayagarh, the state bordered the northern reaches of the Mahanadi River and encompassed fertile agrarian plains and dense surrounding woodlands. The ruling family governed from the capital at Khandapada, promoting local temple architecture and regional trade through the pilgrimage market town of Kantilo before entering into tributary relations with the British East India Company. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Khandapada; Common languages: Odia; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bhanja; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1600; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Khandpara Feudatory State

name: Principality of Transylvania
description: The Principality of Transylvania entered a brief personal union with the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia under the rule of Prince Michael the Brave between 1600 and 1601. Following his victory at the Battle of Șelimbăr in late 1599, Michael established his princely court at Alba Iulia, uniting the administration of Transylvania with Wallachia to create an ephemeral pan-Romanian state. However, aristocratic Hungarian opposition, imperial Habsburg hostility and political intrigue orchestrated by General Giorgio Basta led to Michael's assassination in 1601 and the collapse of the union. \n\n Status: Personal union; Capital: Alba Iulia; Official languages: Latin and Hungarian; Common languages: Hungarian, Romanian and German; Religion: Calvinism, Lutheranism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Principality; Head of state: Michael the Brave; Ruler title: Voivode; Established: 1600; Disestablished: 1602

name: Sarawak Sultanate
description: The Sarawak Sultanate was a traditional Malay kingdom centred in the Kuching and Santubong coastal regions of north-western Borneo. Founded in 1599 by Sultan Tengah, a prince of the royal house of Brunei who established an independent royal court, the kingdom exercised suzerainty over local coastal trade and forged strategic dynastic alliances with neighbouring realms like Sambas and Sukadana. Following the assassination of Sultan Tengah in 1641 without an established royal heir, the independent sultanate was dissolved and its territories were reintegrated directly under Bruneian governors. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Kuching; Common languages: Classical Malay and Dayak languages; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Brunei; Ruler title: Sultan; Established: 1600; Disestablished: 1642; Preceded by: Bruneian Empire; Succeeded by: Bruneian Empire

name: Thanlyin
description: Thanlyin was a Portuguese commercial and military colony situated across the Bago River from modern-day Yangon in lower Burma. Granted governorship over the port following the sacking of Pegu, the Portuguese mercenary commander Filipe de Brito e Nicote transformed the city into an autonomous colonial stronghold supported by Portuguese naval gunboats and local Mon allies. Operating under nominal Portuguese viceregal sanction from Goa, de Brito controlled maritime customs and fortified the city until imperial Burmese forces under King Anaukpetlun besieged and captured Thanlyin in 1613. \n\n Status: Portuguese colonial fief; Capital: Thanlyin; Common languages: Portuguese, Burmese and Mon; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Theravada Buddhism; Government: Colonial military governorship; Ruler title: Governor; Head of state: Filipe de Brito e Nicote; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1600; Disestablished: 1614; Succeeded by: Toungoo Dynasty

name: Lan Na Kingdom
description: The Lan Na Kingdom functioned as an autonomous tributary state in northern Thailand subordinate to the Siamese Kingdom of Ayutthaya during the early seventeenth century. Based at the historic moated capital of Chiang Mai, the kingdom retained its unique Tai Yuan cultural traditions, Buddhist religious establishments and ancestral noble lineages while submitting tribute and acknowledging Siamese suzerainty. name: Principality of Moldavia
description: The Principality of Moldavia was briefly drawn into a personal union with Wallachia and Transylvania under the military leadership of Voivode Michael the Brave during the summer of 1600. After ousting the pro-Polish prince Ieremia Movilă, Michael entered the capital of Iași and declared himself Prince of Wallachia, Transylvania and Moldavia, uniting the three principalities for the first time in Romanian history. name: Bailundo Kingdom
label: ovimbundu kingdoms
description: The Bailundo Kingdom was the largest and most powerful monarchical state among the Ovimbundu peoples in the central highlands of present-day Angola. Centred at the fortified hill capital of Halavala, the kingdom developed an extensive trade network that dominated caravan commerce linking the Atlantic coast at Benguela with the interior plateau. Governed by a supreme monarch titled the soma inene, Bailundo maintained formidable military strength and political sovereignty for centuries until Portuguese military campaigns broke royal resistance during the Bailundo War of 1902 to 1904. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bailundo; Common languages: Umbundu; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Soma inene; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1904; Succeeded by: Portuguese West Africa

name: Dassa
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Dassa was an independent Yoruba kingdom established by the Idaasha subgroup who migrated westwards into the rocky hill country of central Benin. Founded around the naturally fortified redoubts of Dassa-Zoumé, the kingdom established sacred shrines and communal agricultural villages shielded by steep granitic inselbergs. Governed by a traditional monarch known as the oba, Dassa successfully defended its political autonomy and cultural identity against surrounding Dahomey and Mahi invasions throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries before wider regional destabilisation occurred. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dassa-Zoumé; Common languages: Idaasha and Yoruba; Religion: Yoruba religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Oba; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1801; Historical region: Slave Coast

name: Dwaben
description: Dwaben was a prominent Akan chieftaincy located in the forested interior of modern-day southern Ghana. Centred upon its ancestral capital at Dwaben, the state controlled fertile agricultural land and regional gold-trading tracks leading towards coastal commercial networks. Ruled by a paramount chief known as the Juabenhene, the polity retained fierce local independence and distinct military traditions until the political unification of the Ashanti Confederacy transformed power dynamics across the forest kingdoms. \n\n Status: Sovereign chieftaincy; Capital: Dwaben; Common languages: Akan and Twi; Religion: Traditional Akan religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Juabenhene; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1702

name: Emirate of Brakna
description: The Emirate of Brakna was a sovereign nomadic state established by the Hassaniya-speaking Arab and Berber clans in south-western Mauritania. Governed by a hereditary emir from the administrative centre at Aleg, the confederation dominated fertile pastoral plains along the northern bend of the Senegal River. The emirate derived significant economic power through collecting transit taxes on trans-Saharan caravan routes and trading gum arabic with European merchants before French military advances dismantled its sovereignty at the dawn of the twentieth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Aleg; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Hassaniya Arabic, Zenaga and Pulaar; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Tribal emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1901

name: Jukun
description: Jukun was a powerful monarchical state centred in the fertile Benue River valley of central Nigeria, representing the political legacy of the historic Kwararafa confederacy. Governed by a divine ruler titled the Aku Uka from royal settlements near Wukari, the state exercised substantial spiritual authority and tributary hegemony over neighbouring ethnic communities. Jukun power rested upon advanced ironworking, agricultural surplus and strategic control of riverine trade routes until Fulani jihad campaigns and internal fragmentation diminished its regional dominance in the mid-nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Wukari; Common languages: Jukun languages; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Aku Uka; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1856; Preceded by: Kwararafa

name: Kalabari Kingdom
description: The Kalabari Kingdom was a prosperous maritime trading state established by the Ijaw people within the coastal mangrove waterways of the Niger River Delta. Operating from its ancestral capital and later administrative seat at Buguma, the kingdom was organised around competitive commercial canoe houses overseen by a central monarch titled the Amanyanabo. Kalabari merchants dominated regional commerce, initially trading salt, fish and slaves, and later pivoting successfully to palm oil with European ships before entering into a British protectorate treaty in 1885. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Buguma; Common languages: Kalabari and Ijaw; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Amachree; Ruler title: Amanyanabo; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 5 June 1885

name: Kasanze Kingdom
description: The Kasanze Kingdom was an independent Mbundu polity situated near the mouth of the Bengo River in north-western Angola. Having secured full autonomy from the Kingdom of Kongo around the turn of the seventeenth century, Kasanze was ruled by an indigenous sovereign from its stronghold at modern Cacuaco. Occupying a crucial transit corridor between coastal Portuguese settlements at Luanda and the interior kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba, Kasanze vigorously guarded its trade routes until Portuguese military campaigns crushed the kingdom in the mid-seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kasanze; Common languages: Kimbundu; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1650; Preceded by: Kingdom of Kongo

name: Kingdom of Ankole
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Ankole was a sovereign pastoral and agricultural realm situated in south-western Uganda between Lake Edward and Lake Victoria. Governed by a hereditary sacred monarch titled the Omugabe from the royal capital at Mbarara, the kingdom was characterised by an intricate socio-political division between Bahima pastoralists and Bairu cultivators. Ankole defended its territory against powerful lacustrine neighbours such as Bunyoro and Buganda for centuries until concluding a formal protectorate agreement with the British Empire in October 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Mbarara; Common languages: Runyankole; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Omugabe; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 25 October 1901; Historical region: African Great Lakes

name: Kingdom of Buhaya
description: The Kingdom of Buhaya was a sovereign confederation of Haya principalities located across the fertile highland plateau bordering the western shores of Lake Victoria in north-western Tanzania. Administered from royal centres near Bukoba, the realm developed highly productive perennial banana and coffee agroforestry supported by advanced prehistoric iron-smelting traditions. Hereditary monarchs known as bakama led individual constituent realms bound by common clan structures and ancestral deities until imperial Germany established colonial hegemony over the region in 1890. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bukoba; Common languages: Haya; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Mukama; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1 July 1890; Historical region: African Great Lakes

name: Kingdom of Coorg
description: The Kingdom of Coorg was an independent highland realm established among the forested ridges of the Western Ghats in south-western India. Founded by a branch of the Ikkeri Nayaka family who established their capital at Madikeri, the state was defended by the martial Kodava community, renowned for their marksmanship and fiercely autonomous traditions. The Haleri Rajas maintained sovereign status despite recurrent invasions from neighbouring powers such as the Sultanate of Mysore before negotiating a subsidiary protectorate treaty with the British East India Company in 1790. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Madikeri; Common languages: Kodava and Kannada; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Haleri; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 26 October 1790

name: Kingdom of Dahomey
description: The Kingdom of Dahomey was a formidable militaristic state established by the Fon people on the Abomey Plateau in modern-day southern Benin. Headquartered at the fortified palaces of Abomey and ruled by an absolute monarch titled the ahosu, the kingdom developed an exceptionally disciplined standing army featuring famed female regiments known as Mino. Dahomey expanded rapidly by conquering coastal polities such as Ouidah, securing direct participation in Atlantic maritime trade while maintaining royal monopolies over agriculture and commerce until French colonial conquest in 1894. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Abomey; Official languages: Fon; Common languages: Fon; Religion: Vodun; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Ahosu; Currency: Cowrie shells; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 15 January 1894

name: Kingdom of Lagos
description: The Kingdom of Lagos, historically known as Eko, was an autonomous coastal monarchy established on Lagos Island and the surrounding mangrove creeks in south-western Nigeria. Founded originally as an Awori settlement and subsequently reorganised under the influence of the Benin Empire, the realm was governed by an oba supported by hereditary civil and war chiefs. The kingdom flourished as a vital coastal trading entrepôt, connecting inland waterborne commerce along the lagoon system with Atlantic maritime merchants before deeper British imperial intervention reshaped the territory in the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Lagos; Common languages: Yoruba and Awori dialect; Religion: Yoruba religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Oba; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1801; Historical region: Bight of Benin

name: Kyawkku State
label: shan states
description: Kyawkku State was a small autonomous Shan principality situated in the rugged Myelat plateau region of eastern Burma under the suzerainty of the Burmese monarchy. Governed by a hereditary local chieftain bearing the title of ngwegunhmu from the administrative settlement of Kyawkku, the state yielded silver tribute and pledged military levies to the royal court at Ava and later Amarapura. The principality preserved its customary legal codes and Shan agrarian village customs until the British annexation of Upper Burma dissolved the traditional vassalage system in 1886. \n\n Status: Burmese vassal state; Capital: Kyawkku; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Ngwegunhmu; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Mampong
description: Mampong was an independent Akan chieftaincy situated in the rolling hills of the northern forest zone in central Ghana. Guided by a hereditary paramount ruler bearing the title of Mamponghene, the state commanded a key strategic frontier along northern trade routes leading towards the Savanna grasslands. The kingdom maintained extensive gold mines and agricultural settlements until the military integration of the region under Osei Tutu I incorporated Mampong into the newly founded Ashanti Empire, where its ruler served as commander-in-chief of the confederate army. \n\n Status: Sovereign chieftaincy; Capital: Mampong; Common languages: Akan and Twi; Religion: Traditional Akan religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Mamponghene; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1718; Succeeded by: Ashanti Empire

name: Mapuche Chiefdoms
description: The Mapuche Chiefdoms comprised a loose confederation of autonomous indigenous polities inhabiting Araucanía in south-central Chile. Led by hereditary clan chiefs known as lonkos and wartime military commanders titled toquis, the Mapuche successfully repulsed Spanish imperial invasions following the catastrophic disaster of Curalaba in 1598, establishing the Bío Bío River as a formal sovereign frontier. The chiefdoms defended their ancestral lands, livestock and agro-pastoral lifestyle with unyielding resilience for nearly three centuries until Chilean military campaigns gradually incorporated Araucanía during the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign indigenous confederacy; Capital: Temuco; Common languages: Mapudungun; Religion: Traditional Mapuche religion; Government: Decentralised tribal confederation; Ruler title: Toqui and Lonko; Historical era: Colonial and post-colonial period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1900

name: Mbwila
description: Mbwila was an independent mountainous state located around the headwaters of the Lukala River in the rugged Dembos region of northern Angola. Ruled by a sovereign titled the ndembu from a heavily fortified cliffside citadel, the polity occupied an indispensable trade corridor linking the Kingdom of Kongo with the Kingdom of Ndongo. Mbwila skilfully maintained its independence by playing competing regional powers and Portuguese colonial forces against one another, famously resisting subjugation until Portuguese armies achieved formal annexation in the late eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Mbwila; Common languages: Kimbundu and Kikongo; Religion: Traditional African religion and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ndembu; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1759; Historical region: Dembos

name: Niani
description: Niani was a sovereign Mandinka kingdom established along the north bank of the navigable Gambia River in modern-day central Gambia. Governed by a hereditary king bearing the title of mansa from the riverine administrative port of Niani Maru, the polity flourished through its strategic command over regional water transport and inland caravan trails. The kingdom participated actively in regional trade involving groundnuts, beeswax and textiles while maintaining political autonomy from larger Senegambian neighbours throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Niani Maru; Common languages: Mandinka; Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mansa; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1801; Historical region: Senegambia

name: Niumi
description: The Kingdom of Niumi, historically known as the Kingdom of Barra, was an independent West African state situated along the northern Atlantic mouth of the Gambia River. Ruled by a dynasty of Mandinka mansas from their coastal seat at Essau, the kingdom levied substantial customs duties and transit tolls on European merchant vessels entering the Gambia waterway. Niumi leveraged its naval war canoes and commercial position to safeguard its sovereign integrity against European encroachments for three centuries before it was formally absorbed into the British Gambia Protectorate in 1897. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Essau; Common languages: Mandinka, Wolof and Fula; Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mansa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1898; Succeeded by: Gambia Colony and Protectorate

name: Principality of Adonara
description: The Principality of Adonara was an autonomous island realm situated in the Solor Archipelago east of Flores in present-day eastern Indonesia. Governed by an indigenous Lamaholot ruler from the coastal settlement of Adonara, the principality commanded vital maritime passages that funnelled regional trade in sandalwood, beeswax and marine commodities. The realm zealously safeguarded its local sovereignty against rival island principalities and Portuguese Dominican missionaries stationed on neighbouring Solor before formal alliances reshaped political alignments across the Lesser Sunda Islands. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Adonara; Common languages: Lamaholot; Religion: Traditional animism and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional principality; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1614; Historical region: Solor Archipelago

name: Principality of Cooch Behar
description: The Principality of Cooch Behar functioned as a tributary vassal state subordinate to the Mughal Empire across northern Bengal and the lower Brahmaputra basin. Governed by the Koch royal dynasty from their regional administrative base, the principality paid regular imperial tribute and supplied auxiliary military forces to the Mughal subahdar in Bengal. Although acknowledging the paramountcy of the Mughal emperor in Delhi, the ruling Maharajas retained direct domestic jurisdiction over revenue collection, local temple patronage and regional civil administration. \n\n Status: Mughal vassal state; Capital: Bârâkpur; Common languages: Kamatapuri and Bengali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Koch; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1651; Preceded by: Kamata Kingdom

name: Principality of Lamahala
description: The Principality of Lamahala was an independent maritime domain situated on the southern coast of Adonara Island within the Solor Archipelago of eastern Indonesia. Governed by an Islamic raja from the port of Lamahala, the principality functioned as a key member of the Watan Lema, a regional defensive league formed by five allied Muslim coastal states. The domain guarded local coastal waters and dominated maritime commerce in forest goods while fiercely contesting the territorial and religious influence of Portuguese Dominican missionaries on nearby Solor. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Lamahala; Common languages: Lamaholot and Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional principality; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1614; Historical region: Solor Archipelago

name: Principality of Lamakera
description: The Principality of Lamakera was an autonomous Muslim principality located on the eastern tip of Solor Island in the eastern Indonesian archipelago. Based at the seafaring haven of Lamakera, the polity developed an expert maritime culture renowned for open-water whaling, coastal navigation and regional commerce. Lamakera formed an integral pillar of the Watan Lema confederacy, actively mobilising naval forces to protect local trade corridors and resist political encroachment by Portuguese colonial expeditions operating in the Lesser Sunda Islands. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Lamakera; Common languages: Lamaholot and Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional principality; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1614; Historical region: Solor Archipelago

name: Principality of Lohayong
description: The Principality of Lohayong was an independent coastal realm situated on the northern shore of Solor Island in eastern Indonesia. Centred upon the strategic fortified harbour of Lohayong, the principality held a commanding position over the narrow strait separating Solor from neighbouring Adonara. The local ruling dynasty maintained sovereign autonomy while adroitly balancing alliances with rival European trading companies and neighbouring members of the Watan Lema until regional geopolitical restructuring altered the balance of power in 1614. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Lohayong; Common languages: Lamaholot; Religion: Sunni Islam and traditional animism; Government: Traditional principality; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1614; Historical region: Solor Archipelago

name: Principality of Terong
description: The Principality of Terong was a sovereign coastal state located on the south-western coast of Adonara Island within the Solor Archipelago of eastern Indonesia. Governed by a traditional Lamaholot raja from the port of Terong, the polity formed part of the Watan Lema coalition, an alliance of five indigenous Islamic principalities established for mutual defence. Terong fiercely defended its regional waters, engaging in maritime commerce and resisting Portuguese naval expeditions until Dutch commercial expansion transformed the regional geopolitical landscape. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Terong; Common languages: Lamaholot; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional principality; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1614; Historical region: Solor Archipelago

name: South Buha Kingdom
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The South Buha Kingdom was an autonomous monarchical realm established by the Ha people in the rugged highlands of western Tanzania near Lake Tanganyika. Administered from royal enclosures around Kasulu by hereditary rulers bearing the title of mwami, the kingdom relied upon pastoral cattle herding, sorghum farming and local copper trade. The state maintained internal political cohesion and defended its borders against incursions from neighbouring lacustrine powers such as Burundi until eighteenth-century regional transformations reorganised the Buha political landscape. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kasulu; Common languages: Ha; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Mwami; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1751; Historical region: African Great Lakes

name: Sultanate of Rahayta
description: The Sultanate of Rahayta was an independent Afar sultanate situated on the southern Red Sea littoral of modern-day Eritrea near the Bab-el-Mandeb strait. Governed by an Afar sultan from the coastal town of Rahayta, the polity commanded critical maritime surveillance points overlooking the sea passage between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The sultanate prospered by regulating caravan routes from the Danakil interior, trading livestock, salt and marine goods while successfully safeguarding its sovereignty against imperial Ottoman and highland Ethiopian expansion. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Rahayta; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Afar and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sultanate; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 1701; Historical region: Horn of Africa

name: Tortola
description: Tortola was an early English plantation settlement established on the largest island of the Virgin Islands archipelago in the north-eastern Caribbean Sea. Occupied by English adventurers and maritime planters during the final years of the Elizabethan era, the colony was founded to cultivate commercial crops and serve as an anchorage for privateering vessels harassing Spanish shipping in the West Indies. English colonists maintained precarious outposts without substantial royal fortifications until the death of Queen Elizabeth I in 1603 placed the territory under the newly united English and Scottish Crowns. \n\n Status: English colony; Administrative seat: Road Town; Capital: Road Town; Common languages: English; Religion: Church of England; Government: Proprietary settlement; Head of state: Elizabeth I; Historical era: Elizabethan era; Established: 1601; Disestablished: 24 March 1603

name: Kingdom of Palembang
description: The Kingdom of Palembang was an independent realm situated along the lower Musi River basin in southern Sumatra. Ruled by a royal dynasty tracing its lineage to the Javanese court of Demak, the state operated as a thriving riverine emporium connecting the agricultural and pepper-producing interior with regional maritime shipping networks. Palembang maintained commercial relations with both the Sultanate of Banten and incoming Dutch and English merchants, defending its sovereign status until the formal foundation of the Palembang Sultanate consolidated power in the late seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Palembang; Common languages: Palembang Malay and Javanese; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Pangeran and Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1602; Disestablished: 1660; Succeeded by: Palembang Sultanate

name: Principality of Ligne
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Ligne was an imperial estate of the Holy Roman Empire held by the illustrious House of Ligne in the Low Countries. Elevated from a county to an imperial principality by Emperor Rudolf II in 1601, the realm granted its princes imperial immediacy and an influential voice in the Imperial Diet. The princely dynasty played a distinguished diplomatic and military role within the Habsburg administration of the Southern Netherlands, maintaining territorial sovereignty until French revolutionary armies overran and annexed the territory in the late eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Ligny-en-Barrois; Common languages: French and Walloon; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Ligne; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1602; Disestablished: 1796

name: Principality of Moldavia
description: The Principality of Moldavia operated as a feudal dependency of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth during the turbulent opening decades of the seventeenth century. Placed under Polish suzerainty by Grand Hetman Jan Zamoyski, the throne at Iași was occupied by members of the pro-Polish Movilă family, who owed military loyalty and annual tribute to the Polish Crown. This arrangement shielded Moldavia from Ottoman centralisation for nearly two decades, ending when Polish defeats at the Battle of Cecora restored direct Ottoman vassalage in 1620. \n\n Status: Polish-Lithuanian fief; Capital: Iași; Official languages: Church Slavonic, Romanian and Latin; Common languages: Romanian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Movilă; Ruler title: Hospodar; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1602; Disestablished: 1619

name: Ramnad State
description: Ramnad State was an independent Maravar kingdom established in the coastal plains of modern-day southern Tamil Nadu, India. Ruled by hereditary princes bearing the prestigious title of Sethupathi, or protectors of the sacred bridge connecting India to Sri Lanka, the kingdom arose following the fragmentation of the Madurai Nayak domain. The state derived wealth from coastal fisheries, pearl beds and transit taxes paid by Hindu pilgrims visiting Rameswaram, maintaining political autonomy until internal dynastic conflicts enabled the British East India Company to convert the realm into a zamindari estate. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ramanathapuram; Common languages: Tamil; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sethupathi; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1602; Disestablished: 1796; Succeeded by: Madras Presidency

name: Nawngwawn State
label: shan states
description: Nawngwawn State was an autonomous Shan principality situated in the lush upland valleys of eastern Burma under the imperial suzerainty of the Burmese monarchy. Governed by a hereditary local prince bearing the title of myoza from the administrative town of Nawngwawn, the state enjoyed internal administrative freedom in exchange for paying annual tribute and providing military levies to the royal court in Upper Burma. The principality maintained its traditional Shan customary laws, agrarian institutions and Theravada Buddhist religious practices until British colonial authorities annexed Upper Burma in 1886. \n\n Status: Burmese vassal state; Capital: Nawngwawn; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Myoza; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1603; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Bailiwick of Guernsey
description: The Bailiwick of Guernsey was an autonomous British Crown Dependency comprising Guernsey, Alderney, Sark and Herm in the English Channel off the coast of Normandy. Holding distinct constitutional privileges derived from its historic status as part of the Duchy of Normandy, the bailiwick was governed through the Royal Court and the States of Deliberation in Saint Peter Port under a bailiff. While recognising the British monarch as head of state, Guernsey maintained independent fiscal, judicial and legislative institutions that shielded it from direct parliamentary taxation and external interference. \n\n Status: British Crown Dependency; Capital: St Peter Port; Official languages: English and French; Common languages: English, French and Guernésiais; Religion: Church of England; Government: Parliamentary constitutional dependency; Legislature: States of Guernsey; Head of state: British Monarch; Ruler title: Bailiff; Established: 24 March 1603

name: Bailiwick of Jersey
description: The Bailiwick of Jersey was a self-governing British Crown Dependency situated in the Gulf of Saint-Malo off the western coast of the Cotentin Peninsula. Retaining sovereign legal and political liberties originating from the medieval Duchy of Normandy, the island was governed from Saint Helier by the States Assembly and the Royal Court under the presidency of the Bailiff. While remaining loyal to the British Crown, Jersey maintained complete autonomy in taxation and domestic legislation, fortifying its coastlines against recurrent French invasions while fostering a thriving maritime trading economy. \n\n Status: British Crown Dependency; Capital: Saint Helier; Official languages: English and French; Common languages: English, French and Jèrriais; Religion: Church of England; Government: Parliamentary constitutional dependency; Legislature: States Assembly; Head of state: British Monarch; Ruler title: Bailiff; Established: 24 March 1603

name: British North America
description: British North America comprised the collective colonial territories, trading territories and crown domains claimed and governed by the British Crown across northern North America. Administered directly from London through royal governors, chartered commercial enterprises and colonial assemblies, these possessions spanned vast territories from Newfoundland and the Hudson Bay watershed to the eastern seaboard. The territories coordinated naval defence, transatlantic commerce and territorial negotiations with indigenous confederacies and European rivals, evolving steadily until gradual confederation created modern Canada. \n\n Status: Crown colonial territories; Administrative seat: London; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: English and French; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Head of state: British Monarch; Established: 24 March 1603; Preceded by: English North America; Succeeded by: Canada

name: Cautionary Towns
description: Under the newly united English and Scottish Crown of King James I, the Cautionary Towns, consisting of the strategic Dutch ports of Brielle, Vlissingen and Fort Rammekens, remained held by English garrison forces. Functioning as financial surety for substantial loans extended by the late Queen Elizabeth I during the Anglo-Spanish War, the fortresses were overseen by English military governors who collected harbour dues and manned the ramparts. In 1616, King James negotiated a financial settlement with the States General of the Dutch Republic, leading to the liquidation of the mortgage and the full return of the garrisons. \n\n Status: British military possession; Administrative seat: Mobile garrison; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: English and Dutch; Religion: Calvinism and Anglicanism; Government: Military governorship; Head of state: James I; Established: 24 March 1603; Disestablished: 1617; Succeeded by: Dutch Republic

name: Kingdom of England and Kingdom of Scotland
description: The Kingdom of England and Kingdom of Scotland entered a historic personal union on 24 March 1603 when King James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne as King James I following the death of Elizabeth I. Governed from the royal court at Whitehall in London, the two realms remained legally separate nations, each preserving its distinct parliament, legal code, currency and national church. Despite persistent religious turmoil and constitutional crises during the seventeenth century, the Union of the Crowns established the dynastic foundation that ultimately culminated in the 1707 Acts of Union creating Great Britain. \n\n Status: Personal union; Capital: London; Official languages: English, Latin and Scots; Common languages: English, Scots and Scottish Gaelic; Religion: Anglicanism and Presbyterianism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Stuart; Head of state: James I; Legislature: Parliament of England and Parliament of Scotland; Established: 24 March 1603; Disestablished: 1 May 1707; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Great Britain

name: Kingdom of Ireland
description: The Kingdom of Ireland was a dependent client kingdom held by the English Crown in personal union following the accession of King James I in 1603. Administered from Dublin Castle by a royal viceroy designated as the Lord Lieutenant, the kingdom was subordinated to Westminster through Poynings' Law while maintaining its own bicameral parliament in Dublin. British rule during this era was defined by extensive plantation schemes, the consolidation of the Protestant Ascendancy and the systematic disenfranchisement of the Catholic majority until the 1800 Act of Union created a unified United Kingdom. \n\n Status: Crown client kingdom; Capital: Dublin; Official languages: English; Common languages: Irish and English; Religion: Church of Ireland and Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy under viceregal rule; Head of state: British Monarch; Representative title: Lord Lieutenant; Legislature: Parliament of Ireland; Established: 24 March 1603; Disestablished: 1801

name: Macapá
description: Macapá was an ephemeral English colonial trading post and plantation outpost established along the northern mouth of the Amazon River in present-day northern Brazil. Founded by adventurous English merchants seeking lucrative tropical commodities, timber and dyewoods, the settlement operated without a formal administrative capital, relying on temporary riverbank stockades and commercial bartering with indigenous communities. However, persistent naval opposition and armed counter-attacks by Portuguese colonial expeditions operating from Belém overwhelmed the English garrison and extinguished the colony in 1611. \n\n Status: English colonial outpost; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: English and Portuguese; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Proprietary trading post; Head of state: James I; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 24 March 1603; Disestablished: 1611; Succeeded by: Colonial Brazil

name: Tortola
description: Under the newly united English and Scottish Crowns following the accession of King James I, Tortola continued to function as a Caribbean plantation outpost in the British Virgin Islands. Headquartered around the natural harbour at Road Town, the island was settled by small detachments of British planters cultivating tobacco, cotton and provisions while providing provisions to transatlantic shipping. British settlers defended their coastal hamlets against tropical storms and Spanish naval patrols until Dutch privateers and settlers gradually occupied the island in the late 1640s. \n\n Status: British colony; Capital: Road Town; Common languages: English; Religion: Church of England; Government: Proprietary governorship; Head of state: James I; Historical era: Stuart era; Established: 24 March 1603; Disestablished: 1649; Succeeded by: Dutch Virgin Islands

name: Safavid Empire (Military Occupation)
description: The Safavid Empire Military Occupation designated external operational zones and conquered Ottoman frontier provinces held under temporary martial governance by the Safavid Persian royal army. Initiated under Shah Abbas I during his major counter-offensives in the Caucasus and Mesopotamia, Safavid commanders occupied strategic cities including Yerevan, Tabriz and Baghdad without establishing permanent civilian municipal institutions. These martial zones were maintained as fortified strongholds and cavalry staging grounds, functioning until bilateral border settlements such as the Treaty of Nasuh Pasha or Treaty of Zuhab redrew imperial frontiers. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Mobile imperial headquarters; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Persian, Azerbaijani Turkic and Arabic; Religion: Twelver Shia Islam; Government: Military administration; Head of state: Abbas I; Historical era: Ottoman-Safavid Wars; Established: 21 October 1603; Disestablished: 20 November 1612

name: Duchy of Saxe-Altenburg
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine;german confederation
description: The Duchy of Saxe-Altenburg was an autonomous imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire governed by the Ernestine line of the Saxon House of Wettin in eastern Thuringia. Headquartered at the historic residential palace in Altenburg, the duchy was formed in the early seventeenth century following a partition of Saxe-Weimar among royal brothers. The dukes exercised full territorial sovereignty, maintaining an independent court, provincial judiciary and Lutheran church administration until the primary Altenburg ducal line became extinct in 1672, leading to a temporary union with Saxe-Gotha. \n\n Status: Principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Altenburg; Official languages: German; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Wettin (Ernestine line); Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1604

name: Pashalik of Timbuktu
description: The Pashalik of Timbuktu operated as an autonomous West African military republic governed by the Arma, the descendants of the Moroccan expeditionary forces who settled along the middle Niger River. Breaking practical ties with the Saadian court in Marrakech following the death of Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur in 1603, the pashas in Timbuktu were elected directly by local military councils. The state controlled major trans-Saharan riverine ports and trade routes between Djenné and Gao, defending its urban enclaves against Tuareg and Bambara incursions until Fulani conquest in the 1830s. \n\n Status: Sovereign military pashalik; Capital: Timbuktu; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Songhai, Hassaniya Arabic and Soninke; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military elective pashalik; Ruler title: Pasha; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1604; Disestablished: 1834; Preceded by: Pashalik of Timbuktu (Moroccan Vassal)

name: United East India Company
description: The United East India Company, widely known as the VOC, was a chartered Dutch joint-stock corporation that exercised quasi-sovereign administrative and military rule across maritime Asia. Headquartered at the fortified colonial citadel of Batavia, now Jakarta, the company possessed legal charters authorising it to wage offensive warfare, construct fortresses, mint coinage and conclude diplomatic treaties with Asian rulers. By monopolising the global spice trade and seizing strategic coastal ports from Malacca to Ceylon, the company established an extensive maritime commercial empire that lasted until nationalisation by the Batavian Republic in 1800. \n\n Status: Chartered corporate rule; Capital: Jakarta; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch, Malay, Portuguese and Javanese; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Corporate colonial administration; Ruler title: Governor-General; Currency: VOC guilder and real; Established: 1604; Disestablished: 1800; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Oyapoc
description: Oyapoc was an early English colonial outpost and exploratory settlement founded along the banks of the Oyapock River in present-day French Guiana. Established in May 1604 by Captain Charles Leigh aboard the Olive Plant, the colony was intended to exploit reported gold deposits and cultivate tropical commodities in South America. The settlers established their main encampment at Mount Howard, but the colony suffered severe privation, internal mutinies and repeated raids by hostile Caribs from the Cayenne River, leading to its eventual abandonment in 1630. \n\n Status: English colonial settlement; Administrative seat: Mount Howard; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: English and Cariban languages; Religion: Church of England; Government: Proprietary colonial command; Head of state: James I; Historical era: Jacobean era; Established: 22 May 1604; Disestablished: 1630

name: Dutch Coromandel
description: Dutch Coromandel was a directorate and colonial governorate operated by the Dutch East India Company along the Coromandel Coast of south-eastern India.
