Centred at Fort Geldria in Pulicat and later administered from Nagapattinam, the colony served as the primary procurement centre for fine Indian printed cotton textiles bartered across the Indonesian archipelago for valuable spices. The Dutch maintained fortified factories and mercantile warehouses under a company governor until British military occupations during the Napoleonic Wars and the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 permanently transferred the holdings to Great Britain. \n\n Status: Dutch company directorate; Capital: Pulicat; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch, Tamil and Telugu; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church and Hinduism; Government: Colonial directorate; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1606; Disestablished: 1 June 1825; Succeeded by: British India

name: Fernando de Noronha
description: Fernando de Noronha was an isolated South Atlantic island possession held intermittently by the Dutch West India Company off the north-eastern coast of Brazil. Capitalising on its strategic position along transatlantic shipping lanes, Dutch mariners utilised the main island as a naval revictualling base and maritime observation station during their wider commercial campaign in Dutch Brazil. The settlement comprised fortified shore batteries and livestock pastures, sustaining small garrison forces until Portuguese expeditions from Pernambuco permanently re-established Lusitanian control. \n\n Status: Dutch colonial outpost; Capital: Fernando de Noronha; Common languages: Dutch and Portuguese; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Military command; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1606; Disestablished: 1706; Succeeded by: Colonial Brazil

name: Quilombo dos Palmares
description: Quilombo dos Palmares was a sovereign confederation of fortified settlements established by self-liberated enslaved Africans and indigenous allies in the rugged Serra da Barriga mountains of north-eastern Brazil. Centred upon the fortified capital at Macaco near modern União dos Palmares, the community developed an autonomous syncretic society blending Central African governance traditions with local subsistence agriculture and palm harvesting. Governed by elected monarchs such as Ganga Zumba and Zumbi, Palmares repulsed dozens of Portuguese and Dutch colonial assaults before being overrun and destroyed in 1695. \n\n Status: Sovereign maroon confederacy; Capital: União dos Palmares; Common languages: Bantu languages, Portuguese and indigenous languages; Religion: Syncretic African religions and Roman Catholicism; Government: Confederated monarchy; Ruler title: King; Head of state: Zumbi; Established: 1606; Disestablished: 1695

name: Sultanate of Singora
description: The Sultanate of Singora was an independent fortified maritime sultanate situated at the entrance of Songkhla Lake in southern Thailand. Founded by the Persian merchant nobleman Dato Mogol and flourishing under his successor Sultan Sulaiman Shah, the city-state constructed stone ramparts, hilltop forts and a prosperous international harbour. Singora welcomed European, Chinese and regional Malay traders while fiercely asserting its sovereignty against the Siamese Kingdom of Ayutthaya until a massive Siamese naval campaign sacked and demolished the city in 1680. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Songkhla; Common languages: Malay, Thai and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1606; Disestablished: 1681; Succeeded by: Ayutthaya Kingdom

name: Principality of Transylvania
description: Following the conclusion of the Peace of Zsitvatorok and the Treaty of Vienna in 1606, the Principality of Transylvania entered a golden age of sovereign autonomy within Central Europe. Governed from Alba Iulia by illustrious Calvinist princes including Gabriel Bethlen and George I Rákóczi, the principality functioned as a flourishing bastion of religious pluralism, educational advancement and Protestant diplomacy. Transylvania exercised independent foreign policy and intervened militarily in the Thirty Years' War until the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 consolidated direct Habsburg imperial dominance over the province. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Alba Iulia; Official languages: Latin and Hungarian; Common languages: Hungarian, Romanian and German; Religion: Calvinism, Lutheranism, Unitarianism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Elective principality; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 11 November 1606; Disestablished: 26 January 1699

name: New Hebrides
description: New Hebrides designated an early Portuguese and Spanish colonial territorial claim situated across the south-western Pacific archipelago of modern-day Vanuatu. Initiated following the 1606 maritime expedition commanded by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Fernandes de Queirós under the Spanish Crown, European explorers established a short-lived settlement named Nueva Jerusalén near modern Port Olry on Espiritu Santo. Although local resistance, tropical sickness and maritime hardships forced the swift withdrawal of the expedition, the territorial claim remained recorded in Iberian cartography for generations. \n\n Status: Iberian colonial claim; Capital: Port Olry; Common languages: Portuguese, Spanish and indigenous Oceanic languages; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial expeditionary claim; Head of state: Philip III; Historical era: Age of Discovery; Established: 1607; Disestablished: 1801

name: Sultanate of Ternate
description: The Sultanate of Ternate fell under direct Spanish colonial subjugation following an amphibious expedition dispatched from Manila under Governor Pedro Bravo de Acuña in 1606. Operating from the captured royal citadel of Gammalammo, Spanish authorities installed a puppet sultan, garrisoned formidable coastal bastions and enforced royal monopolies over the lucrative clove trade in North Maluku. Spanish rule faced constant resistance from local maritime communities and recurrent military sieges by the Dutch East India Company until Spanish garrisons were finally evacuated to Manila in the 1660s. \n\n Status: Spanish colony; Capital: Ternate; Official languages: Spanish; Common languages: Ternate, Malay and Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Sunni Islam; Government: Colonial governorship; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1607; Disestablished: 1664; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Ternate

name: Popham Colony
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Popham Colony, also known as the Sagadahoc Colony, was an early English colonial settlement founded near the mouth of the Kennebec River in present-day Maine. Backed by the Virginia Company of Plymouth and led by George Popham and Raleigh Gilbert, the settlers constructed Fort Saint George, a storehouse and a seaworthy transatlantic pinnace named the Virginia of Sagadahoc. However, a punishing New England winter, devastating fires, food scarcity and the deaths of key patrons in England prompted the remaining colonists to dismantle the settlement in 1608. \n\n Status: English proprietary colony; Capital: Fort St. George; Common languages: English and Eastern Abenaki; Religion: Church of England; Government: Proprietary council; Ruler title: Colony President; Head of state: James I; Historical era: Jacobean era; Established: 4 May 1607; Disestablished: 1609

name: Colony of Virginia
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Colony of Virginia was the first permanent English settlement established in North America, founded along the James River by the Virginia Company under royal charter from King James I. Beginning at Jamestown and later transferring its seat of government to Williamsburg, the colony surmounted initial famines, endemic diseases and conflicts with the Powhatan Confederacy through the profitable introduction of commercial tobacco farming. Virginia established the House of Burgesses in 1619, nurturing foundational representative legislative traditions that thrived until the colony declared its independence during the American Revolution in 1776. \n\n Status: British Crown colony; Capital: Jamestown and Williamsburg; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Powhatan; Religion: Church of England; Government: Constitutional colonial governorship; Head of state: British Monarch; Representative title: Royal Governor; Legislature: House of Burgesses; Established: 14 May 1607; Disestablished: 23 December 1776

name: Bonaku
description: Bonaku was an independent coastal chieftaincy established by the Duala people along the banks of the Wouri River estuary in modern-day Littoral Cameroon. Governed from the settlement of Bonaku by hereditary lineage leaders and councils of elders, the polity commanded access to rich mangrove fisheries and inland waterways. Bonaku developed into an essential coastal trading hub, bartering ivory, timber and agricultural produce with visiting European merchant vessels while zealously safeguarding its sovereign autonomy and riverine trading monopolies against neighbouring coastal clans. \n\n Status: Sovereign chieftaincy; Capital: Bonaku; Common languages: Duala; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Ruler title: Chief; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1609; Disestablished: 1795; Historical region: Cameroon Coast

name: Ryukyu Kingdom
label: ryuku polities
description: The Ryukyu Kingdom entered a period of dual vassalage following the invasion of Okinawa by the Japanese feudal domain of Satsuma in the spring of 1609. Headquartered at Shuri Castle with its commercial port at Naha, the kingdom preserved its royal dynasty, internal administration and tributary relations with Ming and Qing China, which Satsuma leveraged for indirect international trade. The Ryukyuan monarchs governed their maritime island realm with distinct diplomatic and cultural finesse until the Meiji government annexed the territory directly as Okinawa Prefecture in the 1870s. \n\n Status: Japanese vassal kingdom; Capital: Naha; Official languages: Classical Chinese and Classical Japanese; Common languages: Okinawan and Ryukyuan languages; Religion: Ryukyuan religion, Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Vassal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Second Shō; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 18 April 1609; Disestablished: 1873

name: Electoral Palatinate (Military Occupation)
label: holy roman empire
description: The Electoral Palatinate Military Occupation designated operational combat theatres and garrisoned border sectors held under martial control by troops of the Elector Palatine within north-western Germany. Following the outbreak of the War of the Jülich Succession in 1609, Palatine military commanders occupied strategic forts and river crossings across the Lower Rhine without establishing permanent civilian municipal administrations. These martial footholds functioned as armed garrisons and defensive bastions to protect Protestant interests within the Holy Roman Empire until comprehensive territorial treaties concluded the occupation. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Mobile garrison headquarters; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: German; Religion: Calvinism and Lutheranism; Government: Military administration; Head of state: Elector Palatine; Historical era: War of the Jülich Succession; Established: 1 May 1609; Disestablished: 9 September 1666

name: Electorate of Brandenburg (Military Occupation)
label: holy roman empire
description: The Electorate of Brandenburg Military Occupation encompassed temporary garrison zones and military command districts established by the Hohenzollern electors during the disputed succession of the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg. Operating without a separate civilian administrative capital, Brandenburg field commanders held fortified Rhineland strongholds and riverine crossings in condominium with allied Protestant princes. This armed occupation secured vital strategic footholds for Brandenburg until the formal partition under the 1614 Treaty of Xanten and subsequent administrative consolidation integrated Cleves, Mark and Ravensberg into the Hohenzollern patrimony. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Mobile field command; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: German and Dutch; Religion: Lutheranism and Calvinism; Government: Military governorship; Head of state: Elector of Brandenburg; Historical era: War of the Jülich Succession; Established: 1 May 1609; Disestablished: 1619

name: Hirado Factory
description: The Hirado Factory was a fortified trading post established by the Dutch East India Company on Hirado Island off the north-western coast of Kyushu, Japan. Authorised under an imperial trading pass granted by Shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu, the factory served as the primary Dutch commercial emporium in Japan for over three decades. Dutch merchants imported raw Chinese silk, textiles and spices in exchange for Japanese silver and copper until Tokugawa shogunate sakoku isolation policies forced the relocation of all Dutch operations to Dejima in Nagasaki harbour in 1641. \n\n Status: Dutch trading post; Capital: Hirado; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch and Japanese; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Commercial factory administration; Ruler title: Opperhoofd; Historical era: Edo period; Established: 20 September 1609; Disestablished: 24 June 1641; Succeeded by: Dejima Factory

name: Bermuda
description: Bermuda is a British colonial island territory situated in the North Atlantic Ocean, first settled permanently following the shipwreck of the Sea Venture in 1609. Initially administered by the Somers Isles Company and transferred to direct British Crown governance in 1684, the archipelago established its capital at Saint George and later at Hamilton. Developing an economy centred upon maritime trade, privateering, shipbuilding and salt production, Bermuda established the House of Assembly in 1620, making it one of the oldest continuous representative parliamentary democracies in the world. \n\n Status: British Crown colony; Capital: Hamilton; Largest city: St. George's; Official languages: English; Common languages: English; Religion: Church of England; Government: Parliamentary dependency under constitutional monarchy; Legislature: Parliament of Bermuda; Head of state: British Monarch; Established: 1610

name: Kishangarh State
description: Kishangarh State was an independent Rajput kingdom established in the central Rajputana region of north-western India. Founded in 1611 by Prince Kishan Singh, a younger son of the ruler of Jodhpur, the realm established its capital around the lakeside fortress of Kishangarh. The Rathore rulers defended their sovereign borders against regional neighbours and attained legendary cultural renown in the eighteenth century as celebrated patrons of miniature painting, notably developing the ethereal Kishangarh school of art before concluding a subsidiary alliance with the British in 1818. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Kishangarh; Common languages: Rajasthani, Hindi and Marwari; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rathore Rajput; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1610; Disestablished: 26 March 1818

name: Sagadahoc Colony
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Sagadahoc Colony, also known as the Territory of Sagadahock, was an English colonial domain encompassing the coastal territory between the Kennebec and Saint Croix rivers in eastern Maine. Following the abandonment of the initial Popham settlement, English fishing stations, timber camps and fur-trading posts maintained an enduring commercial presence across the rugged maritime frontier. Governed through loose proprietary charters and trade syndicates, the territory served as a contested boundary between New England settlements and French Acadia until it was incorporated into the ducal patent of the Duke of York in 1664. \n\n Status: English proprietary territory; Capital: Sagadahoc; Common languages: English and Abenaki; Religion: Church of England; Government: Proprietary governorship; Head of state: British Monarch; Historical era: Stuart era; Established: 1610; Disestablished: 1665; Succeeded by: Cornwall County (Province of New York)

name: Sambas Sultanate
description: The Sambas Sultanate was an independent Malay Islamic monarchy situated along the Sambas River basin in western Borneo. Emerging from ancestral ties with the Sultanate of Brunei and the Santubong kingdom, the state adopted Islam under Sultan Muhammad Shafi ud-din I and developed a prosperous maritime economy rooted in gold mining, timber and pepper exports. Sambas maintained sovereign regional authority and defended its coastal waters against rival Bugis and Dayak factions for more than two centuries before Dutch imperial treaties curtailed its autonomy in the 1820s. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Sambas; Common languages: Sambas Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Sambas; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1610; Disestablished: 1820; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Tsardom of Russia
description: During the acute political crisis of the Time of Troubles, the Tsardom of Russia operated as a Polish-Lithuanian protectorate following the military collapse of Tsar Vasili Shuysky in 1610. The governing council of the Seven Boyars in Moscow elected Prince Władysław of Poland as Tsar of Russia, inviting Polish troops under Hetman Stanisław Żółkiewski to garrison the Moscow Kremlin and maintain civil order. However, religious opposition to a Catholic ruler and King Sigismund III Vasa's refusal to let his son convert to Russian Orthodoxy sparked widespread national resistance that ousted the Polish garrison in late 1611. \n\n Status: Polish protectorate; Capital: Moscow; Official languages: Russian and Polish; Common languages: Russian; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism; Government: Protectorate monarchy; Head of state: Władysław Vasa; Legislature: Boyar Duma; Established: 27 July 1610; Disestablished: 8 December 1611

name: BaNgwato
description: BaNgwato was a sovereign Tswana chieftaincy established across the eastern savannah grasslands of modern-day Botswana. Ruled by a hereditary paramount chief titled the kgosi, the state was organised around vast communal cattle-posts, sorghum agriculture and town assemblies known as kgotla. The BaNgwato expanded their territorial hegemony through military resistance against invading Ndebele impis and neighbouring Boer commandos, preserving sovereign independence until Kgosi Khama III successfully petitioned for the establishment of the British Bechuanaland Protectorate in March 1885. \n\n Status: Sovereign chieftaincy; Capital: Serowe; Common languages: Setswana; Religion: Traditional Tswana religion and Christianity; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Kgosi; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1611; Disestablished: 23 March 1885; Succeeded by: Bechuanaland Protectorate

name: Larache
label: european enclaves in north africa before 1830
description: Larache, known to Spaniards as Al-Araiche, was a fortified Spanish colonial presidio situated at the mouth of the Loukkos River on the Atlantic coast of northern Morocco. Ceded to King Philip III by the Saadian claimant Muhammad al-Shaykh al-Ma'mun in exchange for military assistance during a Moroccan succession war, the settlement was transformed into a heavily fortified naval citadel. The Spanish garrison patrolled the straits and suppressed Barbary corsair raids along the coast for eight decades until Moroccan imperial forces under Sultan Moulay Ismail successfully liberated the fortress in 1689. \n\n Status: Spanish colonial presidio; Capital: Larache; Common languages: Spanish and Moroccan Arabic; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Islam; Government: Military governorship; Head of state: King of Spain; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1611; Disestablished: 1690; Succeeded by: Alaouite Dynasty

name: Maragheh Khanate
description: The Maragheh Khanate was a semi-autonomous feudal realm situated east of Lake Urmia in the historic Azerbaijan province of north-western Iran. Founded by the Moqaddam tribe under the patronage of Safavid Shah Abbas I, the hereditary khans governed the fertile agricultural basin and orchards of Maragheh while paying nominal allegiance to the Persian throne. The khanate maintained its own regional cavalry levies and civil administration, exercising substantial local autonomy throughout the turbulent transitions between the Safavid, Afsharid, Zand and early Qajar dynasties until centralised provincial governance was reinstated in 1814. \n\n Status: Semi-autonomous khanate; Capital: Maragheh; Common languages: Azerbaijani Turkic and Persian; Religion: Twelver Shia Islam; Government: Hereditary khanate; Ruling dynasty: Moqaddam; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1611; Disestablished: 1814; Preceded by: Safavid Empire

name: East India Company
description: The East India Company was an English, and later British, chartered corporation that exercised expansive territorial, administrative and military rule across the Indian subcontinent. Commencing territorial operations with its early factories at Surat and Madras and ultimately ruling from fortified administrative capitals at Bombay and Calcutta, the company maintained massive private armies that eclipsed contemporary European state forces. Through military conquests, diplomatic subsidiary alliances and commercial taxation, the company governed hundreds of millions of subjects until the Indian Rebellion of 1857 prompted the British Crown to assume direct rule in 1858. \n\n Status: Chartered corporate rule; Capital: Calcutta and Bombay; Official languages: English and Persian; Common languages: Hindi, Urdu, Bengali, Marathi and Tamil; Religion: Christianity, Hinduism and Islam; Government: Corporate colonial administration; Head of state: Governor-General; Established: 1612; Disestablished: 2 August 1858; Succeeded by: British Raj

name: Equinoctial France
description: Equinoctial France was an ambitious seventeenth-century French colonial settlement established in the Bay of São Marcos along the northern coast of Brazil. Founded on 8 September 1612 by an expedition under Daniel de La Touche, Seigneur de la Ravardière, the colony established the fortified settlement of Saint-Louis in honour of King Louis XIII. Intended to open equatorial South America to French commerce and secure alliances with local Tupinambá warriors, the settlement was fiercely contested by Portuguese military forces from Pernambuco, who besieged and compelled the French to capitulate in late 1615. \n\n Status: French colony; Capital: São Luís; Official languages: French; Common languages: French and Tupí; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Head of state: Louis XIII; Representative title: Governor; Established: 8 September 1612; Disestablished: 1616; Succeeded by: Colonial Brazil

name: Georgian Rebels
description: Georgian Rebels designated the autonomous insurgent administrations established across eastern Georgia during fierce armed uprisings against Safavid Persian domination. Led by King Teimuraz I of Kakheti and King Luarsab II of Kartli, the rebel coalitions mobilised highland Georgian clans, local nobility and Orthodox clergy from mobile mountainous redoubts without establishing a permanent administrative seat. The insurrectionary movement fiercely resisted punitive Persian invasions and forced deportations orchestrated by Shah Abbas I, maintaining guerrilla warfare until coordinated imperial offensives temporarily suppressed regional resistance. \n\n Status: Insurrectionary sovereign state; Administrative seat: Mobile rebel encampment; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Georgian; Religion: Georgian Orthodoxy; Government: Insurgent monarchy; Ruler title: King; Head of state: Teimuraz I; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1613; Disestablished: 1 April 1614

name: Duchy of Savoy (Military Occupation)
description: The Duchy of Savoy Military Occupation encompassed frontline combat theatres and garrisoned fortresses occupied by Savoyard ducal forces within the neighbouring Duchy of Montferrat. Sparked by dynastic inheritance disputes following the death of Duke Francesco IV Gonzaga in 1612, Duke Charles Emmanuel I invaded the region, stationing military garrisons across cities like Alba and Moncalvo without instituting a civilian capital. These martial occupations served as strategic territorial bargaining chips against Spanish and imperial Habsburg armies until negotiated diplomatic treaties enforced Savoyard troop withdrawals. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Mobile field command; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Piedmontese, Italian and French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military administration; Head of state: Duke of Savoy; Historical era: War of the Montferrat Succession; Established: 1 May 1613; Disestablished: 21 June 1615

name: Hirado Trading Post
description: The Hirado Trading Post was an English commercial factory established by the British East India Company on Hirado Island off north-western Kyushu, Japan. Founded in July 1613 by Captain John Saris aboard the Clove with the personal diplomatic assistance of William Adams, the post operated under commercial privileges granted by Shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu. Managed by the merchant factor Richard Cocks, the enterprise sought to trade English broadcloth, spices and lead for silver, but persistent financial losses and intense Dutch rivalry prompted the company to close the trading post in 1623. \n\n Status: British trading factory; Capital: Hirado; Common languages: English and Japanese; Religion: Church of England; Government: Commercial factory administration; Head of state: James I; Representative title: Chief Factor; Historical era: Edo period; Established: 1 July 1613; Disestablished: 1624

name: Surguja State
description: Surguja State was an autonomous princely realm situated across the densely forested and mountainous plateau of modern-day northern Chhattisgarh in central India. Governed by the Raksel Rajput dynasty from their administrative seat at Ambikapur, the state maintained authority over a diverse population comprising Gond, Oraon, Munda and Korwa indigenous communities. The Maharajas preserved their regional autonomy and protected remote upland valleys against imperial encroachment through guerrilla warfare and diplomatic payments until signing a subsidiary treaty with the British East India Company in 1819. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Ambikapur; Common languages: Chhattisgarhi, Surgujia and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism and indigenous animism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Raksel Rajput; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1614; Disestablished: 1819

name: Marquisate of Spigno
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Spigno was an autonomous imperial fief of the Holy Roman Empire nestled in the Bormida valley between Piedmont and Liguria. Held originally by the Del Carretto dynasty and later transferred to noble families including the Asinari and Invrea, the state was administered from the fortified castle of Spigno Monferrato. The rulers held direct imperial immediacy, operating local judicial tribunals and levying transit tolls along strategic mountain passes until territorial consolidations culminated in its cession to the House of Savoy in the early eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Imperial fief of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Spigno Monferrato; Common languages: Piedmontese, Ligurian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: Del Carretto and Asinari; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 5 January 1614; Disestablished: 1724

name: New Netherland
description: New Netherland was a seventeenth-century colonial province of the Dutch Republic established along the Atlantic coast and navigable river systems of eastern North America. Administered by the Dutch West India Company from its administrative seat at New Amsterdam on Manhattan Island, the colony encompassed dynamic fur-trading factories and cosmopolitan farming patroonships spanning the Hudson, Delaware and Connecticut river valleys. Under director-generals including Peter Stuyvesant, the colony prospered through transatlantic maritime trade until English naval expeditions seized New Amsterdam in 1664, transforming the settlement into New York. \n\n Status: Dutch company colony; Capital: New Amsterdam; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch, English, Munsee Delaware and French; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Proprietary governorship; Representative title: Director-General; Currency: Guilder and wampum; Established: 1615; Disestablished: 27 August 1664; Succeeded by: Province of New York

name: Sultanate of Dar Sila
description: The Sultanate of Dar Sila was an independent Islamic monarchy established by the Daju people in the Sahelian borderlands of eastern Chad and western Sudan. Headquartered at Goz Beïda beneath steep granitic hills, the sultanate commanded vital trans-Sahelian trade routes and managed pasture lands supporting large herds of cattle and camels. Guided by hereditary sultans who blended Islamic jurisprudence with ancient Daju customary laws, Dar Sila defended its territorial integrity against powerful neighbours such as Ouaddai and Darfur until French colonial forces subdued the realm in 1917. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Goz Beïda; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Sila Daju and Chadian Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sultanate; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1615; Disestablished: 1917; Succeeded by: French Chad

name: Kingdom of Konta
description: The Kingdom of Konta was an independent Omotic-speaking monarchical realm situated in the rugged highlands of south-western Ethiopia near Mount Damota. Governed from its royal capital at Ameya by a hereditary monarch titled the kati, the kingdom developed a centralised state apparatus characterised by formal royal court etiquette, intensive terraced agriculture and regional tribute collection. Konta retained its distinct cultural traditions and political independence against neighbouring Omotic and Cushitic realms until imperial Ethiopian armies under Emperor Menelik II conquered the kingdom in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ameya; Common languages: Kontatsuwa; Religion: Traditional Omotic religion and Ethiopian Orthodoxy; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Kati; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1616; Disestablished: 1890; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Dirk Hartog Island
description: Dirk Hartog Island was a nominal Dutch territorial landing site and maritime landmark located off the Gascoyne coast of Western Australia within Shark Bay. First recorded on 25 October 1616 by the Dutch sea captain Dirk Hartog aboard the Eendracht, the site was commemorated by leaving an inscribed pewter plate nailed to an oak post at Cape Inscription. The Dutch East India Company charted the surrounding waters as Eendrachtsland, treating the uninhabited windswept island as an important navigational landfall along the Brouwer route without attempting permanent colonial settlement. \n\n Status: Dutch maritime landing claim; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Dutch; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Maritime territorial claim; Head of state: States General of the Netherlands; Historical era: Age of Discovery; Established: 25 October 1616; Disestablished: 28 March 1772

name: Dutch Guiana
description: Dutch Guiana encompassed a cluster of chartered plantation colonies and riverine trading outposts established by the Dutch West India Company along the Wild Coast of north-eastern South America. Centred administratively upon Paramaribo in Surinam and fortified redoubts along the Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice rivers, the colony established a profitable agrarian economy based on sugar cane, coffee, cocoa and enslaved African labour. The colonies withstood repeated naval incursions by British and French squadrons until nineteenth-century diplomatic treaties partitioned the territory between British Guiana and Dutch Suriname. \n\n Status: Dutch company colony; Capital: Paramaribo; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch, Sranan Tongo and Arawak; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Colonial governorship; Representative title: Governor; Currency: Dutch guilder; Established: 1617; Disestablished: 1804

name: Dutch Suratte
description: Dutch Suratte was a commercial directorate of the Dutch East India Company established in the bustling port city of Surat in north-western India. Operating under trading farmans granted by the Mughal emperor, the Dutch company constructed a fortified factory and extensive warehouse complex along the Tapti River. The factory served as a critical nexus for procuring indigo, fine Gujarati cotton piece goods and silk for export to European and Southeast Asian markets until regional political upheavals and British commercial supremacy eclipsed Dutch influence in the mid-eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Dutch company directorate; Capital: Suratte; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch, Gujarati and Persian; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church and Islam; Government: Commercial directorate; Representative title: Director; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1617; Disestablished: 1745; Succeeded by: British India

name: Gorée
description: Gorée was a strategic Dutch fortified island colony situated in the Bay of Dakar off the Cap-Vert peninsula in modern-day Senegal. Acquired by the Dutch West India Company from local Lebou leaders in 1617, the island was fortified with two defensive strongholds named Fort Nassau and Fort Orange. The enclave functioned as a pivotal Atlantic naval revictualling base and commercial depot for the purchase of gum arabic, gold, beeswax and enslaved persons until protracted Anglo-Dutch and Franco-Dutch wars culminated in its capture by French naval forces in 1677. \n\n Status: Dutch colonial enclave; Capital: Goree; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch and Wolof; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Military governorship; Head of state: States General of the Netherlands; Representative title: Commander; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1617; Disestablished: 1 November 1677; Succeeded by: French Senegal

name: Great Jin
description: The Great Jin, also designated in historiography as the Later Jin, was an imperial Jurchen khanate established in Manchuria by the Jianzhou chieftain Nurhaci. Uniting the disparate Jurchen tribes under the martial Eight Banners system, Nurhaci declared independence from the Ming Empire in 1616 and established royal capitals successively at Hetu Ala, Liaoyang and Shenyang. The state expanded rapidly across the Liao River basin, conquering Liaodong and subordinating eastern Mongol tribes until Nurhaci's successor Hong Taiji renamed the ruling house to Great Qing in 1636. \n\n Status: Sovereign khanate; Capital: Shenyang; Official languages: Manchu; Common languages: Manchu, Mongolian and Chinese; Religion: Shamanism, Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Aisin-Gioro; Ruler title: Khan; Established: 1617; Disestablished: 1 May 1636; Succeeded by: Qing Dynasty

name: Kingdom of Kandy (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Kandy Military Occupation designated frontline operational zones and coastal territories briefly held under martial administration by the royal army of Kandy on the island of Sri Lanka. During major counter-offensives against European coastal colonisers, Kandyan forces swept down from the central mountain highlands to capture lowland fortresses and surrounding rural districts without instituting permanent municipal governance. These frontline occupations operated as forward military encampments and blockades, holding strategic positions until colonial counter-attacks or treaty stipulations restored previous boundaries. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Mobile royal field command; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Sinhala; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Military administration; Head of state: King of Kandy; Historical era: Kandyan Wars; Established: 1617; Disestablished: 1 February 1617

name: Nikapitiya's Rebels
description: Nikapitiya's Rebels was a widespread anti-Portuguese insurrectionary movement that erupted across the Seven Korales region of western Sri Lanka in late 1616. Led by a charismatic pretender who assumed the royal identity of Prince Nikapitiya Bandara of the defunct Sitawaka monarchy, the rebellion mobilised thousands of Sinhalese fighters determined to expel Portuguese garrisons and restore native sovereignty. The rebel leadership established mobile encampments and coordinated regional ambushes for nearly a year until seasoned Portuguese colonial troops under Constantino de Sá de Noronha launched decisive punitive offensives that crushed the uprising. \n\n Status: Insurrectionary state; Administrative seat: Mobile military command; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Sinhala; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Insurgent monarchy; Ruler title: Pretender Prince; Head of state: Nikapitiya Bandara; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1617; Disestablished: 1 October 1617

name: Kingdom of Kandy
description: The Kingdom of Kandy operated under a temporary protectorate treaty with the Portuguese Crown between 1617 and 1638 following decades of devastating coastal warfare across Sri Lanka. Concluded by King Senarat to secure a necessary breathing space for his highland realm, the peace treaty required Kandy to pay annual tribute in elephants, recognise nominal Portuguese suzerainty and grant trade concessions while preserving domestic Sinhalese autonomy in the central mountains. However, persistent Portuguese territorial incursions and mutual distrust eventually prompted King Rajasinha II to ally with the Dutch East India Company, expelling the Portuguese. \n\n Status: Portuguese protectorate; Capital: Kandy; Official languages: Sinhala; Common languages: Sinhala and Portuguese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy under tributary treaty; Ruling dynasty: Dinajara; Ruler title: King; Head of state: Senarat; Established: 17 August 1617; Disestablished: 23 May 1638

name: Directorate of the Bohemian Estates
description: The Directorate of the Bohemian Estates was a provisional revolutionary government formed by the Protestant nobility of Bohemia following the Defenestration of Prague on 23 May 1618. Headquartered in Prague and led by Count Jindřich Matyáš Thurn, the body comprised thirty elected directors drawn equally from the estates of the lords, knights and royal towns. The Directorate repudiated Habsburg authority, raised a confederate army and conducted international diplomacy across Protestant Europe until the estates formally adopted the Bohemian Confederation constitution and elected Frederick V of the Palatinate as king in 1619. \n\n Status: Revolutionary provisional government; Capital: Prague; Official languages: Czech, German and Latin; Common languages: Czech and German; Religion: Utraquism, Calvinism and Lutheranism; Government: Confederal directorate; Head of state: Board of Directors; Historical era: Thirty Years' War; Established: 23 May 1618; Disestablished: 31 July 1619; Succeeded by: Bohemian Confederation

name: Brandenburg-Prussia
label: holy roman empire
description: Brandenburg-Prussia was a powerful early modern composite state created through the personal union of the Hohenzollern Margraviate of Brandenburg and the Baltic Duchy of Prussia following the death of Duke Albert Frederick in 1618. Governed from the electoral residence in Berlin, the realm encompassed geographically disparate territories extending from the Rhineland through central Germany to East Prussia. Under the transformative leadership of Frederick William, the Great Elector, Brandenburg-Prussia centralised its state finances, constructed a formidable standing army and established sovereignty outside imperial jurisdiction, culminating in the proclamation of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701. \n\n Status: Personal union of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Berlin; Largest city: Berlin and Königsberg; Official languages: German; Common languages: German and Polish; Religion: Calvinism and Lutheranism; Government: Composite feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenzollern; Ruler title: Elector and Duke; Established: 1619; Disestablished: 18 January 1701; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Prussia

name: Brandenburg-Prussia
description: Brandenburg-Prussia emerged as a composite early modern state following the personal union between the Margraviate of Brandenburg and the Duchy of Prussia under the Hohenzollern dynasty. Governed from Berlin and Königsberg, the realm encompassed disconnected territories stretching from the Lower Rhine across northern Germany to the Baltic littoral. Despite suffering catastrophic devastation during the Thirty Years' War, the electorate expanded its territorial footprint and military administrative apparatus, laying the foundations for its elevation into the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701. \n\n Status: Personal union; Capital: Königsberg; Common languages: German and Polish; Religion: Lutheranism and Calvinism; Government: Composite feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenzollern; Ruler title: Elector and Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Prussia

name: Prussia (Military Occupation)
description: Prussia (Military Occupation) designated operational wartime commands and temporary occupation administrations established by the Hohenzollern military beyond the realm's established frontiers. These emergency garrisons functioned during various European campaigns, including the Thirty Years' War, the Silesian Wars and the Austro-Prussian War, securing logistical lines and collecting wartime contributions. Field commanders administered martial jurisdiction until civilian control was restored or permanent annexations were confirmed by international treaties. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile field command; Common languages: German; Government: Military administration; Ruler title: Elector-Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Central Europe

name: Bohemian Confederation
description: The Bohemian Confederation was a short-lived aristocratic state formed in Prague by Protestant nobles of the Czech lands in opposition to the Catholic Habsburg monarchy. Embracing Bohemia, Moravia, Silesia and Lusatia, the confederates elected Frederick V of the Palatinate as king and mounted fierce resistance against Imperial authority. The rebel government collapsed rapidly after suffering a decisive defeat at the Battle of White Mountain in November 1620, prompting intense imperial re-Catholicisation throughout the realm. \n\n Status: Insurgent confederation; Capital: Prague; Common languages: Czech and German; Religion: Utraquism, Lutheranism and Calvinism; Government: Elective confederal monarchy; Head of state: Frederick V; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Lands of the Bohemian Crown

name: Colony of Nevis
description: The Colony of Nevis was an English settlement established in the Leeward Islands of the eastern Caribbean following royal colonisation patents granted during the reign of James I. Centred at Charlestown, the island developed a plantation economy initially dependent on indentured servants and later sustained by enslaved African labourers producing sugarcane. The settlement maintained its own local legislature and civil administration until being amalgamated administratively with neighbouring Saint Christopher in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Charlestown; Official languages: English; Religion: Anglicanism; Government: Colonial administration; Legislature: Nevis Island Assembly; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Saint Christopher and Nevis

name: Electorate of Saxony (Military Occupation)
label: holy roman empire
description: Electorate of Saxony (Military Occupation) encompassed regions held under martial control by Saxon armies during the initial phases of the Bohemian Revolt and Thirty Years' War. Mobilised by the Albertine Wettin elector John George I, Saxon forces occupied Upper and Lower Lusatia to suppress rebel resistance on behalf of Emperor Ferdinand II. The occupational regime maintained garrisons and levied taxes until the territories were officially ceded to Saxony under the Peace of Prague in 1635. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile military administration; Common languages: German and Sorbian; Religion: Lutheranism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Military command; Ruler title: Prince-Elector; Historical era: Thirty Years' War; Succeeded by: Electorate of Saxony

name: Colony of New Plymouth
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Colony of New Plymouth was the earliest permanent English settlement in New England, founded around Massachusetts Bay by Puritan Separatists arriving on the Mayflower. Governed under the Mayflower Compact and early agreements with the local Wampanoag sachem Massasoit, the settlement expanded across southeastern Massachusetts while maintaining autonomous institutions and agriculture. Rising friction culminated in the devastating King Philip's War, after which the financially weakened colony was absorbed into the newly created Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691. \n\n Status: Self-governing colony; Capital: Plymouth; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Wampanoag; Religion: Congregational Puritanism; Government: Chartered assembly; Legislature: General Court; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Province of Massachusetts Bay

name: Bima Sultanate
description: The Bima Sultanate was an influential maritime Islamic state controlling eastern Sumbawa and neighbouring islets across the Indonesian archipelago. Elevated into a sultanate under Sultan Abdul Kahir in the early seventeenth century, the polity adopted Islamic jurisprudence and fostered close political, cultural and trading ties with the Makassar kingdom of Gowa. Its coastal capital at Bima grew into a vibrant hub for the regional trade in horses, sappanwood and agricultural produce before formal Dutch suzerainty arrived. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Bima; Official languages: Bima; Common languages: Bima and Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1621

name: Danish India
description: Danish India comprised a network of fortified coastal trading enclaves established across the Indian subcontinent by the Danish East India Company. Governed from Fort Dansborg at Tranquebar on the Coromandel Coast and later Serampore in Bengal, the colonies prospered by navigating intra-Asian commerce under neutral shipping flags during European maritime conflicts. Although operating on modest resources compared to rival European empires, these posts endured for over two centuries before their eventual sale to the British Crown in the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Commercial colony; Capital: Tranquebar; Official languages: Danish; Common languages: Danish, Tamil and Bengali; Religion: Lutheranism and Hinduism; Government: Colonial governorship; Currency: Danish Indian rupee; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: British Raj

name: Denkyira
label: akan states
description: Denkyira was a powerful Akan kingdom in the southwestern interior of the Gold Coast that dominated regional trade routes between the forest zones and coastal European trading posts. Ruled from the opulent capital at Abankeseso by the Denkyirahene, the state subjugated neighbouring polities through superior arms and extensive gold mining revenues. Its regional supremacy ended dramatically at the turn of the eighteenth century following a decisive military defeat by the rising Ashanti confederacy at the Battle of Feyiase. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Abankeseso; Common languages: Twi; Religion: Akan traditional religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Denkyirahene; Currency: Gold dust and cowrie shells; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Ashanti Empire

name: Kasanje Kingdom
description: The Kasanje Kingdom was a prominent central African state established in the upper Kwango River basin by Imbangala warriors under the leadership of Kinguri. Known in Portuguese accounts as the Jaga Kingdom, the realm became an indispensable commercial intermediary linking inland trade networks with coastal slave markets at Luanda. Elective monarchs drawn from rival founding clans preserved state independence through skilled military organisation and diplomacy until Portuguese colonial conquest dissolved the monarchy in the early twentieth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kasanje; Common languages: Kimbundu and Imbangala; Religion: Traditional religion; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: Kinguri; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1621; Succeeded by: Portuguese Angola

name: Kingdom of Aja
description: The Kingdom of Aja, known historically as Little Ardra and later as Porto-Novo, was an influential coastal monarchy founded on the Bight of Benin by Aja migrants following dynastic partitions within Allada. Centred on its capital at Ajatche, the polity developed into a bustling Atlantic maritime port trading extensively with Portuguese and French merchant fleets. The kingdom carefully maintained its political autonomy against aggressive inland pressures from neighbouring Dahomey until accepting formal French protectorate status in 1863. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Porto-Novo; Common languages: Aja and Yoruba; Religion: Vodun and traditional beliefs; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: French Dahomey

name: Mbwila
description: Mbwila was a rugged highland principality in the Dembos region of northern Angola, commanding the strategic transit gap between the kingdoms of Kongo and Ndongo. Coerced into signing an act of vassalage with the Portuguese colonial administration at Luanda in 1620, the local ruler, known as the Ndembu, adroitly exploited regional rivalries to preserve practical autonomy. The territory remained a volatile frontier flashpoint, ultimately serving as the battleground for the famous 1665 clash that decimated the Kongo monarchy. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Mbwila; Common languages: Kimbundu and Kikongo; Religion: Traditional beliefs and Roman Catholicism; Government: Chieftaincy under suzerainty; Ruler title: Ndembu; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Portuguese Angola

name: Rajkot State
description: Rajkot State was a Rajput princely state established in the Halar region of the Kathiawar peninsula in western India by Thakur Vibhaji Ajoji of the Jadeja dynasty. Centred along the banks of the Aji River, the state consolidated its administrative territory amid shifts in regional hegemony between the Mughal Empire and the Marathas. Its rulers maintained defensive independence through local alliances and tribute arrangements until entering into subsidiary alliance arrangements with the British East India Company during the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Rajkot; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jadeja Rajput; Ruler title: Thakur Sahib; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1621

name: Saraikela State
description: Saraikela State was a princely principality founded in the Chota Nagpur plateau along the Kharkai River by Bikram Singh, a younger son of the ruler of Porahat. Governed by the Rathore Rajput dynasty, the forest state developed a strong feudal administration that subjugated neighbouring tribal areas while preserving regional autonomy against surrounding powers. It fostered distinctive Odia cultural traditions, including the celebrated Seraikela Chhau masked dance, before eventually being brought into subsidiary contact with the British East India Company. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Saraikela; Common languages: Odia; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Singh Deo; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1621

name: Trincomalee
description: Trincomalee was an ephemeral colonial enclave on the eastern coast of Ceylon claimed briefly by an expeditionary fleet sent by King Christian IV of Denmark-Norway. Commanded by Ove Gjedde, the Danish East India Company landed in late 1620, negotiated local treaties with the Kingdom of Kandy, and attempted to erect defensive fortifications overlooking the natural deep-water harbour. Hampered by sickness and aggressive Portuguese pressure, the Danish contingent evacuated the peninsula within weeks to concentrate colonial ventures on the Coromandel Coast. \n\n Status: Colonial trading post; Capital: Trincomalee; Official languages: Danish; Common languages: Danish, Tamil and Sinhala; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Colonial military post; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Portuguese Ceylon

name: Wankaner State
description: Wankaner State was a princely kingdom established in the rugged hill tracts of the Kathiawar peninsula in western India by Sartanji of the Jhala Rajput dynasty. Established following the fragmentation of the older Jhalavad kingdom, the realm fortified its capital on the Machchhu River and defended its territories against incursions from neighbouring sultanates and Maratha raiding parties. Its rulers governed autonomously for almost two centuries before entering into treaty arrangements with the British East India Company in the early nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Wankaner; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jhala Rajput; Ruler title: Maharana Raj Saheb; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1621

name: Kingdom of Spain and Archduchy of Austria (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Spain and Archduchy of Austria (Military Occupation) designated a joint Habsburg martial command created during the opening stages of the Thirty Years' War in northern Italy and the Alpine valleys. Allied imperial and Spanish garrisons occupied strategic strongpoints across the Valtellina and surrounding territories to safeguard the Spanish Road connecting Milan to the German battlefields. The shared occupation functioned as a wartime military sector until formal diplomacy and subsequent campaigns altered control over the crucial mountain passes. \n\n Status: Joint military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile Habsburg command; Common languages: Spanish, German and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Allied military administration; Historical era: Thirty Years' War; Historical region: Alpine Italy

name: Duchy of Guastalla
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Guastalla was a compact northern Italian state situated along the southern bank of the Po River in the historical Emilia region. Elevated from a county into an imperial duchy by Emperor Ferdinand II in 1621, it was ruled by a cadet branch of the House of Gonzaga. Its strategic location between Mantua, Parma and Modena repeatedly exposed the duchy to sieges and foreign occupations during European dynastic conflicts, until the ruling Gonzaga line died out in the eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign duchy; Capital: Guastalla; Official languages: Italian; Common languages: Emilian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Gonzaga; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period

name: Duchy of Mecklenburg-Güstrow
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Mecklenburg-Güstrow was an imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in northern Germany along the southwestern Baltic littoral. Governed by the House of Mecklenburg from their ducal seat at Güstrow, the state emerged from recurring dynastic partitions of the wider Mecklenburg patrimony. The duchy endured major turmoil during the Thirty Years' War, including temporary expulsion by imperial forces under Wallenstein, before regaining its sovereignty until the Güstrow ducal line became extinct in 1695. \n\n Status: Imperial duchy; Capital: Güstrow; Common languages: German and Low German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Mecklenburg; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Duchy of Mecklenburg; Succeeded by: Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin

name: Ota
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Ota was a prominent precolonial Awori Yoruba kingdom established in southwestern Nigeria, situated strategically between the Yoruba heartland and coastal Atlantic trade hubs. Led by the Olota of Ota, the monarchy maintained fortified settlements that guarded key agricultural and trading paths against rival kingdoms such as Dahomey and Egba. The kingdom preserved its distinct local institutions and rich ceremonial traditions, resisting external expansion until the rapid extension of British colonial authority across Yorubaland in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Ota; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Yoruba traditional religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Olota of Ota; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Yorubaland; Succeeded by: Southern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Province of Maine
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Province of Maine was an early English proprietary colony established along the rugged northeastern coast of North America between the Merrimack and Kennebec rivers. Founded under royal patents issued to Sir Ferdinando Gorges and John Mason, the province fostered dispersed maritime settlements engaged in fishing, timber harvesting and fur trading. The colony faced chronic administrative instability and frontier warfare, which ultimately led to its absorption into the jurisdiction of the neighbouring Massachusetts Bay Colony during the late seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Proprietary colony; Capital: York; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Abenaki; Religion: Anglicanism and Puritanism; Government: Proprietary governorship; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Massachusetts Bay Colony

name: Catholic League
description: The Catholic League was a formidable military and political confederation of Catholic states of the Holy Roman Empire, established in 1609 under the leadership of Duke Maximilian I of Bavaria. During the Thirty Years' War, its unified army, commanded by Johann Tserclaes of Tilly, operated as an autonomous sovereign force, occupying extensive swathes of the Rhineland and the Electoral Palatinate. The league enforced Catholic ecclesiastical claims across central Germany until its military and political structures were dissolved by imperial peace accords. \n\n Status: Military confederation; Administrative seat: Munich; Common languages: German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Confederal military council; Head of state: Maximilian I; Historical era: Thirty Years' War; Disestablished: 1635

name: Pescadores
description: Pescadores was a short-lived maritime colonial outpost established on the Penghu archipelago in the Taiwan Strait by the Dutch East India Company. In 1622, Dutch forces seized the islands to construct a fortified trading base capable of disrupting Portuguese and Spanish shipping while coercing Ming China into commercial concessions. Ming authorities responded with an overwhelming naval and military blockade in 1624, forcing the company to dismantle its fortifications and withdraw its operations eastward to southwestern Formosa. \n\n Status: Dutch trading outpost; Capital: Magong; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch and Hokkien; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Military commercial governorship; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Ming dynasty

name: Wessagusset Colony
label: thirteen colonies
description: Wessagusset Colony was an ill-fated early English trading settlement founded at present-day Weymouth, Massachusetts, by Thomas Weston and a cohort of independent London merchants. Intended as a purely commercial venture without family households or religious organisation, the colony suffered from severe food shortages, mismanagement and mounting friction with local Massachusett leaders. Following a preemptive armed strike by Myles Standish and Plymouth forces against indigenous groups, the settlement fragmented, with survivors scattering to Plymouth or returning to England. \n\n Status: Chartered commercial colony; Capital: Weymouth; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Massachusett; Religion: Church of England; Government: Proprietary administration; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Plymouth Colony

name: Colony of Saint Christopher
description: The Colony of Saint Christopher was the earliest successful English colonial establishment in the Caribbean, founded in 1624 under the leadership of Sir Thomas Warner. Sharing the island uneasy with French settlers, the English colonists cleared land for tobacco and subsequent sugar plantations while violently dispossessing the indigenous Kalinago population. Despite enduring repeated French assaults and changes of sovereignty during intercolonial wars, the settlement remained a cornerstone of British plantation authority in the Leeward Islands. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Basseterre; Official languages: English; Religion: Anglicanism; Government: Colonial administration; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Saint Christopher and Nevis

name: Principality of Hohenzollern-Haigerloch
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Hohenzollern-Haigerloch was a compact imperial state in southwestern Germany, created through the partition of the ancestral County of Zollern among the Swabian Hohenzollerns. Governed from its hillside castle at Haigerloch, the Catholic principality maintained imperial immediacy within the Swabian Circle while preserving modest local self-rule. Plagued by dynastic extinctions on multiple occasions, the small territory reverted to the senior lines of Hohenzollern-Hechingen and Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, ultimately being permanently incorporated into Sigmaringen in 1767. \n\n Status: Imperial principality; Capital: Haigerloch; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenzollern; Ruler title: Count and Prince; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen

name: Principality of Hohenzollern-Hechingen
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine;german confederation
description: The Principality of Hohenzollern-Hechingen was a sovereign principality situated in the Swabian Jura of southwestern Germany, ruled by the senior Catholic branch of the House of Hohenzollern. Elevated to princely rank in 1623, the state preserved its constitutional independence within the Holy Roman Empire, the Confederation of the Rhine and the German Confederation. Confronted with political upheaval during the Revolutions of 1848 and mounting administrative debt, Prince Constantine abdicated his sovereignty, ceding the territory to the Kingdom of Prussia in 1850. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Hechingen; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Semi-constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenzollern-Hechingen; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early modern to modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Prussia

name: Principality of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine;german confederation
description: The Principality of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was an autonomous state along the upper Danube in southwestern Germany, governed by the Catholic junior branch of the Swabian Hohenzollerns. Raised to princely status during the Thirty Years' War, the principality expanded its territory through dynastic inheritances, including the acquisition of neighbouring Haigerloch. After navigating membership in the Confederation of the Rhine and the German Confederation, the reigning prince surrendered sovereign rights to the Prussian Crown in 1850 following revolutionary unrest. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Sigmaringen; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early modern to modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Prussia

name: Dutch Formosa
description: Dutch Formosa was a colonial dominion established across southwestern Taiwan by the Dutch East India Company to anchor trans-Asian commerce with China and Japan. Centred on Fort Zeelandia and Fort Provintia, the colonial administration developed deer-skin exports, commercial sugar cultivation and taxation systems, often suppressing uprisings among indigenous Austronesian and migrant Han Chinese populations. Dutch rule in Formosa collapsed following a prolonged siege by Ming loyalist forces led by Koxinga, who expelled the company to establish the Kingdom of Tungning. \n\n Status: Colony; Capital: Fort Zeelandia; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch, Hokkien and Formosan languages; Religion: Dutch Reformed Protestantism; Government: Colonial governorship; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Tungning

name: Republic of Salé
description: The Republic of Salé, also styled the Bou Regreg Republic, was an autonomous maritime corsair state established at the mouth of the Bou Regreg river on the Atlantic coast of Morocco. Founded by expelled Andalusian Moriscos from Hornachos alongside European renegades and Barbary privateers, the community elected its own diwan and military commanders. The republic amassed immense wealth through extensive privateering and slave trading across the Atlantic and Mediterranean until being subjugated by the ascendant Alawi dynasty in 1668. \n\n Status: Corsair republic; Capital: Salé; Common languages: Arabic, Spanish and Berber; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Oligarchic republic; Ruler title: Governor and Grand Admiral; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Alawi Sultanate

name: Ihangiro
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Ihangiro was an ancient Bantu kingdom situated in the western Victoria basin in present-day northwestern Tanzania, forming part of the historical Haya cultural realm. Governed by a hereditary Omukama belonging to the Ruhinda dynasty, the state possessed sophisticated agrarian terracing, cattle pastoralism and indigenous iron-smelting traditions. The kingdom defended its political autonomy against neighbouring Great Lakes powers such as Karagwe and Buganda before being incorporated into the imperial sphere of German East Africa in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ihangiro (Kagera); Common languages: Haya; Religion: Traditional religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ruhinda; Ruler title: Omukama; Historical era: Precolonial; Historical region: African Great Lakes

name: Kingdom of Kombo
description: The Kingdom of Kombo was a precolonial Mandinka state situated on the southern bank of the Gambia River near the Atlantic coast. Emerging from the decentralisation of the Kaabu and Mali empires, the kingdom was ruled by hereditary mansas alternating between the prominent Jatta and Bojang clans. The realm controlled fertile agrarian lands and coastal trade routes connecting the interior with European riverine merchants, retaining its independence until sectarian turmoil during the Soninke-Marabout wars destabilised the monarchy in the mid-nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Yundum; Common languages: Mandinka; Religion: Traditional religion and Islam; Government: Traditional elective monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jatta and Bojang; Ruler title: Mansa; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: British Gambia

name: Kuba Kingdom
description: The Kuba Kingdom was a flourishing Central African confederal realm established between the Kasai, Sankuru and Lulua rivers in the southern Congo basin. Reorganised in the early seventeenth century by the cultural hero Shyaam a-Mbul a Ngoong, the monarchy comprised over nineteen ethnic groups led by the Bushong royal elite. Governed by the Nyim from the royal capital at Nsheng, the kingdom was renowned for its intricate textile weaving, woodcarving and aristocratic council governance, enduring until colonial subjugation by the Congo Free State. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nsheng; Official languages: Bushong; Common languages: Bushong and Kuba; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Confederal monarchy; Ruler title: Nyim; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Congo Free State

name: Raigarh State
description: Raigarh State was a princely kingdom established in the fertile valley of the Kelo River in eastern central India, within modern Chhattisgarh. Founded by a branch of the Gond Kshatriya dynasty, the state maintained a resilient feudal organisation based on fortified hill strongholds and agrarian revenues. The royal family sustained independence against Maratha dominance from the Bhonsle rulers of Nagpur, eventually establishing formal diplomatic and administrative ties with the British East India Company during the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Raigarh; Common languages: Chhattisgarhi and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gond; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1625

name: Saint Croix
description: Saint Croix was a contested Caribbean island colony whose fertile coastal plains attracted early seventeenth-century English, Dutch and French settlers. In 1625, English colonists established fortified settlements on the island, initially sharing authority before ousting their European competitors to establish exclusive English dominion. The English garrison maintained plantations and local defences until being expelled by a Spanish expeditionary force from Puerto Rico in 1650, after which sovereignty transitioned to French and later Danish colonial authorities. \n\n Status: Colony; Capital: Christiansted; Official languages: English; Common languages: English, Dutch and French; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Spanish West Indies

name: Tortuga
description: Tortuga was a mountainous island enclave situated off the northwestern coast of Hispaniola, jointly settled and administered as a condominium by French and English colonists. Operating from the natural harbour at Basse-Terre, the settlement became an infamous base for buccaneers, indentured runaways and privateers raiding Spanish Caribbean shipping lanes. The dual administration witnessed recurrent Spanish counter-attacks and internal jurisdictional rivalries between English and French governors before France established definitive unilateral control over the island in the mid-seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Condominium colony; Capital: Basse-Terre; Common languages: French and English; Religion: Catholicism and Protestantism; Government: Joint colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Spanish Empire; Succeeded by: Saint-Domingue

name: Datia State
description: Datia State was a Bundela Rajput princely state situated in the northwestern reaches of the Bundelkhand region of central India. Founded in 1626 by Rao Bhagwan Rao, a son of the ruler of Orchha, the principality developed as an autonomous power renowned for its distinctive palace architecture and military traditions. Datia successfully protected its borders against neighbouring Maratha encroachers and Mughal governors, retaining sovereign independence until signing a treaty of subsidiary alliance with the British East India Company in 1804. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Datia; Common languages: Bundeli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bundela Rajput; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1626

name: Dir State
description: Dir State was an autonomous tribal principality situated along the Panjkora River valley in the rugged northwestern frontier between South Asia and eastern Afghanistan. Founded in the seventeenth century by the spiritual leader Akhund Baba, also known as Mulla Ilyas Khan, the state was ruled by the Painda Khel clan of the Pashtun Yusufzai tribe. The khans maintained fierce regional independence against surrounding warlords and Sikh incursions, preserving customary Pashtun law until entering subsidiary relations with British India. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Dir; Official languages: Pashto; Common languages: Pashto; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1626

name: Guadeloupe
description: Guadeloupe was a French Caribbean island colony established across the butterfly-shaped archipelago of Basse-Terre and Grande-Terre in the Lesser Antilles. Initial settlement began under the auspices of the Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique, whose expeditions displaced surviving indigenous Kalinago populations and established permanent fortifications at Basse-Terre. The settlement expanded through the introduction of indentured European labour and enslaved Africans, developing an agricultural export economy centred on tobacco, indigo and sugar under French royal chartered administration. \n\n Status: Chartered colony; Capital: Basse-Terre; Official languages: French; Common languages: French and Antillean Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Colonial period; Preceded by: Kalinago

name: Kingdom of Bhutan
description: The Kingdom of Bhutan was a unified Himalayan theocracy consolidated in the early seventeenth century by the Tibetan religious leader Ngawang Namgyal, who assumed the title of Zhabdrung Rinpoche. Uniting fragmented mountain valleys under the Drukpa Kagyu lineage of Vajrayana Buddhism, the state erected fortified dzongs that functioned as administrative and spiritual citadels. Bhutan successfully repelled repeated Tibetan and Mongol invasions, establishing a dual system of government shared between the Druk Desi for secular administration and the Je Khenpo for ecclesiastical affairs. \n\n Status: Sovereign theocracy; Capital: Thimphu; Official languages: Dzongkha; Common languages: Dzongkha and Choekey; Religion: Vajrayana Buddhism; Government: Dual system of government; Head of state: Zhabdrung Rinpoche; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1626

name: Spanish Formosa
description: Spanish Formosa was a short-lived military and missionary colony established by the Spanish East Indies on the northern tip of Taiwan. Centred on Fort San Salvador at Keelung and Fort Santo Domingo at Tamsui, the settlement aimed to safeguard Spanish trade galleons traversing between Manila and Japan against rival Dutch privateering. Faced with hostility from indigenous tribes, devastating typhoons and declining strategic interest from authorities in Manila, the garrison was besieged and forced to surrender to the Dutch East India Company in 1642. \n\n Status: Military colony; Capital: Keelung; Official languages: Spanish; Common languages: Spanish, Hokkien and Formosan languages; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military governorship; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Age of Discovery; Succeeded by: Dutch Formosa

name: Great Jin (Military Occupation)
description: Great Jin (Military Occupation) designated the military operational zone established by Jurchen forces under Amin during the first Manchu invasion of the Joseon kingdom in early 1627. Crossing the Yalu River, the Later Jin expeditionary army rapidly overwhelmed Korean frontier garrisons, capturing Anju and Pyongyang while pushing the Joseon royal court to seek refuge on Ganghwa Island. The occupational command extracted formal tributary concessions and peace oaths from the Korean court before withdrawing its forces back into southern Manchuria. \n\n Status: Wartime military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile expeditionary command; Common languages: Jurchen and Korean; Religion: Shamanism and Buddhism; Government: Military command; Ruler title: Beile; Historical era: Ming-Qing transition; Succeeded by: Joseon Kingdom

name: Colony of Barbados
description: The Colony of Barbados was an English settlement established in the Lesser Antilles following early proprietary land claims made in the name of King James I. Centred at Bridgetown, the colony quickly evolved from tobacco and cotton farming into the wealthiest sugar plantation society in the seventeenth-century English Atlantic. Sustained by brutal systems of African chattel slavery and governed by its own House of Assembly, Barbados remained a central anchor of British imperial authority until gaining independence in 1966. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Bridgetown; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Bajan Creole; Religion: Anglicanism; Government: Colonial administration; Legislature: House of Assembly; Historical era: Colonial period; Established: 1627; Succeeded by: Barbados

name: Dutch Bengal
description: Dutch Bengal was a prominent trading directorate of the Dutch East India Company established along the Hooghly River in Mughal Bengal. Headquartered at Fort Gustavus in Chinsurah, the directorate coordinated lucrative commercial networks exporting raw silk, saltpetre, opium and fine textiles to Batavia and European markets. Despite intense mercantile competition from English and French companies and shifting fortunes during the Anglo-Dutch wars, Dutch operations persisted until the remaining factories were ceded to the British Crown under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824. \n\n Status: Trading directorate; Capital: Chinsurah; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch and Bengali; Religion: Protestantism and Hinduism; Government: Commercial directorate; Representative title: Director; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: British India
