name: Sawantwadi State
description: Sawantwadi State was an autonomous Maratha principality situated in the Konkan coastal strip of western India, nestled between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea. Founded by the Sawant Bhonsle dynasty, the state commanded formidable hill fortresses and maintained an independent army and naval force. Its rulers engaged in complex diplomacy, navigating shifting alliances with the Sultanate of Bijapur, the emerging Maratha Empire and Portuguese Goa, while fiercely defending their coastal autonomy prior to British ascendancy. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Sawantwadi; Common languages: Marathi and Konkani; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sawant Bhonsle; Ruler title: Raja Bahadur; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1627

name: Tobago
description: Tobago was a contested Antillean island colony settled by the Dutch West India Company, who founded the fortified settlement of Nieuw Walcheren. Located northeast of Trinidad, the island served as an agricultural base for cultivating tobacco, indigo and sugarcane while offering a strategic maritime anchorage in the southern Caribbean. The Dutch settlement faced repeated assaults from Spanish fleets, Carib war parties and rival English and French expeditions before being surrendered during regional colonial conflicts. \n\n Status: Colony; Capital: Scarborough; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch and Kalinago; Religion: Reformed Protestantism; Government: Colonial governorship; Representative title: Commander; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Kingdom of England

name: County of Pappenheim
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Pappenheim was an imperial territory of the Holy Roman Empire located along the Altmühl River in western Bavaria. Held by the hereditary imperial marshals of the empire, the House of Pappenheim exercised immediate sovereignty over its castles, market towns and agrarian holdings. Despite widespread military turmoil during the Thirty Years' War, under commanders such as Gottfried Heinrich zu Pappenheim, the county retained its distinct imperial status until its mediatisation into the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Pappenheim; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Pappenheim; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bavaria

name: Nogai Horde and Crimean Khanate (Military Occupation)
description: The Nogai Horde and Crimean Khanate (Military Occupation) designated coordinated nomadic equestrian campaign theatres across the Pontic steppe and the frontier provinces of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Mobilised for swift seasonal incursions, combined Tatar and Nogai cavalry forces established temporary martial control over rural river valleys to secure captive labour, levy tribute and disrupt Cossack garrisons. These mobile raiding operations avoided sedentary urban governance, dissolving back into the Crimean and Bucak steppe upon concluding their tactical missions. \n\n Status: Joint military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile cavalry command; Common languages: Crimean Tatar and Nogai; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military raiding confederation; Ruler title: Khan and Mirzo; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Pontic-Caspian steppe

name: Sultanate of Morocco
description: The Sultanate of Morocco was a sovereign Islamic empire consolidated in the seventeenth century by the sharifian Alawi dynasty following the fragmentation of Saadi rule. Governed through a mobile imperial court shifting between Fez, Meknes and Marrakesh, the sultanate successfully safeguarded Moroccan independence against Ottoman expansion and European naval incursions. The state maintained extensive trans-Saharan caravan routes and reformed its military apparatus, preserving its territorial sovereignty until being partitioned into French and Spanish protectorates in 1912. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Fez; Administrative seat: Mobile imperial court; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Arabic and Berber; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Alawi dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern to modern; Succeeded by: French Protectorate in Morocco

name: Swedish Livonia
description: Swedish Livonia was a prosperous Baltic dominion acquired by the Swedish Empire following military victories over Poland-Lithuania, formally ratified by the Truce of Altmark. Comprising northern Latvia and southern Estonia, the province was governed from the fortified commercial metropolis of Riga, the second largest city in the Swedish realm. Under Swedish administration, radical agrarian and administrative reforms curtailed Baltic German noble privileges and alleviated serfdom, until the province was ceded to the Russian Empire in 1721 following the Great Northern War. \n\n Status: Baltic dominion; Capital: Riga; Official languages: Swedish and German; Common languages: Latvian, Estonian and Low German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Governor-generalship; Ruler title: King of Sweden; Representative title: Governor-General; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Riga Governorate

name: Ganden Phodrang (Military Occupation)
description: Ganden Phodrang (Military Occupation) encompassed operational frontier zones temporarily placed under martial authority by Tibetan military forces during regional conflicts in the Himalayas and eastern Kham. Coordinated by central monastic officials and allied Mongol regiments, these expeditionary garrisons secured strategic mountain passes, defended Gelug monasteries against rival sects and repelled incursions from Bhutan. The occupational administration enforced emergency fiscal levies and troop billets until peace agreements restored normal regional monastic and secular governance. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile army headquarters; Common languages: Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Theocratic military command; Ruler title: Desi; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Himalayas and Kham

name: Kingdom of Mutapa
description: The Kingdom of Mutapa was a historically celebrated Shona empire on the northern Zimbabwean plateau that entered a period of formal vassalage to the Portuguese Crown during the seventeenth century. Ruled by the Mwenemutapa from the royal court at Zvongombe, the monarchy traded in gold, ivory and agricultural goods along the Zambezi River. Despite substantial Portuguese missionary and mercantile interference, the kingdom preserved its indigenous spiritual institutions until a resurgence by the neighbouring Rozvi Empire drove Portuguese influence out of the plateau. \n\n Status: Protectorate; Capital: Zvongombe; Common languages: Shona; Religion: Shona traditional religion and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mutapa; Ruler title: Mwenemutapa; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Rozvi Empire

name: Nova Scotia
description: Nova Scotia was an early Scottish colonial venture established on the maritime peninsula of eastern Canada under a royal charter granted by King James VI and I to Sir William Alexander. Headquartered at the abandoned French outpost of Port-Royal, named Charles Fort by the settlers, the colony sought to build a permanent New Scotland engaged in fishing, timbering and the fur trade. The nascent Scottish settlement was dismantled in 1632 when King Charles I restored the territory to France under the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye. \n\n Status: Proprietary colony; Capital: Port-Royal; Official languages: Scots and English; Common languages: Scots, English and Mi'kmaq; Religion: Presbyterianism and Anglicanism; Government: Proprietary administration; Ruler title: Lieutenant Governor; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Acadia

name: Province of New Hampshire
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Province of New Hampshire was an English colonial realm established between the Merrimack and Piscataqua rivers on the northeastern coast of North America. Originating from proprietary land patents granted to Captain John Mason, the settlement grew around timber milling, coastal fishing and agricultural trade at Portsmouth. The province experienced periodic jurisdictional incorporation into neighbouring Massachusetts before becoming a distinct royal colony in 1679, ultimately renouncing British authority in 1776 to become one of the founding United States. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Portsmouth; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Abenaki; Religion: Congregationalism and Anglicanism; Government: Royal governorship; Legislature: General Court of New Hampshire; Currency: New Hampshire pound; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: New Hampshire

name: Shahpura State
description: Shahpura State was a Rajput princely state established in central Rajasthan by Sujan Singh, a scion of the Sisodia royal house of Mewar. Endowed with autonomous land grants by the Mughal emperor, the ruler governed from the fortified town of Shahpura, maintaining a delicate double allegiance to both the Sisodia Maharana of Udaipur and the imperial Mughal throne. The state developed refined painting traditions and resilient administrative structures, successfully preserving its territorial integrity through centuries of Maratha instability before British contact. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Shahpura; Common languages: Rajasthani and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sisodia Rajput; Ruler title: Raja Dhiraj; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1629

name: Anziku Kingdom
description: The Anziku Kingdom, known historically as the Tio or Teke Kingdom, was a powerful central African state established across the Bateke Plateau and the banks of the Pool Malebo. Governed by the Onkoo from the royal seat at Monsol, the realm wielded substantial political influence and maintained a formidable warrior caste renowned for skilled metallurgy and weaving. The kingdom controlled lucrative commercial transit routes linking inland riverine trade with coastal European merchants, until King Makoko signed a protectorate treaty with Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza in 1880. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Monsol; Common languages: Teke; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Onkoo; Historical era: Precolonial to early modern; Historical region: Congo River basin; Succeeded by: French Congo

name: Chartered West India Company
description: The Chartered West India Company was a powerful Dutch mercantile enterprise established under charter from the States General of the Dutch Republic to monopolise trade across the Atlantic basin. Governed from Amsterdam through regional chambers, the company operated fortified enclaves and plantation colonies across the Caribbean, the Guianas, northeastern Brazil and New Netherland. It commanded substantial naval armadas, oversaw extensive transatlantic slave trading and directed privateering campaigns against Iberian shipping, until mounting debts led to its liquidation in 1792. \n\n Status: Chartered commercial company; Capital: Amsterdam; Official languages: Dutch; Religion: Dutch Reformed Protestantism; Government: Board of directors; Currency: Dutch guilder; Historical era: Early modern period; Disestablished: 1792

name: Ibom Kingdom
description: The Ibom Kingdom, also known as the Mbot Abasi Kingdom, was an ancient Ibibio polity situated along the boundary between present-day Abia and Akwa Ibom states in southeastern Nigeria. Governed by the Obong from the royal settlement of Obot Okon Ita, the state cultivated thriving agricultural and trade networks across the Cross River basin. In the mid-seventeenth century, the arrival of migrating Igbo groups and subsequent dynastic competition triggered the prolonged Aro-Ibibio Wars, resulting in the dissolution of the kingdom and the emergence of the Aro Confederacy. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Arochukwu; Common languages: Ibibio and Igbo; Religion: Traditional religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Obong; Historical era: Precolonial; Historical region: Cross River basin; Succeeded by: Aro Confederacy

name: Ise-Ekiti
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Ise-Ekiti was an ancient Yoruba kingdom established in the rugged hills of Ekiti in southwestern Nigeria. Governed by a paramount traditional monarch bearing the title of Arinjale of Ise, the kingdom traced its dynastic heritage to legendary warriors from Ile-Ife and maintained a sophisticated tripartite civic division. The state defended its forested territory and fertile agricultural valleys against invasions from surrounding powers during the turbulent Yoruba civil wars of the nineteenth century, until the imposition of British colonial rule in 1901. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Ise Ekiti; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Yoruba traditional religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Arinjale; Historical era: Precolonial; Historical region: Yorubaland; Succeeded by: Southern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Kalmyk Khanate
label: caucasian khanates
description: The Kalmyk Khanate was a powerful nomadic realm established in the North Caucasus and Lower Volga steppes by Western Torghut Oirat Mongols migrating from Dzungaria. Led by Kho Orluk and later by Ayuka Khan, the khanate deployed formidable cavalry armies that dominated the Eurasian plains between the Don and Ural rivers. While serving as vital military allies for Tsarist Russia against Ottoman and Crimean forces, the khans maintained internal autonomy and Vajrayana Buddhist governance until mass migration and Russian imperial annexation dissolved the state in 1771. \n\n Status: Nomadic khanate; Capital: Astrakhan; Common languages: Kalmyk Oirat and Russian; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Nomadic monarchy; Ruler title: Khan; First ruler: Kho Orluk; Subsequent ruler: Ubashi Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Kingdom of Kaarta
description: The Kingdom of Kaarta was an influential precolonial Bambara monarchy established in western Mali following the decline of the imperial Songhai realm. Founded by the Massassi branch of the Coulibaly dynasty, the state was ruled by the Faama from fortified capitals at Guémou and Nioro du Sahel. Kaarta developed an expansive agricultural and cavalry-based military society that resisted Islamic theocratic expansion from neighbouring states, before being overwhelmed by the jihadist campaign of Umar Tall and the Toucouleur Empire in the mid-nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Guémou; Common languages: Bambara; Religion: Traditional religion and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Massassi Coulibaly; Ruler title: Faama; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Toucouleur Empire

name: Lawksawk State
label: shan states
description: Lawksawk State was an autonomous Shan principality situated in the central uplands of the Southern Shan States of eastern Burma. Ruled by a hereditary Saopha, the state governed several hundred agrarian villages and valuable teak-producing forest valleys. As a loyal tributary vassal of the Burmese Konbaung monarchy, Lawksawk contributed levies to royal military campaigns while maintaining internal judicial, fiscal and customary Shan autonomy, until British imperial forces subjugated the Shan highlands following the Third Anglo-Burmese War. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Lawksawk; Common languages: Shan, Danu and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Massachusetts Bay Colony
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Massachusetts Bay Colony was an English settlement established around Massachusetts Bay by the Massachusetts Bay Company under a royal charter granted by King Charles I. Settled primarily by Puritan emigrants led by John Winthrop, the colony instituted an autonomous, theocratically oriented representative government centred at Boston. The colony grew rapidly through the Great Migration, fostering extensive maritime commerce and founding Harvard College, before its independent charter was revoked and merged into the royal Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691. \n\n Status: Chartered colony; Capital: Boston; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Massachusett; Religion: Congregational Puritanism; Government: Self-governing colonial company; Legislature: Great and General Court; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Province of Massachusetts Bay

name: Saint-Christophe
description: Saint-Christophe was a French colonial holding established on the Caribbean island of Saint Kitts, comprising the northern and southern quarters flanking an English central enclave. Administered from Basseterre by the Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique and subsequently by royal governors, the colony built extensive sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans. Intermittent colonial warfare between French and English garrisons led to repeated sieges, expulsions and temporary occupations, culminating in the permanent cession of the French sectors to Great Britain under the Treaty of Utrecht. \n\n Status: Colony; Capital: Basseterre; Official languages: French; Common languages: French and Antillean Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Colony of Saint Christopher

name: Sultanate of Asahan
description: The Sultanate of Asahan was a coastal Malay state situated along the northeastern littoral of Sumatra, established in the early seventeenth century by Raja Abdul Jalil, a son of Sultan Iskandar Muda of Aceh. Governed from Tanjungbalai, the sultanate functioned as a strategic tributary dependency of Aceh, safeguarding maritime trade routes and riverine forest produce. The state retained its internal Malay Islamic administrative hierarchy and dynastic continuity for nearly two centuries, before eventually asserting greater political autonomy from Aceh in the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Vassal sultanate; Capital: Tanjungbalai; Official languages: Malay; Common languages: Malay and Batak; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1630

name: Wadhwan State
description: Wadhwan State was a Rajput princely state established in the fertile Saurashtra peninsula of Gujarat by the Jhala dynasty following the partition of Jhalavad. Fortified at its riverine capital on the Bhogavo River, the state maintained military readiness against neighbouring Kathi raiders, regional Muslim governors and Maratha tribute collectors. Its rulers preserved territorial sovereignty and patronised traditional Jain and Hindu cultural institutions for nearly two centuries, until accepting British protection under the Walker Settlement of 1807. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Wadhwan; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jhala Rajput; Ruler title: Thakur Sahib; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1630

name: Anguilla
description: Anguilla was a short-lived Dutch colonial outpost established in the northern Leeward Islands by the Dutch West India Company in the early 1630s. The company constructed a modest coastal redoubt to shelter passing trade vessels, gather sea salt and secure a strategic observation post overlooking the Anegada Passage. Confronted with poor water resources, agricultural limitations and hostile Spanish naval patrols from Puerto Rico, the Dutch abandoned the settlement after a few years, leaving the island to subsequent English colonisation. \n\n Status: Colonial trading post; Capital: The Valley; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch; Religion: Reformed Protestantism; Government: Commercial trading post; Historical era: Colonial period; Preceded by: Kalinago; Succeeded by: British Leeward Islands

name: British Gold Coast
description: The British Gold Coast originated with seventeenth-century fortified coastal trading posts established along the Gulf of Guinea by chartered English merchant adventurers. Operating from early strongholds such as Fort Kormantin and Cape Coast Castle, the enterprise traded in gold, ivory and enslaved people before the Crown assumed direct jurisdiction in 1821. Through repeated military campaigns against the Ashanti Empire and northern treaties, the colony expanded inland to absorb all rival European forts, until gaining full independence as Ghana on 6 March 1957. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Cape Coast; Official languages: English; Common languages: English, Akan, Ga and Ewe; Religion: Christianity, Islam and traditional beliefs; Government: Colonial governorship; Legislature: Legislative Council; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Ghana

name: Colony of Sint Maarten
description: The Colony of Sint Maarten was a Dutch colonial territory encompassing the southern portion of the Caribbean island of Saint Martin. Established in 1631 with the erection of Fort Amsterdam, the settlement was briefly captured by Spain before being partitioned peacefully with France under the 1648 Treaty of Concordia. The Dutch administration developed lucrative salt extraction and sugar plantations sustained by enslaved African labourers, maintaining its maritime trading hub at Philipsburg across centuries of intermittent Anglo-French warfare. \n\n Status: Colony; Capital: Philipsburg; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch, English and Papiamento; Religion: Reformed Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Netherlands Antilles

name: County of Gimborn
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Gimborn was a small sovereign state of the Holy Roman Empire located in the Bergisches Land of North Rhine-Westphalia. Centred on Schloss Gimborn in the Leppe valley, the lordship was elevated to an imperial county in 1631 under Count Adam von Schwarzenberg, granting its rulers imperial immediacy and a seat in the Westphalian College of Imperial Counts. The dynasty governed the agrarian territory until selling the domain to the Counts of Wallmoden, after which it was mediatised into the Grand Duchy of Berg in 1806. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Gimborn; Common languages: German and Westphalian; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Schwarzenberg; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Berg

name: Kota State
description: Kota State was a prominent Rajput kingdom situated along the eastern bank of the Chambal River in the fertile Hadoti region of Rajasthan. Created in 1631 when Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan granted an independent principality to Rao Madho Singh of the Hada Chauhan clan, the realm became an important military bulwark and a celebrated centre of Rajasthani miniature painting. The state guarded regional trade routes and defended its autonomy against Maratha incursions under the legendary regent Zalim Singh before entering into a British alliance. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Kota; Common languages: Harauti and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hada Chauhan; Ruler title: Maharao; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1631

name: Province of Maryland
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Province of Maryland was an English proprietary colony established around the Chesapeake Bay following a royal charter granted by King Charles I to Cecilius Calvert, second Baron Baltimore. Intended as a refuge for persecuted English Roman Catholics, the colony instituted the landmark Maryland Toleration Act of 1649, granting unprecedented religious liberty to Christian denominations. The colony's tobacco plantation economy relied heavily on indentured servants and enslaved Africans, retaining proprietary governance until Maryland declared independence during the American Revolution. \n\n Status: Proprietary colony; Capital: St. Mary's City; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Anglicanism; Government: Proprietary governorship; Legislature: General Assembly; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Maryland

name: Antigua
description: Antigua was an English colonial possession in the Leeward Islands settled in 1632 by a party of colonists from Saint Christopher led by Edward Warner. Centred on the harbour town of St. Johns, the colony rapidly transformed from cultivating tobacco and ginger into one of Britain's most profitable sugarcane monocultures. Defended by the naval installations of English Harbour and worked by vast populations of enslaved Africans, Antigua served as the administrative hub for the British Leeward Islands until achieving independence in 1981. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: St. Johns; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Antillean Creole; Religion: Anglicanism and Methodism; Government: Colonial administration; Legislature: Legislative Council; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Antigua and Barbuda

name: Lordship of Wismar
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Wismar was a strategic Baltic maritime enclave situated in Mecklenburg, occupied by Swedish forces in 1632 and formally assigned to the Swedish Crown under the Peace of Westphalia. Serving as one of Sweden's principal continental bridgeheads, the fortified Hanseatic port hosted the Royal Swedish High Court for German lands. Sweden maintained strong military fortifications and exercised fiscal control over the harbour until pawning the city to the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin in 1803, with final sovereignty relinquished in 1903. \n\n Status: Swedish dominion; Capital: Wismar; Common languages: Low German, German and Swedish; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Colonial governorship; Ruler title: King of Sweden; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Mecklenburg-Schwerin

name: Montserrat
description: Montserrat was an English colony in the Leeward Islands established in 1632 by Irish Catholic settlers departing nearby Saint Christopher to escape religious discrimination. Governed from Plymouth, the mountainous island developed an economy founded on indigo and sugar plantations, giving rise to an Irish and African Creole heritage. Despite temporary French occupations during transatlantic wars, the settlement remained under British administration, evolving into an overseas territory whose historic capital was later buried by catastrophic volcanic eruptions in the late twentieth century. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Plymouth; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Montserratian Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Anglicanism; Government: Colonial administration; Legislature: Legislative Assembly; Historical era: Colonial period

name: Sultanate of Deli
description: The Sultanate of Deli was an autonomous Malay state established on the eastern coastal plain of North Sumatra by Tuanku Panglima Gocah Pahlawan, a military commander under Sultan Iskandar Muda of Aceh. Originally governing as an Acehnese tributary, the ruling dynasty asserted sovereign autonomy over fertile agricultural territories along the Deli River. The sultanate maintained its traditional Islamic royal court at Medan, transforming in the nineteenth century into a prosperous global hub for tobacco and rubber plantations before integrating into the Republic of Indonesia. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Medan; Official languages: Malay; Common languages: Malay, Karo and Batak; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern to modern; Succeeded by: Indonesia

name: Arguin
label: european enclaves in north africa before 1830
description: Arguin was a fortified island trading enclave situated in the Bay of Arguin off the Atlantic coast of present-day Mauritania. Seized from the Portuguese in 1633 by the Dutch West India Company, the island served as a heavily defended commercial station for trading gum arabic, gold dust and enslaved Africans with local nomadic Moorish confederations. Surrounded by perilous coastal reefs and contested by French naval squadrons, the outpost witnessed frequent violent changes of European control before the Dutch finally yielded authority to France in 1678. \n\n Status: Colonial trading fort; Capital: Arguin; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch, Hassaniya Arabic and Berber; Religion: Reformed Protestantism; Government: Commercial military garrison; Historical era: Colonial period; Preceded by: Portuguese Empire; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Dzungar Khanate
description: The Dzungar Khanate was a powerful nomadic pastoral empire formed in the Dzungarian Basin of northern Xinjiang by Western Oirat Mongols under Erdeni Batur. Ruled by a supreme Khong Tayiji from the valley of Ghulja, the khanate subjugated the Tarim Basin oasis cities, dominated Tibetan Buddhist politics and challenged the regional supremacy of the Qing Empire. The state commanded disciplined nomadic cavalry forces and indigenous artillery until internal civil wars enabled the Qing Emperor Qianlong to launch devastating campaigns that annihilated the empire in the 1750s. \n\n Status: Nomadic empire; Capital: Ghulja; Common languages: Oirat and Chagatai Turkic; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism and Sunni Islam; Government: Nomadic monarchy; Ruler title: Khong Tayiji; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1634; Succeeded by: Qing dynasty

name: Four Oirats
description: The Four Oirats was an enduring confederal alliance of Western Mongol tribes comprising the Choros, Torghut, Dorbet and Khoshut clans roaming across the Altai Mountains and the Dzungarian steppe. Governed through customary tribal councils under the Mongol-Oirat Code, the confederacy maintained pastoral nomadism without establishing a permanent urban capital. The alliance frequently rivalled Eastern Khalkha Mongols and Ming China for supremacy over the Eurasian interior, eventually splintering in the seventeenth century as factions migrated toward the Volga or consolidated into the Dzungar Khanate. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Oirat; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism and Shamanism; Government: Pastoral tribal council; Ruler title: Taishi; Legislature: Mongol-Oirat Code; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Dzungar Khanate

name: Gondal State
description: Gondal State was an autonomous Hindu princely state situated in the Kathiawar peninsula of Gujarat, established in 1634 by Kumbhoji I of the Jadeja Rajput dynasty. Centred on the fortified town of Gondal, the principality expanded through military campaigns and matrimonial alliances, asserting independence from Mughal and regional Muslim governors. Its rulers maintained disciplined agrarian administration and fortified hill strongholds, preserving sovereignty against Maratha incursions until entering into the British subsidiary alliance system in the early nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Gondal; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jadeja Rajput; Ruler title: Thakur Sahib; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1634

name: Khotogoid Khanate
description: The Khotogoid Khanate was a northern Khalkha Mongol principality established in northwestern Mongolia between Uvs Lake and the Delgermörön river. Governed by the Altan Khans of the Khotogoid, also styled Khong Tayiji, the state exercised hegemony over the Yenisei Kirghiz and repelled Western Oirat incursions into the Altai region. Despite acting as an assertive regional power in diplomatic communications with Tsarist Russia, escalating conflict with the neighbouring Zasagtu Khan fractured the confederation, causing its reabsorption into the Khalkha tribal hierarchy. \n\n Status: Nomadic principality; Capital: Urga; Common languages: Khalkha Mongolian; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Nomadic monarchy; Ruler title: Altan Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Zasagtu Khan Aimag

name: Company of the American Islands
description: The Company of the American Islands was a French royal chartered enterprise founded by Cardinal Richelieu to manage and expand French colonisation across the West Indies. Succeeding the earlier Compagnie de Saint-Christophe, the proprietary company oversaw the colonisation of Guadeloupe, Martinique, Saint Lucia and Tortuga. Charged with developing sugar, tobacco and indigo agriculture while converting indigenous populations to Roman Catholicism, the enterprise faced chronic fiscal difficulties and colonial insubordination, leading to the sale of its islands to private proprietors before royal absorption under Colbert. \n\n Status: Chartered proprietary company; Administrative seat: Paris; Official languages: French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Commercial board of directors; Ruler title: Governor-General; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: French West India Company

name: Saybrook Colony
label: thirteen colonies
description: Saybrook Colony was a short-lived English Puritan settlement established at the mouth of the Connecticut River under the authority of the Warwick Patent. Founded by prominent Parliamentary puritan noblemen, including Lord Saye and Sele and Lord Brooke, the colony was commanded by John Winthrop the Younger and Lion Gardiner. Its heavily fortified outpost, Fort Saybrook, played a crucial defensive role during the Pequot War, but lacking proprietary immigration and commercial momentum, the settlement was sold to the Connecticut Colony in 1644. \n\n Status: Proprietary colony; Capital: Old Saybrook; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Quiripi; Religion: Puritanism; Government: Proprietary administration; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Connecticut Colony

name: Sonepur State
description: Sonepur State was a princely kingdom situated along the Mahanadi and Tel rivers in western Odisha, founded in the seventeenth century by Madhukar Deo of the Chauhan Rajput dynasty of Sambalpur. Governed from the riverine capital of Sonepur, the state developed productive rice agriculture, handloom weaving and riverine trade networks. Its rulers maintained territorial autonomy against surrounding forest kingdoms and successfully repelled Maratha raids from Nagpur, preserving independence until entering formal diplomatic and tributary relations with the British East India Company. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Sonepur; Common languages: Odia and Sambalpuri; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chauhan Rajput; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1650

name: Wadai Empire
description: The Wadai Empire was a powerful Muslim sultanate situated east of Lake Chad in present-day Chad, founded in the early seventeenth century by Abd al-Karim after overthrowing the ruling Tunjur dynasty. Governed by the Kolak from his fortified mountain capital at Ouara and later Abéché, the empire developed a formidable cavalry army that conquered extensive tributary territories in Dar Sila and Kanem. Wadai dominated trans-Saharan trade routes exporting ivory, ostrich feathers and captives until French colonial forces conquered the realm in 1912. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Abéché; Common languages: Maba and Chadian Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic monarchy; Ruler title: Kolak; Historical era: Early modern to modern; Succeeded by: French Equatorial Africa

name: Colony of Connecticut
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Colony of Connecticut was an English settlement founded in the fertile Connecticut River valley by Puritan congregations migrating from Massachusetts Bay under the leadership of Thomas Hooker. In 1639, the settlers adopted the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut, widely recognised as an early written democratic constitution that established a representative general court. After securing regional hegemony through the Pequot War and absorbing the neighbouring New Haven and Saybrook colonies, Connecticut received a liberal royal charter in 1662 and maintained self-governance until the American Revolution. \n\n Status: Self-governing colony; Capital: Hartford; Official languages: English; Common languages: English, Mohegan and Quiripi; Religion: Congregational Puritanism; Government: Chartered representative assembly; Legislature: General Court; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Connecticut

name: Colony of Sint Eustatius
description: The Colony of Sint Eustatius was a prominent Caribbean island holding of the Dutch West India Company, situated in the northern Leeward Islands. Centred on Fort Oranje and the port of Oranjestad, the island developed into one of the Atlantic world's busiest free-trade entrepôts, earning the moniker the Golden Rock. Its merchants facilitated neutral arms shipments to the American Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War, precipitating a devastating punitive British capture and sacking led by Admiral George Rodney in 1781. \n\n Status: Colony; Capital: Oranjestad; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch and English; Religion: Reformed Protestantism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Colonial period; Established: 1636; Succeeded by: Netherlands Antilles

name: Great Qing
description: Great Qing was a vast early modern empire founded in Manchuria by the Aisin Gioro clan when Hong Taiji transformed the Later Jin into an imperial dynasty in 1636. Capturing Beijing in 1644 following the collapse of the Ming dynasty, the Manchu Eight Banners conquered China proper and subsequently extended imperial frontiers across Mongolia, Tibet, Central Asia and Taiwan. Governed through a dual Manchu-Chinese bureaucratic system, the empire reached unprecedented demographic and territorial peaks before collapsing during the Xinhai Revolution of 1911. \n\n Status: Imperial dynasty; Capital: Beijing; Official languages: Manchu and Mandarin Chinese; Common languages: Chinese, Mongolian, Tibetan and Uyghur; Religion: Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Aisin Gioro; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Early modern to modern; Succeeded by: Republic of China

name: Aruba
description: Aruba was an arid Caribbean island colony seized from the Spanish Crown in 1636 by the Dutch West India Company during the Eighty Years' War. Situated in the southern Caribbean off the coast of Venezuela, the island was utilised primarily for horse and cattle ranching and wood harvesting rather than large-scale sugarcane plantations. The indigenous Caquetio population retained substantial demographic presence and cultural influence, contributing to the development of Papiamento alongside colonial Dutch authorities before the island entered the Netherlands Antilles in 1954. \n\n Status: Colony; Capital: Oranjestad; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Papiamento, Dutch and Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Reformed Protestantism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Netherlands Antilles

name: Kingdom of Spain and Holy Roman Empire (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Spain and Holy Roman Empire (Military Occupation) designated an aggressive combined Habsburg offensive command operating across northern France during the autumn of 1636. Commanded jointly by the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand of Spain, Johann von Werth and Ottavio Piccolomini, Habsburg forces crossed the Somme, captured the fortress of Corbie and posed an immediate strategic threat to Paris. The occupation maintained strict martial requisitioning across Picardy before being repelled by French royal counter-offensives and forced to retreat toward the Spanish Netherlands. \n\n Status: Joint military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile Habsburg command; Common languages: Spanish, German and French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Allied military command; Historical era: Thirty Years' War; Historical region: Picardy

name: Dejima Trading Post
description: The Dejima Trading Post was an artificial fan-shaped island constructed in Nagasaki harbour by the Tokugawa shogunate to segregate Portuguese merchants from the broader Japanese population. Built to curb Catholic proselytisation while preserving lucrative trade in Chinese silk, gold and regional goods, the enclave was subject to strict surveillance by Tokugawa magistrates. Following the Shimabara Rebellion, the shogunate enacted national isolation edicts, expelling all Portuguese traders from Dejima in 1639 and transferring the trading post exclusively to the Dutch East India Company. \n\n Status: Commercial trading enclave; Capital: Nagasaki; Official languages: Portuguese; Common languages: Portuguese and Japanese; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Merchant factory; Ruler title: Factor; Historical era: Edo period; Succeeded by: Dutch East India Company

name: Providence Plantations
label: thirteen colonies
description: Providence Plantations was an early English colonial refuge founded at the head of Narragansett Bay by the dissenting Puritan theologian Roger Williams following his banishment from Massachusetts Bay. Established on land purchased from the Narragansett sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi, the settlement pioneered absolute liberty of religious conscience and the separation of church and civil government. Governed by democratic town compacts, the community formed the political core of the colony, eventually receiving a comprehensive royal charter from King Charles II in 1663. \n\n Status: Self-governing colony; Capital: Providence; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Narragansett; Religion: Baptist and religious freedom; Government: Democratic town meeting; Head of state: Roger Williams; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations

name: Samka State
label: shan states
description: Samka State was a small Shan principality situated in the southern highlands of the Shan plateau, located south of Inle Lake in eastern Burma. Ruled by a hereditary Saopha, the polity governed agrarian communities situated in a fertile river valley surrounded by steep forested mountains. The principality rendered regular tributary payments and military contingents to the Burmese royal court at Ava and Mandalay, maintaining its traditional Shan customary governance until being incorporated into British Burma in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Samka; Common languages: Shan, Intha and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Mongpan State
label: shan states
description: Mongpan State was an upland Shan principality situated in the eastern Southern Shan States along the Salween River basin in Burma. Governed by a Saopha from its central valley capital at Mong Pan, the territory encompassed valuable teak forests, fertile paddy fields and rugged mountain ridges. As an autonomous tributary state under the Burmese Konbaung monarchy, Mongpan defended its border districts against neighbouring Siamese and Karenni raiding forces until accepting British administrative oversight following the annexation of Upper Burma. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Mong Pan; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: New Courland
description: New Courland was an ambitious colonial enterprise established on the Caribbean island of Tobago by the Baltic Duchy of Courland and Semigallia under Duke Jacob Kettler. Centred on Fort Jacob at Great Courland Bay, Couronian settlers, soldiers and Lutheran pastors founded plantations to cultivate sugarcane, tobacco and ginger. The fledgling Baltic colony suffered severe supply shortages and contested jurisdiction with neighbouring Dutch settlements, ultimately collapsing when Duke Jacob was captured during the Second Northern War in Europe. \n\n Status: Baltic colony; Capital: Fort Jacob; Official languages: German and Latvian; Common languages: German, Latvian and Dutch; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Colonial governorship; Ruler title: Duke of Courland; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Dutch West India Company

name: Pocasset
label: thirteen colonies
description: Pocasset was an early English settlement established on the northern end of Aquidneck Island in Narragansett Bay by religious exiles led by Anne Hutchinson, William Coddington and John Clarke. Following their expulsion from the Massachusetts Bay Colony during the Antinomian Controversy, the settlers drew up the Portsmouth Compact in 1638, creating a civil body politic founded on Christian conscience. Renamed Portsmouth shortly thereafter, the community united with neighbouring Providence, Newport and Warwick under the parliamentary charter and 1663 royal charter of Rhode Island. \n\n Status: Self-governing settlement; Capital: Portsmouth; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Narragansett; Religion: Puritan Antinomianism and Baptist; Government: Democratic civil covenant; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations

name: Valtellina
description: Valtellina was an autonomous Alpine valley territory in northern Lombardy that briefly asserted sovereign independence under the leadership of the Graubünden rebel leader Jürg Jenatsch. Commanding the vital mountain transit passes of the Spanish Road between Habsburg Milan and the Austrian Tyrol, the valley had been violently contested by Spanish, French and Grison armies during the Thirty Years' War. Jenatsch switched allegiances from France to the Catholic Habsburgs, mobilising a local insurrection in 1637 that temporarily secured autonomous self-rule before the valley returned to Three Leagues sovereignty under Spanish treaty terms. \n\n Status: Autonomous valley state; Capital: Sondrio; Common languages: Lombard and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military council; Head of state: Jürg Jenatsch; Historical era: Thirty Years' War; Succeeded by: Three Leagues

name: New Haven Colony
label: thirteen colonies
description: New Haven Colony was an autonomous English settlement established along Long Island Sound by strict Puritan migrants led by the Reverend John Davenport and the merchant Theophilus Eaton. Governed under the Fundamental Agreement of New Haven, the colony restricted political voting and magistracy solely to church members, aiming to build an exemplary mercantile and theological commonwealth. Hampered by the loss of its commercial fleet and lacking a formal royal charter, the financially vulnerable colony was reluctantly absorbed into the expanding Connecticut Colony in 1664. \n\n Status: Self-governing colony; Capital: New Haven; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Quinnipiac; Religion: Strict Congregational Puritanism; Government: Theocratic magistracy; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Colony of Connecticut

name: Dutch Ceylon
description: Dutch Ceylon was an important colonial governorate established across the maritime coasts of Sri Lanka by the Dutch East India Company following alliances with the Kingdom of Kandy to expel the Portuguese. Administered initially from Galle and later from Colombo, the company secured a lucrative international monopoly over the island's cinnamon trade and coastal pearl fisheries. The Dutch instituted Roman-Dutch law and constructed extensive canal networks, preserving coastal rule until British forces captured the colony during the French Revolutionary Wars. \n\n Status: Colonial governorate; Capital: Galle; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch, Sinhala and Tamil; Religion: Reformed Protestantism, Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Colonial governorship; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: British Ceylon

name: British Honduras
description: British Honduras originated with seventeenth-century English buccaneers and woodcutters, known as the Baymen, who established logging camps along the Caribbean coast of Central America to harvest logwood and mahogany. Despite frequent Spanish military attempts to expel the settlers, the inhabitants successfully defended their enclaves, most famously at the Battle of Saint George's Caye in 1798. Officially declared a British Crown colony in 1862, the territory maintained distinct Creole institutions at Belize City until securing internal self-government and adopting the name Belize. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Belize City; Official languages: English; Common languages: English, Belizean Creole and Spanish; Religion: Anglicanism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Belize

name: Mauritius
description: Mauritius was an Indian Ocean island colony established by the Dutch East India Company, who named the territory in honour of Prince Maurice of Nassau. Operating from Fort Frederik Hendrik at Grand Port, the company attempted to harvest ebony forests, introduce sugarcane and breed cattle while providing a vital resupply station for merchant vessels sailing to Batavia. Beset by severe cyclones, droughts, rodent infestations and slave rebellions, the Dutch definitively abandoned the settlement in 1710, leaving the island to subsequent French colonisation. \n\n Status: Commercial colony; Capital: Grand Port; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch and Malagasy; Religion: Reformed Protestantism; Government: Colonial governorship; Representative title: Commander; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Isle de France

name: Mosquito Kingdom
description: The Mosquito Kingdom was an independent indigenous monarchy established along the Caribbean littoral of present-day Nicaragua and eastern Honduras by the Miskito people. Under King Oldman and his successors, the kingdom forged a vital maritime alliance with English privateers and British authorities from Jamaica, providing naval support and timber in exchange for firearms. The realm retained formidable military and political autonomy against Spanish imperial incursions, preserving its traditional kingship and coastal hegemony through dynamic cross-cultural diplomacy until formal British protectorate arrangements evolved. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bluefields; Common languages: Miskito, English and Miskito Creole; Religion: Traditional beliefs and Anglicanism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1638

name: New Sweden
description: New Sweden was an early overseas colonial holding established by the Swedish South Company along the lower Delaware River in North America. Centred on Fort Christina at modern Wilmington, the colony was settled by Swedish and Finnish pioneers who introduced log cabin construction and maintained friendly commercial relations with the local Lenape and Susquehannock nations. The colony traded in tobacco and beaver pelts until 1655, when Dutch Director-General Peter Stuyvesant arrived with an overwhelming military fleet, peacefully absorbing the territory into New Netherland. \n\n Status: Colony; Capital: Wilmington; Official languages: Swedish; Common languages: Swedish, Finnish and Lenape; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Colonial governorship; Ruler title: Queen of Sweden; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: New Netherland

name: Santa Apolónia
description: Santa Apolónia was the historical name applied by early European navigators and the initial French colonial administration to the volcanic island of Réunion in the southwestern Indian Ocean. In 1638, French naval expeditions claimed the uninhabited island for King Louis XIII, establishing a preliminary maritime station and penal outpost along the bay of Saint-Paul. The territory was formally integrated into royal overseas domains and rechristened Île Bourbon in 1649, subsequently transforming into a prosperous plantation colony under the French East India Company. \n\n Status: Colonial outpost; Capital: Saint-Paul; Official languages: French; Common languages: French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Royal colonial claim; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Uninhabited; Succeeded by: Île Bourbon

name: Newport
label: thirteen colonies
description: Newport was an English colonial settlement founded on the southern shore of Aquidneck Island in Narragansett Bay by William Coddington, John Clarke and other religious dissidents from Portsmouth. Boasting a deep and sheltered maritime harbour, the town rapidly emerged as a thriving commercial centre engaged in coastal shipping, shipbuilding and agricultural trade. Dedicated to religious freedom and civil liberty, Newport merged with Portsmouth in 1640 and subsequently joined Providence and Warwick under the parliamentary patent and 1663 royal charter of Rhode Island. \n\n Status: Self-governing colony; Capital: Newport; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Narragansett; Religion: Baptist and religious freedom; Government: Democratic civil covenant; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations

name: Colony of Saba
description: The Colony of Saba was a small Dutch Caribbean settlement established on a sheer volcanic island in the northern Leeward Islands by colonists sent from Sint Eustatius by the Dutch West India Company. Governed from the secluded highland basin known as The Bottom, the settlers engaged in subsistence farming, fishing and boatbuilding in a rugged environment lacking natural harbours. The island experienced intermittent captures by English privateers during European maritime conflicts before permanently stabilising as a loyal dependency of the Dutch Crown. \n\n Status: Colony; Capital: The Bottom; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch and English; Religion: Reformed Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Netherlands Antilles

name: Baghal State
description: Baghal State was a hill princely state situated in the Himalayan foothills of Solan, in present-day Himachal Pradesh, founded by Rana Aje De of the Panwar Rajput clan. Governed from the fortified palace at Arki, the state commanded strategic overland trading routes connecting the Punjab plains with upper Shimla and Tibet. The principality defended its mountainous borders against rival hill raiders and survived brief Gorkha occupation during the early nineteenth century, retaining internal autonomy until acceding to the Indian Union in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Arki; Common languages: Pahari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Panwar Rajput; Ruler title: Rana; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1640

name: Ceuta
label: european enclaves in north africa before 1830
description: Ceuta was a heavily fortified Mediterranean enclave situated on the North African coast directly opposite the Rock of Gibraltar. Originally captured by Portugal in 1415, the garrison and municipal assembly chose to remain loyal to King Philip IV of Spain following the Portuguese Restoration War of 1640. Ceuta functioned as a vital strategic fortress and military outpost, enduring numerous prolonged sieges by Moroccan forces under Sultan Ismail Ibn Sharif before being designated an integral autonomous city of Spain. \n\n Status: Fortress city and military colony; Capital: Ceuta; Official languages: Spanish; Common languages: Spanish and Arabic; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military governorship; Ruler title: King of Spain; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern to modern

name: Duchy of Saxe-Gotha
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Saxe-Gotha was an imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire established in central Thuringia through an Ernestine partition of Saxe-Weimar in 1640. Ruled by Duke Ernest I, known as Ernest the Pious, from Friedenstein Castle in Gotha, the duchy enacted progressive legal codes, rebuilt infrastructure ravaged by the Thirty Years' War and introduced compulsory public schooling. Following Duke Ernest's death and the subsequent inheritance of Saxe-Altenburg, the realm was partitioned among his seven sons, creating several smaller Ernestine duchies. \n\n Status: Imperial duchy; Capital: Villa Gothaha; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Ernestine Wettin; Ruler title: Duke; First ruler: Ernest I; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg

name: Emirate of Trarza
description: The Emirate of Trarza was a powerful nomadic confederation established in southwestern Mauritania along the northern bank of the lower Senegal River by Hassani Arab warriors under the Oulad Ahmed ben Daman. Ruled by an Emir from mobile camps and later Mederdra, the state collected tribute from sedentary Wolof communities and controlled the valuable trans-Saharan trade in gum arabic with European merchants. The emirate retained formidable military independence and Islamic legal administration until French colonial expansion culminated in formal protectorate rule in 1902. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Mederdra; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Hassaniya Arabic, Zenaga and Wolof; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Elective nomadic monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1640

name: Great Xi
description: Great Xi was a short-lived rebel empire established in Sichuan during the Ming-Qing transition by the peasant insurrectionist leader Zhang Xianzhong. Capturing Chengdu in 1644, Zhang proclaimed himself emperor, established imperial bureaucratic offices and minted coinage under the era name Dashun. His regime faced ferocious armed resistance from local Ming loyalist forces and was marked by devastating purges and warfare that severely depopulated Sichuan, before Zhang was killed in battle by invading Manchu Qing armies in early 1647. \n\n Status: Insurgent empire; Capital: Chengdu; Common languages: Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, Buddhism and Daoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Xi dynasty; Ruler title: Emperor; First ruler: Zhang Xianzhong; Historical era: Ming-Qing transition; Succeeded by: Qing dynasty

name: Wahidi Sultanate
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Wahidi Sultanate was a prominent tribal state situated along the Gulf of Aden in the southern Arabian Peninsula, within modern Yemen. Governed from the historic walled commercial town of Habban and the palace at Azzan, the sultanate commanded lucrative incense and coastal trading routes between Aden and the Hadramawt valley. The state retained its political sovereignty under its hereditary sultan until internal dynastic partitions in the late nineteenth century led the fractured branches to accept British protectorate treaties within the Aden Protectorate. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Haban; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: South Arabia; Succeeded by: Aden Protectorate

name: Dejima Factory
description: The Dejima Factory was a restricted commercial trading post operated by the Dutch East India Company on an artificial islet in Nagasaki harbour. Following the expulsion of the Portuguese in 1639, the Tokugawa shogunate transferred Dutch merchants to Dejima in 1641, establishing it as Japan's sole window for European trade and cultural exchange during the isolationist Sakoku period. Operating under constant Japanese surveillance, the factory imported silk, spices and scientific knowledge, known as Rangaku, while exporting copper and silver until Japan opened to international trade in 1858. \n\n Status: Dutch trading post; Capital: Nagasaki; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Dutch and Japanese; Religion: Dutch Reformed Protestantism; Government: Commercial factory; Ruler title: Opperhoofd; Historical era: Edo period; Preceded by: Portuguese Empire; Succeeded by: Empire of Japan

name: Principality of Monaco
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Monaco was a sovereign Mediterranean city-state perched on the rocky coast of the French Riviera, ruled by the House of Grimaldi. In 1641, Prince Honoré II secured recognition of Monaco's sovereign princely status through the Treaty of Péronne, expelling the Spanish garrison and placing the microstate under French royal protection while retaining internal independence. The principality preserved its hereditary monarchy, maritime fortifications and civic institutions, sustaining sovereignty through centuries of European warfare until its temporary annexation during the French Revolution. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Monaco; Official languages: French; Common languages: Monegasque, French, Ligurian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Grimaldi; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early modern period

name: Irish Catholic Confederation
description: The Irish Catholic Confederation was an autonomous confederal state established by Catholic aristocrats, clergy and military leaders in the wake of the 1641 Irish Rebellion. Governed from Kilkenny through a General Assembly and Supreme Council, the confederacy controlled over two-thirds of Ireland during the Eleven Years' War. Minting its own coinage and maintaining diplomatic legations with France and Rome, the confederacy professed nominal loyalty to King Charles I while fighting for religious freedom, until being crushed by the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland. \n\n Status: Insurgent confederation; Capital: Kilkenny; Common languages: Irish and English; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Confederal constitutional monarchy; Legislature: General Assembly; Ruler title: Supreme Council; Historical era: Wars of the Three Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Commonwealth of England

name: Parliamentarians
description: The Parliamentarians, popularly known as Roundheads, were the political and military faction that contested royal absolutism during the English Civil War. Centred in London and controlling the wealthy merchant communities, southeastern ports and the Royal Navy, the Parliamentarian leadership was anchored by prominent Puritan gentry and the Long Parliament. Under military commanders such as Thomas Fairfax and Oliver Cromwell, they established the New Model Army, defeated the Royalist forces of King Charles I, and established the republican Commonwealth of England. \n\n Status: Insurgent republican state; Capital: London; Official languages: English; Common languages: English; Religion: Presbyterianism and Puritanism; Government: Parliamentary republic; Legislature: Long Parliament; Ruler title: Lord General; Historical era: English Civil War; Succeeded by: Commonwealth of England

name: Royalists
description: The Royalists, commonly styled Cavaliers, constituted the loyalist party supporting King Charles I during the English Civil War. Headquartered at the university city of Oxford, the Royalist government assembled a loyal parliament and maintained control over northern and western England, Wales and Cornwall. Backed by traditional landed aristocrats and High Church Anglicans, the Royalist armies waged fierce military campaigns to preserve traditional royal prerogative, before suffering catastrophic defeats at Marston Moor and Naseby that ultimately led to the capture and execution of the king. \n\n Status: Monarchist faction; Capital: Oxford; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Welsh; Religion: Anglicanism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Head of state: Charles I; Ruler title: King; Historical era: English Civil War; Succeeded by: Commonwealth of England

name: Bay Islands
description: The Bay Islands was an English colonial dependency established across the Caribbean archipelago of Roatán, Guanaja and Útila off the northern coast of Honduras. Initially settled by English buccaneers and Puritans from Providence Island in the 1630s, the islands commanded strategic sea routes overlooking Spanish silver fleets departing Central America. Despite recurring Spanish naval attacks and temporary expulsions, British influence persisted through timber cutting and trade with the Miskito Kingdom, culminating in the territory's formal transfer to the Republic of Honduras in 1859. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Coxen Hole; Official languages: English; Common languages: English, Spanish and Garifuna; Religion: Anglicanism and Protestantism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Honduras

name: Gazikumukh Khanate
description: The Gazikumukh Khanate was a sovereign Lak state established in the high mountain valleys of central Dagestan following the disintegration of the Shamkhalate of Gazikumukh in 1642. Governed by a Khan from the ancient fortified fortress town of Kumukh, the khanate united diverse Lak, Lezgin and Avar highland communities. Known for skilled silver craftsmanship, weaponry and formidable mountain cavalry, the state fiercely defended its independence against Persian invasions under Nader Shah, before gradually being integrated into the Russian Empire during the Caucasian War. \n\n Status: Mountain khanate; Capital: Kumukh; Official languages: Lak; Common languages: Lak, Lezgin and Avar; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1642; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Khoshut Khanate
description: The Khoshut Khanate was a Western Mongol Oirat realm established across the Tibetan Plateau and Qinghai in 1642 by Gushi Khan. Intervening in Tibetan sectarian civil wars on behalf of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, Gushi Khan defeated rival princes and established the Fifth Dalai Lama as temporal ruler under the Ganden Phodrang government. The Khoshut khans retained supreme military authority and nomadic patronage over Tibet until their dynasty was extinguished when Dzungar forces invaded Lhasa in 1717. \n\n Status: Nomadic khanate; Capital: Lhasa; Common languages: Oirat and Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Nomadic military protectorate; Ruler title: Khan; First ruler: Gushi Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1642; Succeeded by: Dzungar Khanate

name: Kingdom of Sikkim
description: The Kingdom of Sikkim was an autonomous Himalayan monarchy founded in 1642 when three revered Tibetan lamas consecrated Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal at Yuksom. Governed by the Namgyal dynasty, the kingdom encompassed steep mountain ridges surrounding Mount Kanchenjunga, blending indigenous Lepcha traditions with Tibetan Bhutia culture. The Buddhist state defended its highland sovereignty against recurring incursions from Nepal and Bhutan, maintaining internal self-rule until signing a protectorate treaty with the British Empire in 1861 and eventually acceding to India in 1975. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gangtok; Official languages: Sikkimese and Choekey; Common languages: Bhutia, Lepcha and Nepali; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Namgyal dynasty; Ruler title: Chogyal; First ruler: Phuntsog Namgyal; Historical era: Early modern period

name: Principality of Tabasaran
description: The Principality of Tabasaran was an autonomous monarchical state established in southern Dagestan along the Samur river basin after separating from the Shamkhalate of Gazikumukh in 1642. Governed from the mountain capital of Khuchni under a dual leadership shared between the Ghazi and the Masum, the state commanded vital transit defiles between Derbent and the Shirvan plain. The principality mobilised effective cavalry levies to maintain regional autonomy against Safavid and Ottoman encroachment, enduring until its incorporation into the Russian Empire in 1813. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Khuchni; Common languages: Tabasaran, Lezgin and Azerbaijani; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional diarchy; Ruler title: Ghazi and Masum; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1642; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Shawomet
label: thirteen colonies
description: Shawomet was an early English colonial settlement founded on the western shore of Narragansett Bay by Samuel Gorton and fellow religious dissidents after purchasing land from the Narragansett sachem Miantonomi. Denounced by the authorities of Massachusetts Bay for unorthodox religious opinions, Gorton was arrested and his property ransacked before he sailed to England to secure parliamentary protection. Renamed Warwick in honour of Robert Rich, Earl of Warwick, the settlement defended its independence and merged with Providence, Portsmouth and Newport to create the Colony of Rhode Island. \n\n Status: Self-governing settlement; Capital: Warwick; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Narragansett; Religion: Gortonian Puritanism and religious freedom; Government: Democratic civil covenant; Historical era: Colonial period; Succeeded by: Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations

name: French Guiana
description: French Guiana was a French colonial holding established along the northeastern Atlantic coast of South America between the Oyapock and Maroni rivers. Founded in 1643 by the Compagnie de Rouen with the construction of Fort Cépérou at Cayenne, the nascent colony endured attacks from indigenous Caribs and temporary occupations by Dutch and English expeditionary fleets. French royal authorities revived the settlement with sugarcane, cocoa and coffee plantations worked by enslaved Africans, transforming Cayenne into France's primary continental bridgehead in South America. \n\n Status: Colony; Capital: Cayenne; Official languages: French; Common languages: French, Guianese Creole and indigenous languages; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Colonial period

name: Duchies of Bremen and Verden
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchies of Bremen and Verden were two secularised imperial territories situated between the Elbe and Weser rivers in northern Germany, ceded to the Swedish Crown under the Peace of Westphalia. Administered in personal union from the fortress city of Stade, the duchies formed Sweden's most important continental territory, giving the Swedish monarch seats and voting rights in the imperial Diet. Despite experiencing multiple Danish and Hanoverian wartime occupations, Sweden maintained possession of the territories until finally ceding them to the Electorate of Hanover in 1719. \n\n Status: Swedish imperial dominion; Capital: Stade; Common languages: Low German and German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Principality in personal union; Ruler title: Duke; Representative title: Governor-General; Legislature: Landschaft; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Electorate of Hanover

name: Fort Dauphin
description: Fort Dauphin was the earliest permanent French colonial settlement established in Madagascar, founded in 1643 on the southeastern peninsula of Anosy by the French East India Company. Commanded by Étienne de Flacourt, the colonists erected a palisaded fortress to facilitate trade in cattle, rice and ebony while attempting to spread Roman Catholicism among local Antanosy clans. Strained relations with indigenous rulers, rampant tropical diseases and internal mutinies plagued the outpost, which was abandoned in 1674 after surviving settlers were evacuated following a devastating Antanosy assault. \n\n Status: Colonial trading outpost; Capital: Tolagnaro; Official languages: French; Common languages: French and Malagasy; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Commercial military outpost; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Colonial period; Preceded by: Antanosy; Succeeded by: Anosy kingdom

name: Great Shun
description: Great Shun was an ephemeral Chinese imperial dynasty founded in Xi'an by the charismatic peasant rebellion leader Li Zicheng during the tumultuous Ming-Qing transition. Proclaiming himself the Yongchang Emperor, Li captured the imperial capital of Beijing in April 1644, prompting the suicide of the Chongzhen Emperor and the downfall of the Ming dynasty. Shun rule unraveled within weeks when Ming general Wu Sangui allied with the invading Manchu army, crushing Li's forces at Shanhai Pass and expelling the dynasty back toward central China. \n\n Status: Insurgent dynasty; Capital: Chang'an; Common languages: Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, Buddhism and Daoism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Shun dynasty; Ruler title: Emperor; First ruler: Li Zicheng; Historical era: Ming-Qing transition; Succeeded by: Qing dynasty

name: Babungo
description: Babungo, historically known as Vengo, was an influential precolonial Grassfields kingdom established on the fertile Ndop Plain in present-day northwestern Cameroon. Governed by a hereditary sacred monarch known as the Fon, the kingdom was celebrated throughout the regional trade network as the foremost iron-smelting and artistic woodcarving centre of the western highlands. Babungo defended its agrarian lands and rich metallurgy against regional slave raiders and neighbouring chiefdoms, preserving its sovereign institutions until being subjected to German colonial authority in the early twentieth century. \n\n Status: Traditional fondom; Capital: Babungo; Common languages: Babungo and Vengo; Religion: Traditional religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Precolonial to early modern; Historical region: Cameroon Grassfields; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Dauro
description: Dauro was an autonomous kingdom established in the rugged highlands of south-western Ethiopia, bordered by the Omo and Gojeb river valleys. Governed by dynastic monarchs bearing the title of Kati, the state maintained extensive stone defensive fortifications, celebrated as the Kati Halala walls, to protect against neighbouring expanses and regional rivals. It retained its independence through active trade and agricultural production until its conquest and integration by the Ethiopian Empire during the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Dawro and Omotic languages; Religion: Traditional Omotic religion and Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Kati; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Southwest Ethiopia; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Duchy of Arenberg
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine
description: The Duchy of Arenberg was an imperial estate located in the Eifel region of the Rhineland within the Holy Roman Empire, governed by the prominent House of Arenberg. Elevated from an imperial county to a sovereign duchy, it exercised territorial autonomy and imperial immediacy across the Lower Rhenish-Westphalian Circle. The duchy endured the turbulence of the French Revolutionary Wars before briefly re-emerging within the Confederation of the Rhine prior to its annexation and eventual partition by Prussia and Hanover. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Aremberg; Common languages: Moselle Franconian and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Arenberg; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: County of Arenberg; Succeeded by: First French Empire and Kingdom of Prussia

name: Kingdom of Middag
description: The Kingdom of Middag operated as a supra-tribal indigenous confederation across the central-western coastal plains of Taiwan, centred at Dadu. Formed by an alliance of Papora, Babuza, Pazeh and Hoanya communities under a paramount leader known as the Kamachat, the polity was coerced into acknowledging Dutch East India Company suzerainty in 1645 following armed expeditions. The confederation retained internal autonomy under Dutch protectorate supervision until the Dutch were expelled by Koxinga and the Kingdom of Tungning. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Dutch East India Company; Capital: Dadu; Common languages: Formosan languages; Religion: Formosan animism; Government: Supra-tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Kingdom of Middag (sovereign); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Tungning

name: Great Ming
description: The Great Ming in this volatile interlude functioned as a roving imperial loyalist resistance movement based across the rugged terrain of southern Jiangxi and adjacent provinces following the collapse of the central Ming apparatus. Led by loyalist commanders and regional imperial princes who resisted the expanding Qing forces, the court maintained mobile administrative authority in the face of continuous Manchu campaigns. Its autonomous strongholds sustained stubborn military opposition until Qing armies systematically captured its mountainous redoubts in 1651. \n\n Status: Rump imperial state; Administrative seat: Mobile court; Common languages: Early Mandarin and Literary Chinese; Religion: Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Ming dynasty; Succeeded by: Qing dynasty

name: Kingdom of Madurai
description: The Kingdom of Madurai flourished as an independent sovereign realm across southern Tamil Nadu following the dissolution of the Vijayanagara imperial superstructure. Governed by the Balija warrior dynasty of the Madurai Nayaks, the kingdom asserted regional hegemony through the palaiyakkarar administrative system and fostered extensive monumental architecture, vibrant temple patronage and lucrative maritime trade with European merchants along the Coromandel coast.
