The realm maintained full independence until external pressures forced it into tributary vassalage under the Mughal Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Madurai; Common languages: Tamil and Telugu; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Madurai Nayak dynasty; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Vijayanagara Empire; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire

name: Nayakas of Chitradurga
description: The Nayakas of Chitradurga established an autonomous regional kingdom centred around the formidable hill fortress of Chitradurga in eastern Karnataka after the collapse of the Vijayanagara Empire. Commanding strong garrisons and sophisticated water storage infrastructure, the dynasty defended its territorial integrity against surrounding regional powers including the Bijapur Sultanate and the expanding Marathas. The sovereign chiefdom prospered through regional agricultural revenue and martial prowess until its conquest by the Kingdom of Mysore under Hyder Ali. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Chitradurga; Official languages: Kannada; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Nayaka; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Vijayanagara Empire; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Mysore

name: Nayaks of Gingee
description: The Nayaks of Gingee was a sovereign Hindu principality centred upon the massive triple-citadel fortification of Gingee in northern Tamil Nadu. Having severed ties with the fragmenting Vijayanagara Empire, the ruling Nayak elite maintained temporary independence while contending with intense territorial rivalry against neighbouring Thanjavur and Madurai. This brief period of sovereign autonomy came to an abrupt close around 1649 when the well-fortified stronghold fell to invading forces from the Bijapur Sultanate. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gingee; Common languages: Tamil and Telugu; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Nayaka; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Vijayanagara Empire; Succeeded by: Bijapur Sultanate

name: County of Schaumburg-Lippe
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine
description: The County of Schaumburg-Lippe emerged as an immediate principality of the Holy Roman Empire on 19 July 1647 following the partition of the historic County of Schaumburg. Ruled by the House of Lippe from the residence town of Bückeburg, the small state sustained an effective military tradition and autonomous administrative institutions across Lower Saxony. It preserved its sovereign membership within the Lower Rhenish-Westphalian Circle until its elevation to a principality upon joining the Confederation of the Rhine in 1807. \n\n Status: Imperial county of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Bückeburg; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Lippe; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 19 July 1647; Succeeded by: Principality of Schaumburg-Lippe

name: Amb State
description: Amb State was a sovereign tribal principality positioned along the upper Indus River in the rugged Tanawal region of the north-western subcontinent. Founded and ruled by the Tanoli clan, the realm defended its mountainous frontiers against neighbouring regional warlords and maintained independent authority through traditional tribal levies. The state enjoyed fully autonomous governance during the pre-colonial era and experienced a brief resurgence of sovereign status following Indian independence before formal integration into Pakistan in 1969. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Administrative seat: Darband; Common languages: Hindko and Pashto; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Tanoli; Historical era: Early modern period to modern era; Disestablished: 28 July 1969; Succeeded by: Islamic Republic of Pakistan

name: Emirate of Harar
description: The Emirate of Harar was an independent Muslim commercial realm centred within the fortified walled city of Harar Jugol in eastern Ethiopia. Founded when local leaders broke away from the Imamate of Aussa under the leadership of Ali ibn Daud, the emirate dominated regional trade networks connecting the Ethiopian interior with coastal Red Sea ports. Governed by hereditary emirs and minting its own mahlak currency, the prosperous trading state maintained political autonomy until its conquest by Egyptian forces and eventual annexation by the Ethiopian Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Harar; Common languages: Harari, Arabic, Somali and Oromo; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Imamate of Aussa; Succeeded by: Egyptian Khedivate

name: Swedish Pomerania
label: holy roman empire
description: Swedish Pomerania was an imperial territory along the southern Baltic coast governed as a dominion of the Swedish Crown following the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Centred administratively at Stralsund, the possession gave the Swedish monarch a vote within the Reichstag and served as a vital maritime outpost and military bulwark in northern Germany. Despite repeated occupations by Danish and Brandenburg forces during major regional wars, Sweden retained authority over the duchy until its cession to Denmark and Prussia in 1814. \n\n Status: Dominion of the Swedish Empire; Administrative seat: Stralsund; Common languages: Low German, German and Swedish; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Duchy under royal governor-general; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 24 October 1648; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Prussia

name: Bahama Islands
description: The Bahama Islands constituted an English and subsequently British colonial possession extending across the Lucayan Archipelago in the tropical western Atlantic Ocean. Initial European settlement commenced when Bermudian Puritans established plantations on Eleuthera in 1648, after which administration expanded to New Providence with its administrative seat at Nassau. The archipelago endured periods of proprietary mismanagement and rampant maritime privateering before direct crown administration was instituted to safeguard imperial sea routes until independence in 1973. \n\n Status: Crown colony of Great Britain; Capital: Nassau; Official languages: English; Religion: Anglicanism and Protestantism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Colonial period; Established: 1649; Disestablished: 10 July 1973; Succeeded by: Commonwealth of The Bahamas

name: Prince-Bishopric of Münster
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Münster during this era designates the period of Swedish military occupation and diplomatic influence following the conclusion of the Thirty Years' War in Westphalia. Although an ecclesiastical state of the Holy Roman Empire administered from the cathedral city of Münster, its strategic fortresses and revenue systems were placed under the custody of Swedish forces to guarantee peace terms and wartime reparations. The prince-bishops struggled persistently to reassert territorial sovereignty and remove foreign garrisons across the region. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality under Swedish military oversight; Capital: Münster; Common languages: Low German and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Westphalia; Preceded by: Prince-Bishopric of Münster (sovereign)

name: Virgin Islands
description: The Virgin Islands during this period formed a colonial plantation outpost of the Dutch West India Company, centred on the island of Tortola with its main port at Road Town. Established to facilitate maritime contraband trade and supply Dutch shipping routes between New Netherland and South America, the settlement featured defensive earthworks and sugar cane plantations. The enclave was recurrently targeted by Spanish and English privateers before English forces permanently captured the island in 1672 during the Third Anglo-Dutch War. \n\n Status: Colony of the Dutch West India Company; Capital: Road Town; Common languages: Dutch and Negerhollands; Religion: Dutch Reformed; Government: Colonial directorship; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: British Virgin Islands

name: Noble Rebels
description: The Noble Rebels comprised the shifting insurrectionary coalitions of dissident French aristocrats, grandees and regional parlements who mounted armed resistance against the centralising regency of Anne of Austria and Cardinal Mazarin during the Fronde. Operating without a fixed capital, the rebels coordinated provincial armies from strongholds in the Île-de-France, Guyenne and Normandy while seeking alliances with the Spanish monarchy. Royal forces under Marshal Turenne ultimately fragmented the noble factions, terminating their autonomous military resistance in 1652. \n\n Status: Aristocratic rebel confederation; Administrative seat: None (decentralised); Common languages: French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military insurrectionary alliance; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Kingdom of France; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Zaporozhian Host
description: The Zaporozhian Host during this autonomous phase operated as an independent Cossack stratocracy established across central Ukraine following the successful Khmelnytsky Uprising against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Formalised by the Treaty of Zboriv in August 1649 and led by Hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky from Baturyn and Chyhyryn, the state maintained a militarised regimental administration and defended Orthodox religious rights. Confronting persistent Polish military counter-offensives, the Host retained complete sovereignty until concluding the Treaty of Pereyaslav in 1654 to secure Muscovite suzerainty. \n\n Status: Sovereign Cossack stratocracy; Capital: Baturyn; Common languages: Ruthenian and Polish; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Stratocratic elective hetmanate; Ruler title: Hetman; Head of state: Bohdan Khmelnytsky; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth; Succeeded by: Cossack Hetmanate (Russian protectorate)

name: Commonwealth of England
description: The Commonwealth of England was a revolutionary republic established across England and Wales following the execution of King Charles I and the formal abolition of the monarchy in 1649. Headquartered in London and governed by the Rump Parliament and an executive Council of State, the republican regime suppressed domestic royalist insurgencies, subjugated Ireland through military conquest and conducted naval warfare against the Dutch Republic. Internal political discord between parliamentary factions and the New Model Army culminated in 1653 with the establishment of the Protectorate. \n\n Status: Unitary republican commonwealth; Capital: London; Official languages: English; Religion: Puritanism and Protestantism; Government: Parliamentary republic; Legislature: Rump Parliament; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Kingdom of England; Succeeded by: Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland

name: Île Bourbon
description: Île Bourbon was a French overseas island colony in the south-western Indian Ocean, forming part of the Mascarene Archipelago east of Madagascar. Administered from its primary port at Saint-Denis, the island was settled by French colonists and quickly transitioned into an intensive plantation economy dependent on the labour of enslaved Africans and Malagasies for coffee, spices and sugar cane. The settlement served as a strategic maritime station for French merchant fleets traversing the route between Europe and India until its reorganisation into the modern department of Réunion. \n\n Status: Crown colony of the Kingdom of France; Capital: Saint-Denis; Official languages: French; Common languages: French and Reunionese Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Department of Réunion

name: Maldives
description: The Maldives during this span operated as a tributary island sultanate under the commercial and maritime hegemony of the Dutch East India Company. Governed from the coral-island capital of Male by traditional hereditary sultans, the archipelago offered lucrative exports of cowrie shells, coir rope and dried fish to Dutch merchants stationed in nearby Ceylon. The Dutch maintained indirect oversight through regular tributary exchanges and naval supremacy across the Laccadive Sea without directly dismantling native political or religious institutions until British expansion eclipsed Dutch control. \n\n Status: Tributary sultanate under Dutch suzerainty; Capital: Male; Official languages: Dhivehi; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Elective sultanate; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Sultanate of the Maldives; Succeeded by: British protectorate of the Maldives

name: Swedish Gold Coast
description: The Swedish Gold Coast comprised a network of fortified coastal trading settlements founded in April 1650 along the Gulf of Guinea in modern-day Ghana by the Swedish Africa Company. Centred at Fort Carolusborg near Cape Coast, the colony was established under the direction of Hendrik Carloff to export timber, gold dust and enslaved captives for the Swedish transatlantic trade. Competing fiercely with neighbouring Dutch and Danish merchants, the Swedish enterprise endured local rebellions and armed naval assaults before being permanently absorbed by the Dutch Gold Coast in 1663. \n\n Status: Trading colony of the Swedish Africa Company; Capital: Cape Coast; Common languages: Swedish and Fante; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Colonial trading company administration; Ruler title: Administrator; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 22 April 1650; Disestablished: 22 April 1663; Succeeded by: Dutch Gold Coast

name: Adanse
description: Adanse was an influential Akan forest kingdom located in the southern interior of modern Ghana, with its traditional royal seat at Fomena. Regarded by Akan oral tradition as a foundational ancestral cradle and cultural epicentre, the realm derived substantial wealth from alluvial gold extraction and intermediate trade between northern savannah routes and the Atlantic coast. Ruled by the Adansehene, the state shaped early Akan clan institutions and political philosophy until regional dominance shifted to Denkyira and the emerging Ashanti confederation. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Fomena; Common languages: Twi; Religion: Akan traditional religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Adansehene; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Gold Coast; Succeeded by: Denkyira

name: Anguilla
description: Anguilla is a British overseas island dependency situated at the northern periphery of the Leeward Islands in the north-eastern Caribbean, centred on its administrative capital at The Valley. Colonised by English planters in the mid-seventeenth century, the small limestone island developed a subsistence and smallholder plantation economy that struggled with arid soils and recurring tropical storms. Although briefly captured during intermittent Anglo-French conflicts, the island remained under steady British colonial oversight, eventually maintaining a separate colonial administration into the modern era. \n\n Status: British overseas possession; Capital: The Valley; Official languages: English; Religion: Anglicanism and Protestantism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period to modern era; Historical region: Leeward Islands; Preceded by: Indigenous Arawak territory

name: Anlo
description: Anlo was a sovereign coastal polity established by the Anlo Ewe people between the Keta Lagoon and the Atlantic seaboard in south-eastern Ghana. Governed from the sacred capital of Anloga by the Awomefia as both spiritual and political sovereign, the state maintained a centralised military structure and controlled lucrative regional trade in sea salt, smoked fish and coastal merchandise. The kingdom defended its territorial sovereignty against rival inland confederacies and European encroachment until its incorporation into the British Gold Coast in 1902. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Anloga; Common languages: Ewe; Religion: Traditional Ewe religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Awomefia; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Slave Coast; Succeeded by: Gold Coast

name: Bamenda-Nkwe
description: Bamenda-Nkwe was a sovereign fondom established in the volcanic high plateau of the Western Grassfields in north-western Cameroon, with its royal seat at Baéza. Governed by a hereditary Fon assisted by an influential council of titled elders and secret societies, the kingdom developed intensive terraced farming, ironworking and craft industries across its undulating mountain valleys. The polity guarded its independence through diplomacy and traditional defensive alliances with neighbouring Grassfields chiefdoms until the advent of German colonial expansion at the turn of the twentieth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign fondom; Capital: Baéza; Common languages: Ngemba and Grassfields Bantu languages; Religion: Traditional Grassfields beliefs; Government: Traditional sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: Western High Plateau; Succeeded by: Kamerun

name: BaNgwaketse
description: The BaNgwaketse was a sovereign Tswana kingdom established across the arid scrublands of southern Botswana, centred upon the rocky defensive stronghold of Kanye. Led by hereditary monarchs titled the Kgosi, the polity exercised dominion over large cattle herds and coordinated communal agriculture through the traditional kgotla assembly system. The kingdom successfully repelled migratory invaders during the Difaqane and maintained its political autonomy against Boer incursions until accepting British protectorate status under the Bechuanaland Protectorate in March 1885. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kanye; Common languages: Setswana; Religion: Traditional Tswana religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Kgosi; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: Southern Africa; Succeeded by: Bechuanaland Protectorate

name: Barra
description: Barra, known natively as the Kingdom of Niumi, was a sovereign Mandinka state situated along the northern shore of the Gambia River estuary, centred at Barbastro. Governed by a hereditary Mansa, the realm exerted commanding control over transatlantic riverine navigation, levying tolls on European trading vessels and conducting profitable commerce in beeswax, grains and captives. The kingdom defended its coastline against foreign incursions until British colonial expansion gradually diminished its trade revenues, resulting in direct annexation into the Gambia Protectorate in 1893. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Barbastro; Common languages: Mandinka, Wolof and Serer; Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Mansa; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: Senegambia; Succeeded by: British Gambia

name: Bukerewe
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Bukerewe was an autonomous island kingdom situated in south-eastern Lake Victoria within the African Great Lakes region, centred at the royal capital of Bukerewe on Ukerewe Island. Ruled by hereditary kings bearing the title of Omukama from the Silanga dynasty, the polity flourished through fertile volcanic agriculture, lacustrine fishing and vital inter-island canoe commerce. The state retained its political independence and distinct cultural identity amid regional warfare until the arrival of European explorers and its incorporation into German East Africa in 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bukerewe; Common languages: Kerewe and Bantu languages; Religion: Traditional Great Lakes religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Omukama; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: African Great Lakes; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: County of Rantzau
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Rantzau was an immediate imperial territory of the Holy Roman Empire established in southern Holstein around its administrative seat at Barmstedt. Created when Emperor Ferdinand III elevated Christian Rantzau to the rank of imperial count, the small enclave exercised territorial immediacy and held a seat within the Lower Saxon Circle. The county was governed by the noble Rantzau family until dynastic murder and legal disputes prompted Danish royal intervention, leading to its permanent absorption into Danish Holstein in April 1726. \n\n Status: Imperial county of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Barmstedt; Common languages: Low German and German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Feudal county; Ruling dynasty: House of Rantzau; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1651; Disestablished: 9 April 1726; Succeeded by: Duchy of Holstein

name: Greater Kyamutwara
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Greater Kyamutwara was a prominent precolonial Haya kingdom situated on the western shore of Lake Victoria in north-western Tanzania, with its administrative court established at Bukoba. Governed by a sacred monarch titled the Omukama, the realm integrated intensive banana horticulture with pastoralism and fostered sophisticated iron smelting traditions that commanded regional renown. The expansive kingdom formed the dominant political power in the Kagera basin until internal dynastic rivalries fragmented its territory into smaller successor principalities at the opening of the eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bukoba; Common languages: Haya and Bantu languages; Religion: Traditional Great Lakes religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Omukama; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: African Great Lakes; Succeeded by: Kyamutwara

name: Grenada
description: Grenada was a French overseas island colony in the southern Windward Islands of the eastern Caribbean, governed from the port town of Saint George's. Following the subjugation and displacement of the indigenous Kalinago population in the early 1650s, French chartered companies and subsequent royal governors established lucrative plantations for cocoa, coffee and sugar cane cultivated by enslaved Africans. The colony grew into a prosperous agricultural possession of the French West Indies until British naval forces captured the island in March 1762 during the Seven Years' War. \n\n Status: French crown colony; Capital: Saint George's; Official languages: French; Common languages: French and Antillean Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Colonial period; Established: 1651; Disestablished: 3 March 1762; Succeeded by: British Windward Islands

name: Hadimu
label: polities of the swahili coast
description: Hadimu was an indigenous sovereign realm established by the Wahadimu people across the central and southern reaches of Zanzibar Island, centred upon the royal estate at Dunga. Governed by a traditional paramount ruler titled the Mwinyi Mkuu, the state maintained customary land rights, communal agriculture and vibrant maritime trade along the Swahili coast. The ruling dynasty exercised sovereign territorial jurisdiction and collected agricultural tributes from local villages until the Omani Busaidi dynasty gradually subordinated native authorities to established sultanate rule in Zanzibar. \n\n Status: Sovereign chiefdom; Capital: Dunga; Common languages: Swahili; Religion: Sunni Islam and traditional Swahili beliefs; Government: Traditional sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Mwinyi Mkuu; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Swahili Coast; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Zanzibar

name: Ibara Kingdom
description: The Ibara Kingdom was an autonomous precolonial realm established by the Bara people across the vast semi-arid plains and savannahs of south-central Madagascar, with its recorded royal seat at Abeokuta. Organised around powerful warrior clans and vast zebu cattle herds, the state defended its territorial independence through mobile warfare and tactical alliances among localised lineages. The kingdom preserved its sovereign character and resisted external domination for nearly two centuries until the expanding Merina Kingdom conquered and unified the central highlands and peripheral territories during the 1820s. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Abeokuta; Common languages: Malagasy; Religion: Traditional Malagasy beliefs; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: Southern Madagascar; Succeeded by: Merina Kingdom

name: Imamate of Bundu
description: The Imamate of Bundu was an autonomous Islamic theocratic state established by the Torodbe Fulani scholar Malik Sy in the borderlands between the Falémé and upper Gambia rivers, centred at Bulibani. Governed by an elected spiritual and secular ruler known as the Almamy, the imamate maintained a well-organised network of Islamic schools and controlled strategic overland commerce in gold, iron and gum arabic. The state defended its independence against neighbouring Bambara and Mandinka polities for two centuries before succumbing to French colonial subjugation in 1859. \n\n Status: Sovereign Islamic state; Capital: Bulibani; Common languages: Fula and Mandinka; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Theocratic elective monarchy; Ruler title: Almamy; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Kingdom of Gajaaga; Succeeded by: French Senegal

name: Jafarabad State
description: Jafarabad State was an autonomous maritime princely principality situated on the southern coast of the Kathiawar Peninsula in Gujarat, centred around the fortified harbour town of Jafrabad. Founded in the mid-seventeenth century and closely linked with the Siddis of Janjira, the state maintained a capable coastal naval squadron and derived considerable revenue from Indian Ocean trade, fisheries and regional tariffs. The principality preserved its internal autonomy and maritime influence through strategic agreements until entering into a subsidiary treaty relationship with the British East India Company in 1835. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Jafrabad; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Sunni Islam and Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Kathiawar; Succeeded by: Jafarabad State (British protectorate)

name: Kénédougou Kingdom
description: The Kénédougou Kingdom was a prominent West African state founded by the Traoré dynasty of the Senoufo people, encompassing portions of southern Mali, northern Ivory Coast and western Burkina Faso. Initially governed from Bougoula and later from the strongly fortified city of Sikasso, the kingdom developed a powerful standing army and defended its agricultural heartland behind massive mud-brick ramparts known as the Tata of Sikasso. The realm resisted the expansionist Toucouleur and Wassoulou empires until French colonial forces stormed Sikasso in May 1898. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sikasso; Common languages: Senoufo and Bambara; Religion: Traditional Senoufo religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Faama; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1651; Disestablished: 1 May 1898; Succeeded by: French Sudan

name: Kharsawan State
description: Kharsawan State was an independent Rajput princely realm situated in the rugged Chota Nagpur plateau of eastern India, centred at the town of Kharsawan. Founded by a branch of the Rathore dynasty who separated from Porahat, the state held sway over extensive mineral-rich forested lands and maintained authority through traditional feudal levies and agricultural rents. The ruling chiefs, bearing the title of Thakur and later Raja, maintained territorial independence against regional Maratha raids until accepting British protectorate supervision in the aftermath of the 1857 rebellion. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Kharsawan; Common languages: Odia, Ho and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Ruling dynasty: Singh Deo; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Chota Nagpur; Succeeded by: British Raj

name: Kingdom of Barotse
description: The Kingdom of Barotse, also known as Barotseland, was a sovereign realm established by the Lozi people across the vast Bulozi floodplain of the upper Zambezi River in western Zambia, with its dry-season royal capital at Lealui. Governed by a revered paramount monarch titled the Litunga alongside a representative national council known as the Kuta, the state managed sophisticated flood-plain canal irrigation, cattle pastoralism and fishing. The kingdom maintained extensive regional tributary networks until King Lewanika concluded treaties with the British South Africa Company in June 1890. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Lealui; Common languages: Siluyana and Silozi; Religion: Traditional Lozi religion; Government: Traditional constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: Litunga; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Lunda Empire; Succeeded by: British South Africa Company

name: Kingdom of Kaarta
description: The Kingdom of Kaarta was a powerful Bambara militarised state established in western Mali following the disintegration of imperial authority in the middle Niger basin, with its administrative seats at Diangounte and Ka'arta. Governed by the Massassi dynasty under the royal title of Faama, the kingdom relied on a formidable standing cavalry to assert hegemony across surrounding Sahelian trade routes and resist neighbouring Fula empires. Kaarta remained a dominant regional power until its fortified strongholds were besieged and conquered by the Toucouleur Empire of El Hadj Umar Tall in 1855. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ka'arta; Common languages: Bambara; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Faama; Ruling dynasty: Massassi dynasty; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Toucouleur Empire

name: Kingdom of Mpororo
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Mpororo was an autonomous pastoralist realm in the African Great Lakes region, spanning portions of south-western Uganda and northern Rwanda with its royal court at Mpororo. Governed by a sacred monarch bearing the title of Omukama, the kingdom maintained a strong pastoral economy based on Ankole long-horned cattle and wielded considerable regional military influence. Although dynastic succession disputes eventually divided its core territories into several smaller autonomous chiefdoms, the entity preserved its cultural identity until final colonial demarcation placed it under the British Uganda Protectorate in 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Mpororo; Common languages: Runyankole and Bantu languages; Religion: Traditional Great Lakes religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Omukama; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: African Great Lakes; Succeeded by: Uganda Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Wala
description: The Kingdom of Wala was an autonomous realm established in north-western Ghana between the Black Volta and Kulpawn rivers, centred at the historic commercial hub of Wa. Ruled by the Wa Naa in close cooperation with a respected Islamic scholarly elite and local earth-priests, the kingdom operated as a vital trans-Saharan trading crossroad for kola nuts, salt and gold dust. The state maintained political autonomy and cultural cohesion despite regional conflicts until British colonial forces formally incorporated the territory into the Northern Territories of the Gold Coast in 1902. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Wa; Common languages: Wali; Religion: Sunni Islam and traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Wa Naa; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Northern Ghana; Succeeded by: Gold Coast

name: Korea State
description: Korea State, also known as Koriya, was an autonomous Rajput princely realm situated amidst the densely forested hills of the modern Chhattisgarh region in central India, centred at Baikunthpur. Founded by the Chauhan dynasty, the state exercised independent governance over indigenous tribal populations and controlled strategic mountain passes connecting the Gangetic plain to the Deccan. The ruling Rajas maintained sovereignty through local feudal militias until the expanding Maratha Empire of the Bhonsles of Nagpur subjugated the territory into tributary status in 1791. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Baikunthpur; Common languages: Chhattisgarhi and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Ruling dynasty: Chauhan dynasty; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Maratha Empire

name: Kuthar State
description: Kuthar State was an autonomous hill principality located in the lower Himalayan foothills of modern Himachal Pradesh, governed from the fortress estate of Krishan Nagar. Ruled by a hereditary line of Chandravanshi Rajput Ranas, the small state sustained its independent authority through terrace cultivation, timber harvesting and control of regional mountain pilgrim tracks. The principality successfully preserved its autonomy against neighbouring hill states until the Gurkha invasion of 1804 disrupted regional order, which was subsequently restored under British paramountcy following the Anglo-Nepalese War. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Krishan Nagar; Common languages: Pahari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Rana; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Simla Hills; Succeeded by: British Raj

name: Manandriana Kingdom
description: The Manandriana Kingdom was an autonomous highland realm established by the Betsileo people in the central plateau of Madagascar, centred at the settlement of Ambositra. Governed by hereditary sacred kings who supervised extensive irrigated rice terraces and cattle husbandry across the mountain valleys, the state maintained distinct cultural rituals and local craft industries including wood carving. The kingdom retained sovereign independence amidst intense regional skirmishes among highland polities until the expanding Merina Kingdom under King Andrianampoinimerina conquered and incorporated the region in 1795. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ambositra; Common languages: Malagasy; Religion: Traditional Malagasy beliefs; Government: Traditional sacred monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: Central Highlands of Madagascar; Succeeded by: Merina Kingdom

name: Mongnai State
label: shan states
description: Mongnai State was a major Shan principality located in the undulating hills of eastern Burma, centred at the walled town of Mongnai. Ruled by a hereditary Shan saopha, the state functioned as a prominent regional vassal of the Konbaung and earlier Toungoo dynasties of Burma, serving as the primary headquarters for the Burmese military governor of the southern Shan States. It maintained local feudal administration and tribute networks until British colonial forces occupied the Shan highlands in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Burmese Empire; Capital: Mongnai; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Shan States; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Okpe
description: Okpe was an autonomous kingdom established by the Okpe sub-group of the Urhobo people in the western Niger Delta region of southern Nigeria, centred at Orerokpe. Governed by a traditional monarch titled the Orodje alongside a rotating council drawn from four ruling houses, the kingdom coordinated agricultural production, palm oil gathering and riverine trade. The realm successfully guarded its political sovereignty and customary judicial institutions until the British established direct imperial control under the Oil Rivers Protectorate in 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Orerokpe; Common languages: Urhobo; Religion: Traditional Urhobo religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Orodje; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: Niger Delta; Succeeded by: Oil Rivers Protectorate

name: Oku
description: Oku was a sovereign Grassfields kingdom established in the rugged volcanic highlands surrounding Mount Oku and Lake Oku in north-western Cameroon, with its capital at Elak Oku. Governed by a revered hereditary monarch bearing the title of Fon, the state was structured around powerful secret regulatory societies such as the Kwifon, which enforced customary law and preserved social balance. The polity sustained its independent culture, medicinal plant trade and highland agriculture until the establishment of German colonial administration in 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign fondom; Capital: Elak Oku; Common languages: Oku and Grassfields Bantu languages; Religion: Traditional Grassfields beliefs; Government: Traditional sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: Western High Plateau; Succeeded by: Kamerun

name: Ondonga
description: Ondonga was an independent Ovambo kingdom situated in the fertile flood plains of northern Namibia, with its traditional royal court established at Olukonda. Governed by a sacred monarch titled the Omukwaniilwa, who was assisted by a council of respected senior headmen, the state organised efficient communal grain cultivation, cattle grazing and seasonal trade across the Cuvelai basin. Ondonga maintained its sovereignty against outside pressures and European missionary influence until the extension of German colonial control through German South West Africa in 1896. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Olukonda; Common languages: Oshindonga; Religion: Traditional Ovambo religion; Government: Traditional sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Omukwaniilwa; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: Ovamboland; Succeeded by: German South West Africa

name: Pomeroon
description: Pomeroon was a Dutch plantation colony established along the banks of the Pomeroon River in the Guiana region of northern South America, centred around the fortified settlement of Nieuw Middelburg. Founded under the auspices of the Dutch West India Company and settled by Dutch and Sephardic Jewish planters, the colony focused on the cultivation of sugar cane and annatto dyes through enslaved labour. Despite early commercial promise, the exposed settlement suffered from devastating raids by French privateers and indigenous warriors, leading to its destruction and abandonment by 1690. \n\n Status: Colony of the Dutch West India Company; Capital: Nieuw Middelburg; Common languages: Dutch; Religion: Dutch Reformed and Judaism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1651; Disestablished: 1690; Succeeded by: Essequibo (colony)

name: Ranasan State
description: Ranasan State was an autonomous Rajput princely domain situated in the Mahi Kantha region of northern Gujarat, centred at the fortified settlement of Ranasan. Ruled by a lineage of Parmar Rajputs who held the hereditary title of Thakur, the state commanded defensive terrain along local river tributaries and maintained order through clan-based martial retinues. The principality successfully defended its local prerogatives and customary revenues against regional overlords until the onset of Maratha Gaekwad hegemony and British political treaties in 1802. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Ranasan; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Thakur; Ruling dynasty: Parmar; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Mahi Kantha; Succeeded by: Baroda State and British Raj

name: Savalu
description: Savalu was an autonomous precolonial kingdom established by the Mahi people amongst the granite hills of central Benin, centred at the settlement of Savalou. Governed by a traditional monarch titled the Ahosu, the kingdom served as a vital bastion of Mahi resistance against the aggressive military raids of the neighbouring Kingdom of Dahomey. The state maintained its political sovereignty and regional commercial exchanges through alliances with neighbouring inland confederacies until French expeditionary forces annexed the territory into French Dahomey in 1895. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Savalou; Common languages: Fon and Mahi; Religion: Traditional Vodun beliefs; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Ahosu; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: Slave Coast; Succeeded by: French Dahomey

name: Sefwi
description: Sefwi was an independent Akan kingdom established in the dense tropical forests of south-western Ghana along the upper Tano and Bia river basins, with its royal capital at Sefwi Wiawso. Governed by a paramount king known as the Sefwihene, the realm absorbed successive waves of Akan migrants fleeing regional conflicts and accumulated wealth through alluvial gold extraction, timber and trade. The kingdom preserved its sovereignty while navigating intense geopolitical pressures from Denkyira and the Asante Empire until British colonial annexation in 1902. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sefwi Wiawso; Common languages: Sehwi and Twi; Religion: Akan traditional religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Sefwihene; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Gold Coast; Succeeded by: Gold Coast

name: Shilluk Kingdom
description: The Shilluk Kingdom was a powerful, centralised Nilotic realm that extended along the banks of the White Nile in present-day South Sudan, governed from its royal capital at Fashoda. Headed by a sacred king titled the Reth, whose spiritual vitality was traditionally intertwined with the health and prosperity of the land, the kingdom commanded riverine commerce with a formidable fleet of war canoes. Shilluk military power held off neighbouring nomadic tribes and Funj encroachments until Ottoman-Egyptian expeditions overwhelmed and dismantled the state in the 1860s. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Fashoda; Common languages: Shilluk; Religion: Traditional Shilluk religion; Government: Sacred divine monarchy; Ruler title: Reth; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Nilotic migrations; Succeeded by: Ottoman Egypt

name: Sultanate of Darfur
description: The Sultanate of Darfur was an independent Islamic empire that dominated the vast arid savannahs and highlands of western Sudan, centred at the desert metropolis of El Fasher. Founded by the Keira dynasty and ruling over the Fur and Arab populations, the sultanate maintained a powerful cavalry army and prospered through trans-Saharan trade along the Forty Days Road to Egypt. The state fiercely guarded its autonomy until falling to Turco-Egyptian forces under warlord Al-Zubayr Rahma Mansur in 1874, before a final revival ended under British conquest in 1916. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: El Fasher; Common languages: Fur and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Keira dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Turco-Egyptian Sudan

name: Sultanate of Kutai Kartanegara ing Martadipura
description: The Sultanate of Kutai Kartanegara ing Martadipura was a sovereign Islamic maritime kingdom situated along the Mahakam River in eastern Borneo, with its royal court established at Tenggarong. Formed through the consolidation of Kutai Kartanegara with the older Hindu kingdom of Kutai Martadipura, the state controlled lucrative riverine commerce in forest resins, rattan, gold and edible bird nests. Ruled by hereditary sultans who balanced relations between Bugis settlers and indigenous Dayak groups, the realm maintained independent trade until Dutch colonial treaties established formal protectorate oversight in 1845. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Tenggarong; Common languages: Kutai and Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Kutai Martadipura; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Surinam
description: Surinam during this timeframe existed as an English plantation colony, popularly known as Willoughbyland, situated along the northern coast of South America and centred at Paramaribo. Established by Lord Willoughby of Parham with royalist settlers from Barbados, the settlement developed expansive sugar estates worked by enslaved Africans along the Surinam and Commewijne rivers. The colony established a local House of Burgesses and small sugar mills before a Dutch naval expedition under Abraham Crijnssen captured the settlements in February 1667, leading to permanent Dutch cession. \n\n Status: Colony of the Kingdom of England; Capital: Paramaribo; Official languages: English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Proprietary colonial administration; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1651; Disestablished: 26 February 1667; Succeeded by: Colony of Suriname (Dutch colony)

name: Saint Barthélemy
description: Saint Barthélemy during this era constituted a Caribbean island dependency administered by the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, operating under French royal sovereignty from its recorded settlement at Wanganui. Acquired by the Knights Hospitaller under Grand Prior Phillippe de Longvilliers de Poincy through purchase from the Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique, the arid island was settled by small groups of French mariners and farmers. The Order maintained rudimentary colonial governance and maritime supply posts until economic unprofitability and Poincy's death prompted the sale of the island to the French West India Company in 1665. \n\n Status: Colony of the Sovereign Military Order of Saint John; Capital: Wanganui; Official languages: French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Hospitaller colonial governorship; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 24 May 1651; Disestablished: 10 August 1665; Succeeded by: French West India Company

name: Saint Christopher
description: Saint Christopher during this transitional phase was governed by the Knights Hospitaller of the Order of Saint John, which acquired the French sector of the partitioned island from the Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique. Administered from its recorded colonial command at Cartagena by the Order's governor Phillippe de Longvilliers de Poincy, the colony oversaw profitable sugar plantations and maintained uneasy coexistence with the neighbouring English partition. The Knights exercised civil and military authority until mounting debts led to the transfer of all Hospitaller holdings to the newly chartered French West India Company in 1666. \n\n Status: Colony of the Sovereign Military Order of Saint John; Capital: Cartagena; Official languages: French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Hospitaller colonial governorship; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 24 May 1651; Disestablished: 4 January 1666; Succeeded by: French West India Company

name: Saint Martin

description: The Province of Carolina was an English and subsequently British proprietary colony chartered in March 1663 across the south-eastern seaboard of North America, governed from its capital at Charleston. Created under the proprietary patent granted to James, Duke of York, the territory exercised civil and military authority over scattered fishing settlements, timber camps and fur-trading stations between the Kennebec and St Croix rivers. Captured from the Dutch in 1664, the territory was subsequently leased to William Penn and administered alongside Pennsylvania before acquiring its own separate legislative assembly in 1704 while sharing the same proprietary governor. name: Duchy of Massa and Carrara
label: holy roman empire

name: Province of New Jersey
label: thirteen colonies

Initially established as a proprietary grant given to Sir George Carteret and Lord Berkeley of Stratton following the capture of New Netherland, the territory fostered smallholder agriculture, religious diversity and bustling river commerce. name: Province of New York
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Province of New York was an English and subsequently British proprietary and royal colony situated in north-eastern North America, centred at the bustling seaport of New York City on Manhattan Island. Established after English naval forces captured New Netherland from the Dutch in 1664 and named for James, Duke of York, the colony extended along the Hudson and Mohawk river valleys to the Great Lakes. name: Bana

Governed by a sacred monarch titled the Fon, the state maintained a stratified social hierarchy coordinated by traditional regulatory societies such as the Kum'nji, which oversaw agricultural lands, market commerce and ancestral rituals. The kingdom preserved its independence through diplomatic alliances with neighbouring Grassfields kingdoms until German colonial expeditions established imperial control over the region in 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign fondom; Capital: Bamnoli; Common languages: Fe'fe' and Bamileke languages; Religion: Traditional Bamileke beliefs; Government: Traditional sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Historical region: Western High Plateau; Succeeded by: Kamerun

name: Banganapalle State

Founded by Muhammad Beg Khan Najm-i-Sani under a jagir grant from the Sultan of Bijapur and later confirmed by the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, the state was ruled by a distinguished Shia Muslim dynasty who bore the title of Nawab. The principality preserved its internal autonomy and regional agricultural revenue through volatile Deccan conflicts until entering into protective treaty relations with the British in 1800. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Banganapalle; Common languages: Telugu, Urdu and Persian; Religion: Shia Islam and Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Rayalaseema; Succeeded by: British East India Company

name: Jaxa State
description: Jaxa State was a remarkable fugitive micro-state established on the northern banks of the Amur River along the contested Russo-Qing frontier, with its wooden citadel at Albazin. Founded by Nicefor Czernichowski, an exiled Polish-Lithuanian nobleman who assassinated the tsarist governor of Ilimsk and fled eastward with Cossack followers, the community erected strong timber ramparts, negotiated with local Daurs and Evenks, and developed agricultural settlements. name: Kingdom of Cotiote
description: The Kingdom of Cotiote, natively known as Kottayam, was an autonomous feudal principality situated in the lush Malabar region of present-day Kerala, centred at Kottayam. Governed by a royal lineage belonging to the Kshatriya Padinjare Kovilakam, the state commanded lucrative spice-growing valleys that produced black pepper, cardamom and ginger for Indian Ocean trade. Under the legendary warrior prince Pazhassi Raja, the kingdom mounted fierce guerrilla resistance against Hyder Ali of Mysore and later against British East India Company armies until Pazhassi Raja was killed in battle in 1805. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kottayam; Common languages: Malayalam; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Malabar; Disestablished: 30 November 1805; Succeeded by: British East India Company

name: Lunda Empire

name: County of Soyo (Military Occupation)

name: French Establishments in India

name: Colony of Tobago

name: Principality of East Frisia

description: The Principality of East Frisia was an immediate sovereign principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in the coastal lowlands of north-western Germany, governed from its capital at Aurich. Ruled by a cadet branch of the House of Hesse-Darmstadt, the state secured sovereign independence in 1668, earning renown through its warrior prince Frederick II, the famous Prince of Homburg. Höhe; Common languages: German; Religion: Calvinism and Lutheranism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Hesse; Ruler title: Landgrave; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Prussia

name: Cayman Islands

Transformed into one of the Atlantic world's most lucrative export centres, the island produced vast quantities of sugar, rum and molasses through an immense system of enslaved labour. Despite frequent slave uprisings and protracted conflicts with the interior Maroons, Jamaica remained under British colonial rule until achieving full sovereign independence in August 1962. \n\n Status: Crown colony of Great Britain; Capital: Spanish Town and Kingston; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Jamaican Patois; Religion: Anglicanism and Protestantism; Government: Constitutional royal colony; Representative title: Governor; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Colonial period; Established: 1 August 1670; Disestablished: 6 August 1962; Succeeded by: Jamaica

name: Bani Khalid Emirate

Established under the leadership of Barrak ibn Ghurayr of the Al Humaid clan after expelling Ottoman garrisons from the Lahsa Eyalet in 1670, the emirate controlled lucrative date oasis agriculture, coastal pearl fisheries and trans-Arabian caravan routes. name: Kingdom of Bolaang Mongondow
description: The Kingdom of Bolaang Mongondow was an autonomous maritime and highland state that held dominion across the northern peninsula of Sulawesi, with its royal coastal court at Bola'ang. Founded in 1670 when Prince Datu Loloda Mokoagow succeeded paramount chief Tadohe and assumed the royal title of Datu, the kingdom conquered surrounding Minahasan territories and controlled regional commerce in forest resins, gold and rice. name: Danish West Indies
description: The Danish West Indies was a chartered and subsequent crown colony of Denmark-Norway in the Caribbean Sea, comprising the islands of Saint Thomas, Saint John and later Saint Croix, with its capital at Charlotte Amalie. Established by the Danish West India Company in 1672, the colony developed into a thriving international trading hub and plantation economy producing sugar cane and rum cultivated by enslaved Africans. Denmark maintained administrative control over the islands through periods of British wartime occupation until selling the territory to the United States in March 1917. \n\n Status: Crown colony of Denmark; Capital: Charlotte Amalie; Official languages: Danish; Common languages: Danish, English, Negerhollands and Virgin Islands Creole; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Colonial governorship; Representative title: Governor-General; Historical era: Colonial period; Established: 1672; Disestablished: 31 March 1917; Succeeded by: United States Virgin Islands

name: Colony of Saint-Martin

Formally partitioned with the Dutch under the 1648 Treaty of Concordia, French settlement consolidated under royal authority in May 1672. The colony developed plantation agriculture dependent on enslaved African labour, repeatedly changing hands during imperial wars with Great Britain before lasting territorial stability was restored in the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: French colony; Capital: Marigot; Common languages: French and Antillean Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 May 1672; Disestablished: 19 March 1946; Succeeded by: Overseas Department of Guadeloupe

English planters established control following the expulsion of Dutch settlers in 1672, developing sugar cane plantations heavily reliant on chattel slavery. Administered from Road Town on Tortola, the archipelago evolved into a distinct civilian dependency within the broader British Leeward Islands administrative framework. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Road Town; Official languages: English; Religion: Protestantism and Anglicanism; Government: Colonial dependency; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1672; Legislature: House of Assembly; Currency: British pound sterling and United States dollar

name: Savanur State
description: Savanur State was an autonomous Muslim principality situated across the northern Karnataka region of south-western India. Established in 1672 by Abdul Karim Khan, an Afghan military commander of the Miyana tribe, the realm maintained a delicate independence between the expanding Maratha Empire and the Sultans of Mysore. The nawabs governed from their fortified seat at Savanur, fostering local commerce and defending their agricultural lands until regional conflicts curtailed their sovereignty. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Savanur; Common languages: Kannada, Urdu and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1672; Succeeded by: Princely State of Savanur

name: Republic of the Seven United Netherlands (Military Occupation)
description: The Republic of the Seven United Netherlands (Military Occupation) comprised foreign districts and strategic frontier strongpoints temporarily seized by Dutch States armed forces during the Franco-Dutch and Nine Years' wars. Directed by military commanders under the authority of the States General at The Hague, these occupied zones served as defensive security buffers and diplomatic leverage. Dutch garrisons maintained martial law and levied logistical contributions until peace treaties mandated territorial restitutions. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: Dutch States Army field headquarters; Common languages: Dutch, French and German; Religion: Calvinism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 February 1673; Succeeded by: Republic of the Seven United Netherlands

name: Duchy of Saxe-Jena
label: holy roman empire

Beset by tropical diseases, poor provisioning and Spanish naval blockades, the Scottish settlers surrendered to Spanish forces in 1700, a catastrophe that severely impaired Scotland's economy and accelerated union with England. \n\n Status: Scottish colony; Capital: Puerto Inmortal; Common languages: Scots and English; Religion: Presbyterianism; Government: Chartered colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1697; Disestablished: 1700; Succeeded by: New Spain

name: Kumul Khanate
description: The Kumul Khanate was a semi-autonomous Muslim Chagatai realm located in the Hami oasis of eastern Xinjiang, operating as a hereditary vassal under the Qing Empire and later the Republic of China. Established in 1696 when Prince Muhammad Shah submitted to the Kangxi Emperor, the khans traced direct descent from Chagatai Khan and the Mongol imperial line. The khanate governed local Uyghur agrarian and oasis communities, providing military contingents and intelligence to the Chinese imperial court until provincial governor Jin Shuren abolished the monarchy in 1930. \n\n Status: Feudal vassal khanate; Capital: Kumul; Common languages: Chagatai, Uyghur and Mandarin Chinese; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chagatai; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1697; Disestablished: 1931; Succeeded by: Republic of China

name: Tertholen
description: Tertholen was a short-lived Caribbean colonial outpost established by the Margraviate of Brandenburg on the island of Tortola in the Virgin Islands. Seeking to expand Brandenburg's transatlantic mercantile network following maritime ventures on Saint Thomas, colonial agents occupied the island in 1697, naming it after the Dutch island of Tholen. The small garrison established a transient trading station to barter tropical goods and refit slave ships, but abandoned the outpost by 1698 due to British diplomatic pressure and lack of sustainable provisioning. \n\n Status: Brandenburg colonial outpost; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: Brandenburg naval station; Common languages: German and English; Religion: Lutheranism and Calvinism; Government: Commercial outpost; Ruler title: Elector of Brandenburg; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1697; Disestablished: 1698; Succeeded by: British Virgin Islands

name: Principality of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen
