description: The Principality of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen was an imperial estate of the Holy Roman Empire and subsequently a sovereign German state situated in northern Thuringia. Elevated from an imperial county to a principality in September 1697 under Count Christian William, the realm was governed from the baroque residence of Sondershausen Castle. The principality preserved its domestic legal institutions, army contingents and civic administration throughout the Napoleonic upheavals and German Confederation, flourishing as a cultural and musical centre before joining the German Empire in 1871. \n\n Status: Principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Sondershausen; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Schwarzburg; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 13 September 1697; Disestablished: 18 January 1871; Succeeded by: German Empire

name: Antankarana Kingdom
description: The Antankarana Kingdom was an autonomous precolonial monarchy established across the rugged limestone karst and coastal plains of northern Madagascar. Originating in the late seventeenth century after a dynastic dispute led a branch of the Sakalava royal house to migrate north, the kingdom established its spiritual and political redoubts around the natural caves of Ankarana. The kings governed coastal fishing and inland agrarian communities, fiercely resisting highland Merina expansion by utilising cavern fortresses until negotiating French military protection in the 1840s. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Antandroy; Common languages: Malagasy (Antankarana); Religion: Traditional Malagasy religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zafimbolamena; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1698; Disestablished: 1844; Succeeded by: French Madagascar

name: Bhor State
description: Bhor State was an autonomous Maratha jagir principality located along the eastern slopes of the Western Ghats in modern Maharashtra, India. Founded in 1697 when Chhatrapati Rajaram granted the estate to Shankarji Narayan Gandekar for outstanding administrative and military service during the Mughal-Maratha wars, the realm was governed from the palace at Bhor. The hereditary Pant Sachivs administered surrounding mountain forts and agricultural valleys, providing vital military contingents to the Maratha Empire until entering the British subsidiary alliance system in 1819. \n\n Status: Maratha jagir state; Capital: Bhor; Common languages: Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Gandekar; Ruler title: Pant Sachiv; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1697; Disestablished: 1819; Succeeded by: Princely State of Bhor

name: Vieques
description: Vieques under British Scottish control was a short-lived colonial settlement established on the Caribbean island of Vieques in 1698. Dispatched in connection with the Darien enterprise of the Company of Scotland, Scottish settlers landed on Crab Island to establish an agricultural plantation colony and regional trading post. The small encampment struggled with tropical illness and food shortages, and within months Spanish colonial authorities from neighbouring Puerto Rico launched an armed expedition that dismantled the Scottish settlement. \n\n Status: Scottish colony; Capital: San Juan; Common languages: Scots and English; Religion: Presbyterianism; Government: Colonial military settlement; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1698; Disestablished: 1699; Succeeded by: Danish West Indies

name: Chitral State
description: Chitral State was an autonomous mountain kingdom established in the rugged Hindu Kush valleys of north-western South Asia. Ruled by the Katur branch of the Kator dynasty founded by Shah Katur around the late seventeenth century, the realm maintained independent governance from its palace citadel at Chitral. The mehtars governed multi-ethnic mountain communities, controlling strategic passes between Central Asia and the Indus plains while repelling Afghan and Badakhshani raids until regional tributary relationships evolved in the late eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Chitral; Common languages: Khowar and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam and Isma'ilism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kator; Ruler title: Mehtar; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1699; Disestablished: 1779

name: Morvi State
description: Morvi State was an autonomous princely realm situated across the northern Kathiawar peninsula of Gujarat in western India. Established in 1698 by Kanyoji, a prince of the Jadeja Rajput dynasty following succession struggles in Kutch, the kingdom established its capital at Morvi on the Machhu River. The Jadeja rulers developed coastal salt flats, agricultural estates and riverine commerce, defending their independence against regional Maratha and Mughal incursions until concluding the Walker Treaty of subsidiary alliance with the British in 1807. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Morbi; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jadeja Rajput; Ruler title: Thakur Sahib; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1698; Disestablished: 1808; Succeeded by: Princely State of Morvi

name: Pratapgarh State
description: Pratapgarh State, historically known as Kanthal, was an autonomous Rajput principality situated in the rugged highlands of southern Rajasthan in north-western India. Governed by the Sisodia Rajput dynasty who claimed kinship with the Maharanas of Mewar, the realm was revitalised when Maharawat Pratap Singh founded the new fortified capital of Pratapgarh in 1698. The rulers levied tributes from neighbouring forest tribes and defended their hill domains against Mughal forces and Maratha predatory raids until entering British subsidiary protection in 1818. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Pratapgarh; Common languages: Rajasthani (Harauti) and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sisodia Rajput; Ruler title: Maharawat; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1699; Disestablished: 1851; Succeeded by: Princely State of Pratapgarh

name: Vieques
description: Vieques under Danish colonial administration was a brief Caribbean outpost established on the island of Vieques in 1699. Following the expulsion of Scottish settlers, the Danish West India Company dispatched expeditions from neighbouring Saint Thomas to assert sovereignty and develop sugar plantations on the fertile island. Danish colonists erected temporary dwellings and storehouses, but persistent diplomatic protests and naval threats from Spanish Puerto Rico forced the Danish authorities to abandon their settlement on Crab Island in 1701. \n\n Status: Danish colony; Capital: Bambrugge; Common languages: Danish and Dutch; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Chartered colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1699; Disestablished: 1701; Preceded by: Scottish colony; Succeeded by: Spanish Puerto Rico

name: Aundh State
description: Aundh State was an autonomous Maratha jagir principality located in the Deccan tablelands of modern Maharashtra, India. Founded in 1699 when Chhatrapati Rajaram conferred the jagir upon Parshuram Trimbak Pant Pratinidhi for his exceptional leadership and loyalty during the prolonged wars against Aurangzeb, the domain was governed from Aundh. The hereditary Pratinidhis administered fertile agricultural lands, patronised Hindu temple scholarship and maintained military detachments for the Maratha Empire until accepting British paramountcy under the Deccan States Agency in 1820. \n\n Status: Maratha jagir state; Capital: Aundh; Common languages: Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Pant Pratinidhi; Ruler title: Pant Pratinidhi; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1699; Disestablished: 1821; Succeeded by: Princely State of Aundh

name: Mbunda Kingdom
description: The Mbunda Kingdom was an autonomous Bantu monarchy situated in south-eastern Angola along the upper reaches of the Cuando and Lungwebungu rivers. Governed by sacred monarchs titled Mwene Mbunda from royal courts at Lumbala Nguimbo, the kingdom unified multiple matrilineal clans through sophisticated judicial assemblies. The realm prospered through extensive regional trade in iron tools, beeswax, ivory and rubber, successfully defending its borders against Chokwe and Luvale raiders until Portuguese colonial military campaigns subjugated the monarchy in 1917. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Lumbala Nguimbo; Common languages: Mbunda; Religion: Traditional Mbunda religion and Christianity; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Mwene Mbunda; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1700; Disestablished: 1915; Succeeded by: Portuguese Angola

name: AbaThembu
description: AbaThembu was an autonomous Bantu kingdom established by the Thembu nation across the rolling uplands of the modern Eastern Cape in South Africa. Dating its consolidation to the reign of King Nxeko in the early eighteenth century, the state was governed by a paramount royal dynasty of the Hala clan through regional subordinate chiefs. The kingdom maintained an agrarian and pastoralist economy centred on cattle wealth, defending its territorial integrity against neighbouring Xhosa rivals and European settlers until British colonial authorities annexed Thembuland in 1876. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: Thembuland royal great place; Common languages: isiXhosa; Religion: Traditional Thembu religion; Government: Traditional paramount monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hala; Ruler title: King (Kumkani); Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1876; Succeeded by: Cape Colony

name: Ajasse Ipo
description: Ajasse Ipo was an autonomous Yoruba kingdom located in the Igbomina cultural region of present-day Kwara State in north-central Nigeria. Founded during the late seventeenth century and governed by a traditional monarch titled the Olupo, the town served as a pivotal commercial crossroad linking the northern savannas with the southern Yoruba forest states. The kingdom preserved its cultural heritage, judicial councils and agricultural markets through decades of Fulani and Nupe military encroachment until British colonial forces established administrative control over Kwara in 1900. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Ajasse Ipo; Common languages: Yoruba (Igbomina); Religion: Traditional Yoruba religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Olupo; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1900; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Akuapem
description: Akuapem was an autonomous kingdom situated along the scenic Akuapem Ridge in south-eastern Ghana. Formed following the 1733 Abotakyi Accord, which united indigenous Guan communities with Akan Akyem warriors against Akwamu dominance, the state was governed by the Okuapehene from the royal palace at Akropong. The kingdom controlled important trade paths connecting coastal ports to the inland forest belt, fostering palm-oil cultivation and welcoming early Basel Christian missionaries before British colonial authorities formally incorporated the realm into the Gold Coast colony in 1902. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Akropong; Common languages: Akuapem Twi and Guan; Religion: Traditional Akan religion and Christianity; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Okuapehene; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1902; Succeeded by: British Gold Coast

name: Akyem Kotoku
description: Akyem Kotoku was an autonomous Akan kingdom located in the dense forest country of the Eastern Region of Ghana, forming one of the three historic divisions of the Akyem nation. Governed by a paramount king known as the Kotokuhene from the capital at Akyem Oda, the kingdom flourished through gold panning, kola nut trading and fertile agricultural cultivation. The state vigorously defended its autonomy against expansionist Ashanti invasions during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, maintaining independent military regiments until British colonial authorities annexed the region in 1902. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Akyem Oda; Common languages: Akan (Twi); Religion: Traditional Akan religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Kotokuhene; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1902; Succeeded by: British Gold Coast

name: Assin Apimenem
description: Assin Apimenem was an autonomous Akan state situated in the forested interior of modern central Ghana, occupying strategic territory along the Pra River corridor. Governed from its historic capital at Manso, the realm functioned as a critical transit hub and commercial buffer between the coastal Fante confederacies and the inland Ashanti Empire. The kingdom regulated regional trade routes for gold, ivory and agricultural commodities, defending its political autonomy through changing alliances until the British colonial administration annexed the Assin territories into the Gold Coast Protectorate in 1902. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Manso; Common languages: Akan (Fante and Twi); Religion: Traditional Akan religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1902; Succeeded by: British Gold Coast

name: Awa-Khoi
description: Awa-Khoi, widely known as the Red Nation or Khaun, was the paramount clan polity of the Nama people in south-central Namibia. Headquartered at the historic oasis of Hoachanas, the polity was governed by a hereditary kaptein whose supreme moral and political seniority was recognised across all central Nama tribes. The clan managed extensive pastoral cattle herds across semi-arid plains, defending grazing lands against Herero expansion and rival Oorlam groups until German imperial troops defeated their forces and established colonial rule in 1896. \n\n Status: Traditional pastoral chieftaincy; Capital: Hoachanas; Common languages: Khoekhoe (Nama); Religion: Traditional Nama religion and Christianity; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Ruler title: Kaptein; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1896; Succeeded by: German South West Africa

name: Baddibu
description: Baddibu, also known historically as Rip, was an autonomous Mandinka kingdom situated along the northern bank of the Gambia River in modern The Gambia and Senegal. Governed by a traditional monarch titled the Mansa from regional royal residences, the state derived significant economic wealth from riverine commerce, salt trading and groundnut cultivation. During the nineteenth century, the kingdom was transformed by the Soninke-Marabout religious wars led by Islamic reformer Maba Diakhou Bâ, maintaining sovereignty until British and French colonial partitioning dissolved the state in 1898. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Baddibu; Common languages: Mandinka and Wolof; Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mansa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1898; Succeeded by: British Gambia Colony and Protectorate

name: Bafilo
description: Bafilo was an autonomous Kotokoli kingdom situated along the mountainous trade routes of north-central Togo. Centred around the prominent commercial settlement of Bafilo, the polity was ruled by traditional Tem chieftains who coordinated regional agricultural production, artisanal weaving and cattle trade. The town became a regional centre of Islamic learning and commerce along trans-Volta caravan trails, preserving its domestic autonomy and civic customs until German colonial forces incorporated the territory into the Togoland protectorate in 1896. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Bafilo; Common languages: Tem (Kotokoli); Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Ruler title: Chief; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1896; Succeeded by: German Togoland

name: BaKgatla
description: BaKgatla was an autonomous Tswana polity established by the bagaKgafêla branch of the Sotho-Tswana peoples across south-eastern Botswana and the adjacent western Transvaal. Guided by hereditary paramount chiefs known as the Kgosi, the society was organised into disciplined age-regiments that managed communal cattle herding and defended arable territory. Centred at Mochudi along the Notwane River, the BaKgatla successfully resisted Boer encroachment and protected their sovereignty until Great Britain established the Bechuanaland Protectorate in March 1885. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Mochudi; Common languages: Setswana; Religion: Traditional Tswana religion and Christianity; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Kgosi; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 23 March 1885; Succeeded by: Bechuanaland Protectorate

name: Bandjoun
description: Bandjoun was an influential and autonomous Bamileke kingdom established in the Western Highlands of Cameroon by King Notouom I in the early eighteenth century. Centred at the royal palace and grand compound at Hialah in Bandjoun, the monarchy was governed by the Fo alongside a powerful council of nine notables and secretive societies. The realm commanded productive agricultural hillsides, flourishing palm groves and celebrated woodcarving ateliers, defending its territorial sovereignty against regional neighbours until German colonial forces occupied the region in 1901. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Bandjoun; Administrative seat: Hialah; Common languages: Ghomala (Bamileke); Religion: Traditional Bamileke religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Fo; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Batcham
description: Batcham was an autonomous Bamileke chiefdom located in the Bamboutos mountain range of the Western Highlands in modern Cameroon. Governed by a sacred hereditary monarch titled the Fo, the polity was structured around matrilineal clan compounds, agricultural terraces and ancestral religious shrines. The kingdom fostered regional commerce in iron tools, agricultural produce and ceremonial crafts, maintaining political independence from neighbouring chiefdoms through fortified hill passes until German colonial expeditions subjugated the Bamboutos region and established colonial administrative control in 1901. \n\n Status: Traditional chiefdom; Capital: Batcham; Common languages: Ngomba (Bamileke); Religion: Traditional Bamileke religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Fo; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Bemba
description: The Bemba Kingdom was a powerful and centralised Bantu realm established across the northern plateau of modern Zambia between the Luapula River and Lake Tanganyika. Governed by a supreme paramount monarch titled the Chitimukulu from the crocodile clan, known as the Abena Ng'andu, the kingdom expanded rapidly through a disciplined military system of territorial chiefs. Centred near modern Kasama, the Bemba controlled lucrative transcontinental caravan routes for ivory, copper and cloth, maintaining their sovereignty until the British South Africa Company established colonial rule in 1891. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Kasama; Common languages: Bemba (iciBemba); Religion: Traditional Bemba religion; Government: Traditional paramount monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Abena Ng'andu; Ruler title: Chitimukulu; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: British South Africa Company

name: Buddu
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Buddu was an autonomous Bantu kingdom situated along the fertile north-western shores of Lake Victoria in modern southern Uganda. Originally a prominent province and tributary principality affiliated with the Bunyoro-Kitara empire, the state was governed from administrative centres around Masaka by hereditary chiefs who controlled lucrative banana groves and cattle pastures. Buddu maintained its regional autonomy and distinct cultural identity until the late eighteenth century, when Kabaka Junju of Buganda invaded and permanently annexed the territory into the Buganda Kingdom in 1798. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Masaka; Common languages: Luganda; Religion: Traditional Bantu religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Pokino; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1798; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Buganda

name: Bukunzi
description: Bukunzi, also known as Mbirizi, was an autonomous kingdom situated in the rugged highlands east of the Ruzizi River in extreme south-western Rwanda. Founded by an exiled branch of the Shi royal dynasty from across the Congolese border, the state was celebrated throughout the Great Lakes region for the legendary rainmaking powers of its hereditary monarchs. Bukunzi maintained strong cultural and commercial ties with Bushi, successfully preserving its complete independence from the central court of Rwanda until Belgian colonial troops forcibly integrated the realm in 1925. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Bukunzi; Common languages: Kinyarwanda and Shi; Religion: Traditional Great Lakes religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1926; Succeeded by: Ruanda-Urundi

name: Buna
description: Buna, historically known as Bouna, was an autonomous kingdom established in north-eastern Ivory Coast near the confluence of the Comoé and Black Volta rivers. Founded by a branch of Dagomba migrants under Bounkani in the late seventeenth century, the kingdom established its fortified capital at Buna. The realm derived substantial wealth as an entrepôt for kola nuts, gold dust and Saharan livestock, welcoming Muslim Dyula merchants alongside indigenous Lobi communities until the Mandinka forces of Samori Ture conquered and sacked the kingdom in 1884. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Buna; Common languages: Kulango and Dyula; Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1884; Succeeded by: Wassoulou Empire

name: Bungu
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Bungu, also known as the Wungu Kingdom, was an autonomous Bantu state situated in the Rukwa basin of south-western Tanzania. Governed by hereditary clan monarchs from their capital at Bungu in modern Chunya District, the polity developed intensive sorghum farming, iron smelting and regional livestock husbandry. The kingdom maintained strategic control over trade routes linking Lake Rukwa with the central Tanzanian plateau, defending its territory against neighbouring Sangu and Ngoni invasions until German colonial forces incorporated the area into German East Africa in 1891. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Bungu; Common languages: Bungu and Swahili; Religion: Traditional Bantu religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Mwene; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Bushiru
description: Bushiru was an independent highland kingdom located across the forested volcanic ridges of north-western Rwanda. Ruled by sacred hereditary monarchs known as the Abahinza, who belonged to indigenous Hutu clans, the state maintained complete autonomy from the neighbouring Tutsi-led Nyiginya dynasty of central Rwanda. The kingdom was renowned for its rich agricultural production, sacred forest shrines and independent legal traditions, resisting royal Rwandan expansion for over two centuries until Belgian colonial authorities coordinated military campaigns that annexed Bushiru to the central Rwandan court in 1926. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Bushiru; Common languages: Kinyarwanda; Religion: Traditional Rwandan religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Mwhinza; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1926; Succeeded by: Ruanda-Urundi

name: Busozo
description: Busozo was a small autonomous mountain kingdom situated in the rugged terrain of south-western Rwanda, bordering the Ruzizi valley and Lake Kivu. Governed by hereditary monarchs who maintained close cultural and political ties with neighbouring Bukunzi and eastern Congolese polities, the kingdom operated outside the jurisdiction of the central Rwandan Mwami. The population engaged in terraced farming, cattle keeping and ritual traditions centred on rainmaking, preserving their political sovereignty until Belgian colonial forces launched administrative expeditions that merged Busozo into the unified Rwandan kingdom in 1926. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Busozo; Common languages: Kinyarwanda and Shi; Religion: Traditional Great Lakes religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1926; Succeeded by: Ruanda-Urundi

name: Bussa
description: Bussa was an ancient and autonomous Borgu kingdom situated along the rapids of the middle Niger River in west-central Nigeria. Tracing its founding to the legendary hero Kisra, the state was governed by the Kabbah of Bussa and held recognised spiritual and genealogical primacy over all Borgu states. The kingdom commanded strategic river crossings and agricultural trade, famously resisting Fulani jihadi expansion from the Sokoto Caliphate throughout the nineteenth century until the British Royal Niger Company signed a protective treaty in February 1897. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Bussa; Common languages: Busa (Borgu) and Hausa; Religion: Traditional Borgu religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Kabbah; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1 February 1897; Succeeded by: Royal Niger Company

name: Buzinja
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Buzinja was an autonomous Bantu kingdom situated along the south-western shoreline and islands of Lake Victoria in modern Geita Region, Tanzania. Formed as one of the historic kingdoms of the African Great Lakes, the realm was governed by hereditary monarchs who integrated agricultural Zinza communities with pastoral lineages. The kingdom prospered through lake fishing, banana cultivation and regional iron trade, maintaining its independence against expanding Buganda and Mirambo's Nyamwezi confederacy until German colonial forces occupied the lake basin and incorporated Buzinja into German East Africa in 1891. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Buzinja; Common languages: Zinza and Swahili; Religion: Traditional Great Lakes religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Omukama; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Cokossi
description: Cokossi, also known as the Anufo Kingdom, was an autonomous precolonial state established around Sansanné-Mango in northern Togo. Founded by Akan warrior cavalry migrants originating from the Ivory Coast who settled along the Oti River basin, the kingdom integrated indigenous Moba and Gourma populations through martial superiority. Governed by a paramount king assisted by military captains, the realm dominated regional caravan routes, levying transit tolls on horse and kola trading until German colonial representative Gustav Nachtigal negotiated a protectorate treaty in July 1884. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Mango; Common languages: Anufo (Chokossi); Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional military monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 5 July 1884; Succeeded by: German Togoland

name: Dargol
description: Dargol was an autonomous precolonial kingdom and chieftaincy situated along the Dargol River valley in the Tillabéri region of western Niger. Inhabited primarily by Songhai and Zarma communities alongside semi-nomadic Tuareg pastoralists, the polity was governed by traditional chiefs who supervised agricultural floodplain irrigation and seasonal cattle grazing. The realm maintained local independence amidst shifting conflicts between the neighbouring Songhai successor states and expanding Tuareg confederacies until French colonial military columns occupied the Middle Niger basin and established civil administration in 1900. \n\n Status: Traditional chieftaincy; Capital: Dargol; Common languages: Songhai and Zarma; Religion: Sunni Islam and traditional animism; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Ruler title: Chief; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1900; Succeeded by: French West Africa

name: Diara Kingdom
description: The Diara Kingdom, also known as Jarra, was an autonomous precolonial Mandinka state situated on the southern bank of the lower Gambia River across parts of modern Gambia and Senegal. Governed by a traditional monarch titled the Mansa from the fortified town of Diara, the state flourished through riverine trade, millet cultivation and livestock husbandry. The kingdom maintained its political autonomy despite recurrent regional conflicts during the nineteenth-century Soninke-Marabout wars, retaining its traditional chieftaincy structures until British colonial forces formally established the Gambia Protectorate in 1901. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Diara; Common languages: Mandinka; Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mansa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: British Gambia Colony and Protectorate

name: Dominica
description: Dominica under French colonial rule was an insular Caribbean possession situated in the Windward Islands between Guadeloupe and Martinique. Establishing permanent settlements around Roseau with the tacit consent of indigenous Kalinago inhabitants, French planters developed coffee, cocoa and timber estates operated by enslaved African labourers. Governed by a resident French commandant subordinate to the Governor-General of Martinique, the colony remained contested with Great Britain throughout the eighteenth century, experiencing British occupation during the Seven Years' War before final British acquisition under the 1783 Treaty of Paris. \n\n Status: French colony; Capital: Roseau; Common languages: French and Antillean Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 3 September 1783; Succeeded by: British Dominica

name: Fadhli Sultanate
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Fadhli Sultanate was an autonomous tribal monarchy situated along the Gulf of Aden coastline in southern Yemen. Ruled by the Fadhli clan from their coastal capital at Shuqrah, the sultanate commanded strategic littoral highways and the fertile wadi valleys of Abyan. Renowned as a formidable military power in Southern Arabia, the sultans levied transit tolls on regional trade caravans bound for the port of Aden and maintained independence against neighbouring Sharifian and Zaidi incursions until Great Britain captured Aden in August 1839. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Shuqrah; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Fadhli; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1 August 1839; Succeeded by: Aden Protectorate

name: Fogny
description: Fogny, also known historically as Foni, was an autonomous kingdom established by Mandinka and Jola communities in the fertile Casamance basin south of the Gambia River. Governed from regional settlements such as Bignona, the polity integrated agricultural rice cultivation with forest rubber collection and riverine trade. The realm maintained political self-rule through traditional village councils and warrior leaders, resisting encroachment from neighbouring Fula jihadists until British and French colonial boundary commissions partitioned the region between the Gambia Protectorate and French Senegal in 1901. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Bignona; Common languages: Mandinka and Jola; Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Ruler title: Mansa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: British Gambia Colony and Protectorate

name: Fonfuka
description: Fonfuka was an autonomous precolonial kingdom situated in the rugged Grassfields region of the Boyo Division in north-western Cameroon. Serving as the historic seat of the Bum kingdom along the Kimbi River, the realm was governed by a traditional sacred monarch titled the Fon. The kingdom developed thriving agricultural terracing for food crops and palm oil, controlling lucrative regional trade networks linking the montane highlands to the Benue valley until German colonial forces occupied the Grassfields and imposed administrative control in 1901. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Fonfuka; Common languages: Bum (Grassfields Bantu); Religion: Traditional Grassfields religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Geledi Sultanate
description: The Geledi Sultanate, governed by the aristocratic Gobroon dynasty, was a powerful Somali kingdom established along the lower Shebelle River basin in southern Somalia. Founded by Ibrahim Adeer following the overthrow of the Ajuran Sultanate, the realm established its capital at the fortified trading crossroads of Afgooye. The sultanate maintained a formidable standing army, regulated lucrative agricultural plantations and collected tribute from coastal Swahili cities until signing a protectorate agreement with the Kingdom of Italy in November 1894. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Afgooye; Common languages: Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gobroon; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 3 November 1894; Succeeded by: Italian Somaliland

name: Goure
description: Goure was an autonomous Kanuri and Toubou sultanate located across the semi-arid grasslands of south-eastern Niger in the modern Zinder Region. Governed by a traditional hereditary ruler from the oasis town of Goure, the state prospered as an important caravan station along trans-Saharan trading routes between Lake Chad and the Hausa city-states. The polity maintained thriving livestock markets and defended its wells against desert raiders, preserving domestic autonomy until French colonial military columns occupied the region and incorporated Goure into French West Africa in 1900. \n\n Status: Traditional sultanate; Capital: Goure; Common languages: Kanuri and Daza; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1900; Succeeded by: French West Africa

name: Herero
description: The Herero Kingdom was an autonomous pastoralist realm established across the central plateau and savannahs of modern Namibia by the Ovaherero nation. Governed by supreme paramount chiefs and clan elders seated at the historic capital of Okahandja, the state commanded immense cattle herds that formed the spiritual and economic lifeblood of the community. The Herero waged protracted defensive wars against encroaching Oorlam commandos to preserve their ancestral grazing lands, maintaining independence until Chief Maharero signed a treaty of protection with the German Empire in October 1885. \n\n Status: Traditional pastoral kingdom; Capital: Okahandja; Common languages: Otjiherero; Religion: Traditional Herero religion and Christianity; Government: Traditional paramount chieftaincy; Ruler title: Paramount Chief; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 21 October 1885; Succeeded by: German South West Africa

name: Hiraab Imamate
description: The Hiraab Imamate, ruled by the Yacquub dynasty, was an autonomous Somali theocratic monarchy established along the southern Banadir coast and central hinterlands of Somalia. Founded in the late seventeenth century by Imam Omar after successfully overthrowing the Ajuran Sultanate, the state was governed from the historic maritime city of Mogadishu. The imamate integrated coastal merchant clans with interior nomadic pastoralists, patronising Islamic scholarship and defending port commerce against external powers until Italian colonial authorities established the Italian Somaliland protectorate in February 1889. \n\n Status: Theocratic imamate; Capital: Mogadishu; Common languages: Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam (Sufi); Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yacquub; Ruler title: Imam; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 8 February 1889; Succeeded by: Italian Somaliland

Operating as a tributary vassal under the Burmese Konbaung dynasty, the realm was governed from Hsamonghkam and Aungpan by hereditary Shan rulers titled myosas. The state collected agricultural revenues from highland farming valleys and supplied military levies to the Burmese royal army, maintaining local customary governance until British colonial forces annexed the Shan States following the third Anglo-Burmese war in 1886. \n\n Status: Tributary Shan state; Capital: Hsamonghkam; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Myosa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Jimara
description: Jimara, known historically as Diamaru or Jemarrow, was an autonomous Mandinka kingdom situated along the southern bank of the upper Gambia River in modern The Gambia. Governed by a traditional monarch titled the Mansa from regional royal residences at Jimara, the state derived prosperity from riverine canoe transport, rice cultivation and groundnut agriculture. The kingdom maintained its domestic institutions and defended its territory through decades of regional conflict during the Soninke-Marabout religious wars until British colonial authorities formally established the Gambia Protectorate in 1901. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Jimara; Common languages: Mandinka; Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mansa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: British Gambia Colony and Protectorate

description: Kandi was an autonomous Bariba kingdom situated across the northern savannahs of modern Benin in the historic Borgu region. Founded as an offshoot of the Nikki kingdom and governed by a traditional monarch titled the Saka, the realm centred on the fortified commercial town of Kandi. The kingdom derived economic vitality from trans-Saharan caravan trade routes in cattle, grain and kola nuts, preserving its martial independence against regional invaders until French colonial forces occupied northern Dahomey and annexed Kandi in 1895. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Kandi; Common languages: Bariba (Baatonum) and Dendi; Religion: Traditional Bariba religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Saka; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1895; Succeeded by: French Dahomey

name: Kantora
description: Kantora was an autonomous Mandinka kingdom located at the eastern extremity of modern The Gambia along the upper reaches of the Gambia River. Originating as a historic eastern province of the Kaabu Empire, the realm maintained independent governance from royal settlements including Songkunda and Kantora. The state flourished through riverine trade in ivory, wax and agricultural produce, preserving its traditional political structures and communal assemblies until British colonial expansion incorporated the district into the Upper River Division of the Gambia Protectorate in 1901. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Kantora; Common languages: Mandinka; Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mansa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: British Gambia Colony and Protectorate
